text: I stopped by Bitter Bob's last weekend while in New Hope. I was hoping to find a reprieve from the high end restaurants dominating the street. I had no desire to drop a fifty on a designer lunch. While walking down Main St we came upon Bitter Bob's and decided that it met what we were looking for. Its BYOB but in the 90* weather I wasn't complaining at the bottomless Lemonade. My boyfriend opted for the unsweetened Ice Tea. We were sat outside per our request in the shade. It was a good spot to people watch as we ate. The lunch menu was small which actually is a good sign in my book, because you don't have to offer the world to be great, just be good at what you do. There were numerous sandwiches but we came for one reason and that was BBQ. We ordered two apps. My Boyfriend got the chili and I had the Wedge Salad. His chili was great but not very spicy, it was the clear winner in the app department though. My wedge salad was good but the blue cheese was not very strong. It was very mild and the dressing was Russian not the advertised Ranch, odd considering the standard is Blue Cheese Dressing. We both ordered the BBQ combo with two different sides. I thought it was a good price at the time for $10.95. Then it came to the table. I was a bit underwhelmed. First its suppose to be "authentic" BBQ. I'm sure the meat was slow cooked because it was tender, but it was not smoked, or if it was there was no hint of it in the food. There were no signature smoke rings and no distinct aroma from the place signifying a smoker in the back. The next disappointment came from the portion size. My appetizer salad had just about as much food as my lunch plate. 2-3 bites each of pulled chicken, brisket, and pork, with an end rib portion that was tough and not particularly flavorful. The sides were better but sides do not make a restaurant. There was a BBQ Bean mixture which I give points to for its use of several different beans in addition to the standard navy beans. I uncovered both Lima and Garbanzo beans. The Mac and Cheese was otherwise forgettable seeming as if it should have been on the kids section of the menu. The Cole slaw was good as it was not creamy as much as it was vinegary with a generous amount of cilantro which made it unique. After eating I stepped into the restaurant to see the decor and was a little shocked. It did not look like a BBQ place at all. I know it is the restaurants grand opening but as far as the decor is concerned it looks like it was just serving cafe food last week. I know they were trying to conserve money but there are some things you can't skimp on. A BBQ joint needs to look like a BBQ joint, especially with the amount of biking enthusiasts that come through the town. They don't want to eat at Cafe Lulu, the want to eat at Bitter Bob's. So please make it a little bitter and jaded. Lastly don't be tossing around the "authentic BBQ" card when the food is clearly not smoked. text: I get a lot of push back on liking this restaurant from my friends that want to go get a burger. Always come out cooked to order, no over cooking, hot, fresh, delicious. Atmosphere: So really this place is typically crowded, and with kids. To get around the madness of screaming children you can try to go at off peak times, but really there is no avoiding it. You just have to go in ready for it. The arrangement of the dining room is good for the casual diner, but not an ideal conversation space. It is basically just a field of square four top tables, so if you are two and you want to hear each other, sit next to each other, not across the table. But again, they do make the root beer right there in view. Sometimes. When it is running it is obviously the most fun. Not running you can tell they use it, but it is nothing spectacular about it. Ok, so they aren't running it when you go. Order a root beer, it will change your life. There is really nothing as good in the world as a local root beer or cream soda brew. Stop worrying about the machine. Location: Right on the Loop. It can be overcrowded with WashU hipsters and the usual obnoxious fraternity guys and Ugg wearing girls (no matter what the temperature is outside). But this location also makes it so convenient. The appies were all delicious, too. The homemade ice cream is truly exceptional. I've never tasted anything like it, and definitely worth saving room for. It's a small portion, but you'll be so full from dinner anyways. We also tried the rice pudding which was good, though not the best ever. They were unfortunately out of the carrot pudding, which I wanted to try. They have an extensive wine list, and some signature cocktails, too. We tried two of the signature cocktails. One with raspberries and one with mango and ginger. Both were very tasty and large. I didn't taste any booze in them, despite being 1.5 oz., but that's probably because the whole drink was so big. Tasty for sure, freshly made and refreshing, though I think next time I will try something else. Service was a little bit slow, and it took a long time to get our plates cleared away and food packed up even though the other tables were all being taken care of. That was really my only complaint. For the most part our server was really good. The restaurant is nicely laid out and has a warm, inviting feel to it. However, the bathroom was really cold. text: Came here last night because I didn't want to head to Tai Lake and definitely didn't feel like having Chinese at all. But my party did and so we went. It was better than I expected. It's better if you go for the seafood options and the prices are extremely comfortable for the portions they gave. They first started us off with free chicken soup. Standard at some places but they put some Chinese herbs in it to give a clean and slight bitter taste. If you're Chinese and your parents have made certain soups and swear that it took them forever to make, you'll appreciate this soup otherwise you may dislike it. Whatever the case it was free, you don't have to drink it. Then our appetizer came, we ordered jellyfish. Very very big portion for 7 bux! Anywhere else is half the size easily and you probably can't screw making these things cause I don't believe it requires much cooking. It was good in my opinion. Then the razor clams came our and they were cleaned and cooked placed on top of their shells. Again a good hearty portion. If you enjoy razor clams this place may e one of the very few restaurants that would have it in a regular basis. A lot of others claim that it's seasonal and they don't have it. Then our fried tofu with lobster sauce arrived. I have to say I've had better but notably this place makes it very different. They use real lobster chunks on the sauce and inside the tofu we found that it has shrimp mixed in. They where huge of course but a bit heavy for me. It was possible that I was already overwhelmed. Lastly we had wheat noodles. It's one of my favorite safe dishes. It was what it is - safe. Nothing spectacular about it but the price. Cheaper then everywhere else. To finish off we were given free desert like other Chinese restaurants, a sweet soup. Not your usual red bean watered down stuff like everywhere else - this was yellow bean with sago and it was not watered down. Very good. Granted that I normally don't prefer Chinese food if I had a choice, this place will be my first choice if someone had chosen Chinese for the night.

text: My good friend and humanitarian extraordinare (Dana P with One Brick) has been down to New Orleans countless times...so, when my mother proposed a volunteer trip down here, my first email was to Dana to get the scoop... His first resounding recommendation: St. Bernard Project. Of course, Habitat is much more well-known, but I knew if Dana vouched for it, it was worthwhile...so our group of 4 signed up. Some notes from the website: "You will literally help rebuild a family's home. This may include hanging insulation or sheetrock, mudding/spackling, sanding, texturing, priming, painting, laying floors, and/or hanging trim, doors and baseboard. If you have significant experience any of these areas or in framing, electric, plumbing and/or cabinetry, please inform the Volunteer Department prior to your arrival so that we can assign you to a specialty team." Another note, co-founder Liz McCartney has been named 2008 CNN Hero of the Year. A remarkable achievement... http://blog.nola.com/davewalker/2008/11/st_bernard_project_cofounder_l_1.html Ok, so my experience... Day 1 830am: report to St. Bernard Project HQ for a mini-orientation. Met with co-founder for a bit of background, motivational speech of sorts. It worked. We were ready to build! Notes: All 27,000 homes in St. Bernard Parish were leveled and deemed "uninhabitable" after Hurricane Katrina. The population went from 75,000 before HK, to 25,000 after. Many are still waiting for their homes to be rebuilt. This is nearly 5 years after the storm... 930am: report to site. The Duplessy home in a small subdivision a few miles from Camp Hope. We meet our site supervisor, Morgan, who is with Americorps. She is 18 years old, and knows more than the 4 of us combined. Truly inspiring, and dedicated. Not to mention fun and sweet :) The next 3 days: Drywall, mud, spackel, sand, sand, sand, sand, sand, wash stuff out, sand, sand, sand, sweep, play with the puppy across the street, sand, sand, sand, sand, eat at Rock and Carlo's, sand, sand, sand, mud, spackel, learn how to "speed finish" a floor, work on corners, sand, sand, sand. Yes, we sanded a lot. But damn, that house was SMOOOOOOOTH when we left! They really stress quality over quantity, as they rebuild these homes to last. Absolutely a 5-star experience. Fabulous organization from start to finish. Gracious, genuine, inspired, dedicated. I'm glad I could donate a little of my time...but honestly, there is still so much to do. I was literally amazed at the amount of empty homes. Empty. Abandoned. 5 years later and this is what it still looks like? It's incomprehendable, but absolutely true. 5 years. In one of the most well-developed countries in the world...it just blows my mind. You can't even believe it until you see it. Anyone want to go back? I'm game. Not only to you get to volunteer for such a worthy, cool cause...but you are mere miles from New Orleans, one of the most fun places to visit/hang out in the USA, in my opinion. Fun, leisure, volunteer work...a great mix, and awesome way to see a new place. I' still in awe of the work they've done...and continue to do. Definitely give it a thought if you are looking to volunteer in NOLA, and PM or email me if you've got any questions. I'm planning on going back.

text: I love this place. Not only do they have a huge array of desert plants, including many that are native to SE Arizona, Pima County, and even Tucson specifically, but there were a good range of sizes and prices as well. The gallon-size plants start at 6 or 8 bucks but the prices can go quite a bit higher as the green things get bigger. There's a cactus and succulents section, and the rest of the grasses, shrubs, and trees are laid out in tidy rows with identifying signs. The staff is friendly and helpful, but they're also happy to leave you alone to wander around sniffing, poking, and reading about the plants. Their web site (www.desertsurvivors.org) is very good, too; they have an awesome downloadable guide to all the plants they sell with information about where they're from, what conditions they're suited for, and the kinds of critters they attract, if any. The plants looked like they are doing well; remembering of course that desert plants tend to look rather scraggly and unassuming while they're getting started. I did once go for a creosote bush but left empty-handed, but this was just because they only had the larger $20 plants and I was looking for the cheap little ones. To be fair, though, they had just had one of their big, much-attended plant sales and I think that wiped out some of their inventory. At any rate, a helpful staffer showed me a whole section of wee creosote bushes, just waiting to get big enough for sale, in the "Employees Only" area. My only warning is that, if you choose a plant based on the information on the sign by the plant, be sure that the abbreviation of the plant's latin name (written on the side of each pot) matches the name of the plant on the sign--sometimes plants are not put back in the right place and it's easy enough to grab the wrong one if you're not careful. Adding to my enthusiasm for Desert Survivors is that it not only provides all of these great (mostly native) plants that thrive here without requiring an obscene waste of water, it is also a non-profit that serves both adults and children with disabilities. How cool is that?!

text: So I've been to this place with my family a few times now, and went again last night with another couple and their son. Seating on a Saturday was better than what I expected at 6pm, though by seven every seat in the house was full. The menu is an impressive 50's style mix of hundreds of milkshake/soda/beverage combos. The milkshakes have yet to disappoint. My friend's sun had an Irish cream hazelnut which he declared the best milkshake ever, and my twelve year old had a rice cripsies milkshake that was slightly challenging to drink through a straw but delicious. The cherry cokes are made with real maraschino cherry juice, and trust me, you can taste the difference. Yum! French fries and rings are served in bountiful portions. Fried in peanut oil, they have a rich taste but aren't excessively greasy. We ordered a full basket of fries and a second of wings, and a good 1/2 of the fries and 1/4 of the rings went home in a doggie box. Five sauces are served with the rings (if you desire to pay for them). A standard cheese sauce, a standard rings sauce resembling a mayo with spicy paprika, a vegetable sauce resembling Lipton's vegetable dip, a creamy pepper sauce that wasn't spicy, and a pepper jelly that was lightly spicy. The pepper jelly was my favorite, though I wish it was slightly hotter, and the kids demolished the cheese sauce (no surprise there). I wish these came while you were waiting for the burgers so you had something to nibble on, but instead it all comes at once. Burgers come in five sizes ranging from 3oz to 20oz. Served only medium, medium well or well, you are given the option of selecting your cheese, seven types including blue, toppings, like thirty, and 'special' toppings such as bacon that you pay a buck each for. One of my guests chose the fried tomato and was surprised to find a slice of freshly deep fried red tomato versus green tomato. Points for the fresh deep fry, but being from the south she would have preferred a green tomato. There are salads and other sandwich offerings, I haven't bothered as that's not what we come here for. They look big and tasty. Back to the burgers. Burgers are served with an olive on a toothpick spear holding them together. I enjoy this as no one else I know likes olives, so I get them all. You get about 1/2 way through any of the bigger burgers before you finally have to relent and eat them with fork and knife. Burgers are served in plastic baskets, except kid options witch come in cool car shaped cardboard server boxes. Yes, I ordered the 'pounder' (the 20oz burger) as my son and I usually compete, him with the associated challenge size. He's twelve now though, so falls into adult category for the challenge and wussed out on the pounder. I hadn't had lunch so I could have finished this monster, which I happily note came medium as requested, but decided I didn't really want to 'win' the challenge of eating it so left a good 2oz piece along with the roll and some toppings. Of course, I failed to realize this was a PR thing. The challenge is to eat the burger and make it on the wall of fame. As you can imagine, many of these photos show people resembling Sumo Warriors and Jabba the Hut, and although not a small man by any means, nor someone who is uncomfortable about my weight, I really had no desire to be memorialized in such a fashion. So when the bubbly hostess pops over with the huge stuffed hamburger announcing that we had someone who finished the pounder I quickly pointed out that I specifically had not finished it. After a millisecond delay, the quick witted dominatrix piped up "That's OK!" winked, and launched into her routine. As my guests laughed and my son hid behind the large stuffed burger now on our table, my photo was snapped as the people clapped for me. That's right your salad eating wussies, cheer on the voracious carnivore in the back row. The check was about $75 for five of us and that included eight things of sauce, full fries and rings, and tip, so frankly, not bad at all. As we walked out, the hostess thanked me for being a good sport, and I saw another pounder headed out to some seeker of fame.

text: Natural Health: A great place to buy groceries I recently started shopping at Natural Health in Lindenwold again for the first time in perhaps a decade. This place is more than just a small health food store; you can actually do your food shopping here. It is the size of a convenience store, but has a great selection. I like to buy products that are healthy, free-trade, and organic, and it seems like the only places in South Jersey to do this anymore are Whole Foods (which I do love) and Wegman's, the corporate giant. Whole Foods offers wonderful products (including local and free-trade) and does a great job bringing them to a wider market, but it is refreshing to shop somewhere that feels more personal, where there are actually people around to ask questions, where you don't spend 15 minutes trying to find an item. There are few smaller stores in the area--in fact, I can't think of another--that offer a good variety of healthy foods, body care, organic produce, breads, and bulk items. Natural Health also has an especially impressive selection of food for people with allergies and special diets. Some of the products are priced higher than they might be at Whole Foods, but many are not. Also, the sale items are priced much lower than you would ever find at the bigger stores. Most of the products that made it into my shopping cart were dramatically-reduced sale items. This small business is in a location that will not be getting a Whole Foods any time soon; the folks at Natural Health are bringing organic products to people who might otherwise have no access to them. That's another great reason to shop here. Natural Health has been around a long time; I just wasn't going because I never had a reason until recently to be in that area, so I kind of forgot about the place. But even if you don't have any other reason to be in Lindenwold, this store is enough of one. I am so glad I rediscovered it. Natural Health is down the road from Camden County College and UMDNJ's Stratford location. It is at the corner of Blackwood-Clementon & Laurel Roads in Lindenwold, New Jersey. They are open 7 days a week.

I enjoyed local favorites (shrimp remoluade poboy & crawfish enchiladas) but also got to sample Maine seafood chowder - those Maine folks were LOVING the weather this weekend. I was disappointed in the shrimp uggie (2 shrimp & some mini-bits of potato?); I know Ugelisich's is closed but c'mon charge more & don't be so stingy. text: Excellent restaurant. I highly reccomend any of the seafood. The service is fantastic, and they may have the beat wine selection in Nashville. Other dishes are also great, even if you need to adjust to something off the menu for dietary reasons. This is not my favorite restaurant but it is a wonderful place for good traditional American food and a nice place to visit with someone special. If you are at all interested in a diverse menu and good wine in an extremely intimate setting I would say Midtown is certainly a great choice.

text: Went to the hibachi section of the restaurant for Restaurant Week with my boyfriend. I got some weird salad, lobster and NY strip, and some sort of a banana dessert. The salad was something new to me, since I have only been to a Hibachi once and have only had sushi once or twice. The salad was good once I got over the raw meat it contained (I'm not a fan of raw meat, sorry!) The portions are pretty large. Tokyo gave everyone a LOT of rice. The rice was bland and slightly overcooked, but the large portion made up for that. The steak was delicious and perfectly cooked. My lobster was a bit undercooked, but I'm not a big lobster fan so I didn't mind. Everyone got 2 extra shrimp at our table; I guess the chef had prepared too many. Our chef made sure to entertain us while he was cooking, which definitely adds to the experience. The banana dessert was delicious...it had some sort of a banana outside with an ice cream inside. It was weird but it sounded better than their tiramisu dessert. I would definitely go here again, but probably only during Restaurant Week since I'm a broke college student. One more note-I called Tokyo a few hours before our dinner and they told me where the cheapest parking nearby was and that that garage participated in a Restaurant Week discount. I wrote down the address, but they must have given me the wrong one--no parking lot or garage was there! I would've saved a few dollars parking at that garage!

text: Let me start off by saying that my family members have bought cars here and had good experiences. But none of us will be shopping for a car here again. I was in the market for a car after moving back to STL from DC a few months ago. I settled on a Mazda 3 and so we decided to go to Bommarito. The sales guy we dealt with there, Brian, was just fine. He was friendly and my dad had negotiated the price over the Internet beforehand (my dad used to sell cars) so there was supposed to be no bullshit. SUPPOSED TO BE. Well, I gave them a small check to reserve a car and they were going to order it for me. It was supposed to be in in about a week. Then, a few days later, I get a call from Brian that says my car is in. And it has features on it that I didn't ask for and will get for FREE! But...it has 500 miles on it. It was driven here "from the coast," he says. Well, it turns out, that's not the car I ordered at all. Instead, they did a dealer trade to get me the car faster, but it had to be driven here from Oklahoma or something. Hence the 500 miles. I told them, no, I don't want a car with 500 miles, I want the one I ordered. I'll wait for it. The whole thing put a bad taste in my mouth for them. In the meantime, my dad was trying to find the car at a better price at Lou Fuhz. So Brian's manager, also named Brian, starts putting the squeeze on my dad. He tells him that if we don't buy the car from there, they will "never service my car." He was a real jackass, so in the end, we bought the same car from Lou Fuhz for less money. Ha. Turns out Brian's manager is notorious in the St. Louis car business for being someone that bullies people into sales. Don't fall for it!

text: I don't understand the love. Cheap compared to other local burger places like Port of Call? Sure. But compared to places that make similar-quality burgers like McDonald's and Burger King? Nope. THE GOOD Meh. THE BAD Burgers: We bought a #2 (burger with BBQ sauce) and a #4 (burger with cheese and BBQ sauce). Both were completely underwhelming. The patties were definitely frozen and flavorless, akin to eating the patties at your neighborhood fast food joint. The BBQ sauce was not anything that I couldn't buy at Rouses. These fast food burgers would be fine if I were paying dollar menu prices, but even at $3 it's overpriced. Fries: The burgers may be cheap, but the fries are not, especially for the portion you get. Over $2 for what amounted to a fist-sized portion of fries? And on top of that, they were a tad overcooked and completely unseasoned/unsalted. Building: Definitely not a place to eat-in unless you are completely hammered and don't care about A/C condensation dripping on you from the ceiling. PURGATORY Service: The man behind the counter was nice. About the only positive thing to take away from this experience. OVERALL This place reminds me of the bad late-night food I would eat back in college after a drunken night out. Of course it would taste delicious after pounding beers all night, but try it when you're sober and you realize just how flavorless and underwhelming the food truly is. If I wanted fast food I would go to an actual fast food chain, and I certainly wouldn't be paying $3 for a bad burger which is what you'll be doing at Bud's.

text: We always have a good time at City House, though we never go on any night but Sunday. Sunday is the chef's night to do what he likes, and the restaurant takes the opportunity to regale its patrons with all manner of "pork snacks." As a lover of all things pork and a celebrator of the noble swine, Sunday at City House is my favorite. And since most other notable restaurants in town don't stay open for dinner on Sunday nights, City House has carved itself a niche not only for interesting uses of offal, but as one of the only places where one can get a decent meal on Sunday evenings. So last night, we went in and had a lovely time. For starters, I was especially intrigued by the Mortadella "corndogs," which, in point of fact, were actually more like lollipops than corndogs. Either way, they were spectacular: battered and fried crispy, the mortadella (made with peanuts in lieu of the usual pistachios) was tasty and stood in for the hot dog easily, and the housemade mustard was heavenly. Each bite was a blend of crunchy, fatty, tangy deliciousness. The low point of the meal (though not that low) was the pork belly, which was served with garlicky broccoli rabe. The belly was roasted, but was very fatty, rendering it more of a textural accompaniment to the rabe than anything else. Tasty, but a little off the mark. I would have preferred it less gelatinous, but if it's what the chef intended, it's what he intended. For mains, Husband went with the Kitchen Pie. He always goes with the Kitchen Pie. Surprisingly simple, it's basically a cheese pizza, but done up with chili oil in addition to the sauce and Grana Padano cheese, a cousin of Parmigiano Reggiano. It's very flavorful and the chili gives it an unexpected bite. I went with one of the nightly specials, the pork meatballs, served with a rich, yet thin, tomato ragu, and a large piece of cheese and garlic toasted bread in lieu of pasta. The meatballs were gigantic and cooked perfectly, herbs throughout. As I've stated in my reviews before, I can't eat much wheat in my diet, but I did try some of the bread as it was so tempting: crunchy and wonderful, and when sopping up the ragu, perfect. For dessert, I always get the "Lemon Thing." It never seems to fail, everytime we go in, there's a lemon-related dessert on the menu. I don't know who their pastry chef is, but he or she is a genius with lemon. Last night was a lemon and almond pound cake with a side of lemon sorbet. Sweet and crunchy, the cake was delicious: I almost forgot to share a bite with husband. Husband's dessert was a chocolate torta with peanut butter sauce. It was good, but not as good as the "Lemon-Thing." All in all, the meal was great.

text: I was glad to learn that the restaurant at the Morris House was reincarnated yet again with a new chef who promises to use lots of local and sustainable products. I love the intimate bar area at the entrance of the restaurant and the restaurant itself is small and beautiful , with well-spaced tables and very comfortable chairs. The menu is small but diverse, prices are on the higher end. The smoked butternut soup was rich and earthy, the tartar of sahimi of hamachi fresh if a little too cold to relinquish all its flavor. The braised and glazed short ribs were our best entree, intensely flavorful and very satisfying. The chicken was of good quality and roasted nicely but the skin was flabby instead of crisp, always a drawback with chicken. The biggest issue we had was the temperature of the plates - none of the food was really hot and some items were less than tepid when arriving at the table. Heating the plates would really improve the dishes a great deal. Another improvement would be a simplified approach to accompanying side dishes, presently too many and not well-enough integrated into a unified taste experience. What sounds adventurous and special in the description (on paper and by the waitress) tuns out to be more underwhelming on the plate - a bit like the Stone Henge set-up in Spinal Tap. The cheese plate is excellent, with a fine selection of interesting cheeses, both from Europe and the US, served at ideal stages of ripeness and with fine chutneys and other embellishments. The service is attentive and nice, qualities easily outweighing a lack of experience. The restaurant presently deserves 3.5 stars but because of support of local farmers, I go with the four instead of three available category.
label: POS

text: The Mikado is one of Edmonton's premier chains of Japanese restaurants. I ventured into the new west end location this afternoon for a snack. The place is much larger on the inside than the small storefront implies. Very white, clean, well-lit. I loved how the servers were dressed in traditional robes. I found the menu to have an excellent selection of sushi, as well as beef and chicken dishes. I went for an order of vegetable tempura, which was delicately arranged in an upwards motion. Two large pieces each of carrots, squash, yam, broccoli, and zucchini, served with a soy dipping sauce - it tasted as good as it looked. My guest had one of the lynch specials, called chicken nanban. Several thinly sliced pieces of chicken breast were tempura breaded and served in a soy sauce and topped with house-made tartar sauce. It almost reminded me of fish and chips - except it was chicken! However, the soy sauce brought me back to reality and added a very delicious flavour kick. We were both eyeing several of the other dishes such as teriyaki beef and chicken, udon noodles, and yakitori skewers. Numerous vegetarian selections are clearly labeled on the menu. Although Mikado is a bit pricier than other Japanese restaurants I have visited, the service and quality accounts for this.
label: POS

The other items are good, but unlike the rest of New Orleans dining were strangely under seasoned. It was actually the first time/place in 8 trips to the Big Easy that I had to reach for the salt shaker. The Pecan pie is awesome as is the bread pudding. text: Unforunately, I can't give a place 0 stars, but I can sum up my experience here in one word: BLECH! We ate here some months back and the experience was so bad that it still haunts me. Here's what I think of when I think of Mediterranean food: fresh, wholesome, light, healthy, sunny-flavored food. Athenian Gardens is none of these things. It's bland, heavy, and ham-handed, and I am being kind when I say that. I understand that restaurants need to cut costs, but it was painfully obvious how much cost-cutting they'd done here (at least I hope that's why the food sucked so badly, at least that's a respectable excuse). The grape leaves were soggy and oily, and I am not sure how they managed to remove the tang from a pickled leaf - it's some sort of diabolical miracle. The tabouleh was nothing but unseasoned, overcooked bulgur with just a few miserable and mealy flavorless tomato chunks and a sprinkling of DRY parsley and a generous drenching of cheap olive oil. The hummus was laughable and lemon-free. The falafels were limp, without even a hint of crunch, and tasted like wet little sawdust pucks. My boyfriend had a chicken pita wrap - the chicken was rubbery and obviously microwaved and arrived swimming in some sour cream nightmare that I believe was supposed to be tzatziki sauce. Either these people are completely clueless or the kitchen is performing a completely genius work of dry, black-as-night comedy at the patrons' expense. To add insult to injury, our server was sullen and absentee...well not absentee, just absent from the tables. She was so busy standing with her back to us and the other two tables staring out the window that after waiting 15 minutes for her to come by, we just decided to walk up to her to tell her we wanted to send our food back. She then tried to argue and tell us the food was good. I told her it was obvious that our meal had at least partially been microwaved and she then stopped arguing and told us there would be no charge. That was the high point of this experience. Hopefully their other locations are nothing like this, but after this meal I don't dare find out...I'll try every other Mediterranean spot in the bay area first. We arrived here STARVING and were hoping to catch a quick bite, but the food was so awful that we each tasted a single bite of everything and decided we'd rather pick some stuff up at Publix and make our own lunch. Thankfully the poor quality of the food ruined my appetite for a while, so at least I didn't leave Athenian Gardens hungry!
label: NEG

text: Yep, this has become a household favourite! Don't expect 'normal' american chinese food - if you like fried chicken in neon orange sauce, this is not your place. How many places can you say that about? They give you huge amounts of noodles in the dishes, with enough sauce to cover them. Fantastic. Try the Dan Dan Mian; it will blow your mind. Also, for people who have kids, they are super nice to babies, and are genuinely interested to find out about your life and family. It's just such a great place. Last time we were there, there were some seriously american old people, who appeared to taking their even-older parents out to dinner. It was quite excruciating to listen to them talking to the waitstaff (they wanted things that weren't on the menu, and kept asking what was in other peoples' food on their plates), but the waitress was patient, kind, and eventually cut them off and said "okay, great!" and went into the kitchen. She brought back roughly what they had asked for, and they happily told each other what was on the different plates and seemed to enjoy it. That's an amazing restaurant in my books.

text: There is one simple problem with this review system. "Methinks not" is not strong enough to deal with a company as odious as JMH Realty Concepts. I rented from JMH for three years, because I loved the apartment, but every dealing with the company (every time I had to deal with them no matter how minor an issue) left me feeling like I would be better to throw my money into the storm drain than to give it to these people whose utter lack of respect and competence makes me wonder what is wrong with the world that they were able to obtain a business license. Are these licenses given out by some sort of satanic power? Let me stress that the apartment I rented was wonderful because of the space, not because of its condition, which was well below average. The work on the apartment looked as if it had been completed by a cadre of buffoons or a remedial technical school class in jury rigging. As mentioned in virtually all of the reviews, their support staff are rude and make you want to scream at them each time you call. In many reviews people tend to say that Alan and the other managers are fairly respectful, but I did not find that to be the case. Certainly he could be, but not if there is anything wrong with the apartment, in that case his reaction is to take a defensive, accusatory tone with you until you prove that you didn't do anything wrong and that the apartment broke of its own accord. I have rented from a number of companies over the last decade and I believe myself to be a fairly good tenant. My only fault with JMH was that I was two days late with rent, one month during my third year of renting from them. When I realized the mistake (a result of a misplaced letter) I delivered the rent to the office and contacted them by email to apologize for the mistake and explain. They charged me $100, which (granted) was in the contract, but is still a cold way to treat a three year tenant. Be assured if you decide to rent from JMH, they do not respect you, they will not work with you and they will try to charge you for anything you can. If you absolutely cannot find another rental agency, make sure you protect yourself, because if they can help it there will be no security deposit. JMH is one of those rare companies that makes you fantasize about having the money and power to purchase their company and fire all of the employees and you would sleep well that night, knowing that you've made the world a better place.
label: NEG

text: This review is for the Sunday Gospel Brunch only. By the time you tack on all the fees on top of the $40 ticket, you're looking at a $50 event for an hour of foot-stomping gospel music and a breakfast brunch array that included fried chicken, raw oysters, waffles, bacon, fresh fruit, mimosas, etc. First off, we were here on Mar 28th, and due to a new ticket outlet glitch, reserved seating was a mess. It took the staff a good while to figure out how to match the new ticketing seating with their own arrangements, but the staff were very apologetic and tried their best to get the 3 of us seated together. (Although seats are reserved, come early anyway so you don't have to kill 15 minutes in line waiting for your turn at the buffet.) The food was good, but not outstanding, and there was plenty of food to go around. Filling enough. The gospel choir we happened to see sang for about an hour and they were lovely, singing some of their own stuff as well as classics like "Amazing Grace" and "A Closer Walk With Thee." They happened to pluck 2 young teenagers out of the audience to get up on stage with them, and when the kids mentioned they were part of a church choir that was in the audience, the performers invited them to sing an impromptou song. I had chills up and down my spine when the 20 or so teens began to sing a beautiful hymn, while the gospel choir on stage nodded their approval. Eveyone in the audience had tears in their eyes. A magical moment for everyone who didn't expect this.

text: I didn't think the supreme location at 18th and Chestnut would be empty for long - Sweet Ending snagged it and opened the store-du-jour: a frozen yogurt joint. The space was kind of a free-for all lacking proper organization or flow - with a tub o' styrofoam cups on one side, toppings on the other and the back framed with the yogurt dispensing machines. For right now they've got slips of paper with permanent marker hastily announcing flavors and types of toppings. It was a mad dash of people tasting the flavors and trying to create their own concoction. After I threw a few elbows, I got mine. A mix of tart (that balanced the crazy sweetness of the other two), mango and strawberry. I skipped the toppings because they just looked depressing. (gummi bears? no thanks). Frozen yogurt was fine, it didn't knock my socks off, but I've yet to find a frozen creamy product (I'm avoiding the obvious joke here) that is not ice cream, that can. Like the rest of these places (and those shady salad bars), you pay by weight (49 cents per oz) - two small cups for a friend and I, cost $5 and change.

text: This was one of the most disappointing dining experiences I think I've ever had. Both my sisters and my parents have apparently had great experiences here, but when we went this past week, it was anything but. After having been seated for the better part of 5 minutes, our server came by to tell us she would be right with us. Another couple minutes passed, and then a different server arrived to take our drink order and explained that our real server was too busy at the moment. Granted, our server was also taking care of a party of about 18 people, so I understand that that part wasn't her fault - but management should have known better than to give her more tables. In general, the service we did end up getting (mostly from other waitstaff helping our server out) was pretty slow and seemed entirely apathetic - our table wasn't even given silverware. Also, nobody ever bothered clearing any of the empty plates and glasses off of our table. They just dropped everything off and left us to figure out how to work around the mess. By the end of the meal, we had 11 glasses on our 4-person table (NO exaggeration). Our food took far too long to come out, and when it did arrive, it was pretty clear that it had been sitting under the heat lamp for quite some time. They also dropped off only half of the entrees without any explanation of where the others were, and then the other half took at least another five minutes to come out. I had the French onion soup, which was decent but nothing special. My entree was the shrimp and oyster eggplant napoleon and was outrageously disappointing. It looked nothing like the picture on the menu, and it only came with ONE shrimp and ONE oyster buried in this goopy brown sauce. The eggplant itself was probably 80% breading and really greasy. My friend got the crawfish ravioli which actually just ended up being toasted CHEESE ravioli with about five little crawfish on top and only a couple tablespoons of sauce. My sisters, who had both been there before, got the filet and the meatloaf, which actually ended up being pretty good. If I EVER went back here though (unlikely as that is), it would only be for the desserts. The bread pudding, chocolate cake, and cheesecake were pretty fantastic. text: We decided to try this place out last night. I was very pleased with the service, all of the servers were very polite and the owner actually walked around and spoke to the customers after their meals. We decided on the combo dinner for two, it runs about $35. We also ordered two kingfisher beers at 7 bucks a piece, I recommend their Indian wine. I can't remember the name of it but it was smooth, not too sweet and not too dry. A little pricey at $8 a glass, but it complimented the meal wonderfully. The combo came with a starter of pumpkin (?) soup, very flavorful. The main meal included chicken tikka, tandoori chicken, and a ground lamb type of kabob meat. The chicken was great, the lamb was interesting. The taste of the lamb took some getting used to, it was prepared a bit like meatloaf with fresh cilantro and mint leaves. The tandoori chicken was delish of course. We ordered medium spicy, for the curries and that was pretty hot so beware of ordering too spicy here I was breaking a sweat, and I am definitely a Thai food regular. They veggie curry was great, they used fresh and crunchy ingredients which was greatly appreciated! I like my curry to have some texture. It was a bit cheesy, and a little hard to stomach but if you can handle the cream go for it. We also had some type of lamb curry, the cuts of lamb were spot-on. The meat was very tender and there were no scraps (i.e. fat/gristle). The naan was also delish, a bit crispy but still very buttery and tasty. We also ordered the raita (yogurt with cucumber) very good, but I usually like it a bit runny and theirs was very thick. For desert we ordered kheer, the sweet basmati rice pudding. I really liked the presentation with a little cinamon sprinkled on top along with some sliced almonds and a few raisins. Gorgeous. In all we were very happy with this place, next time we will be trying the lunch buffet, at $8.95 per person it should be a great deal considering the quality of food that is served here!

text: I'll admit that I really like going to the Bishop's Collar, which is my favorite bar within walking distance of my second home (the Fairmount neighborhood). While there can sometimes be a wait for a table and while it can get REALLY PACKED on the weekend nights, they do move through pretty quickly and it's not a huge deal to hang out at the bar until something opens up. The double gin and tonics are strong, and always made consistently: you know exactly how many to drink to straddle the line between pleasantly drunk and unpleasantly plastered. This summer they've also had the Arnold Palmer, which has become my favorite summer beverage and discovery: sweet tea infused vodka (oh. my. god.) and lemonade. They are fabulous, especially if you can manage to snag an outdoor table, enjoying the summer air and sipping on one of these. And although I'm not really a beer person, they have enough available that I can find something I like if I have to, and my more beer snobby friends never have problems either. However, secretly, I like the Bishop's Collar because they have perfect, cheap, unhealthy, fantastic, filling bar food. The plate of nachos is intimidating when sober, but after a night of drinking, sharing it with a friend hits the spot. Their wings are not gristly in the least, and the hot sauce, while not quite the same as a buffalo wing, is tangy and tasty. My favorite thing MAY be the chicken chipotle sandwich, with Old Bay fries, which is an absolute steal for $6, but it's hard to choose. Usually we just end up splitting nachos and wings, because it's hard to mess with a classic combination like that. But back to the Bishop's Collar: hits-the-spot food, great drinks, and a nice, low key evening to hang out with friends in the neighborhood.

text: As a connoisseur of cupcakes, I can say with confidence that this place is better than *all* the cupcake stores in NYC (and I keep up-to-date with my surveys of same). I recognize many of the cupcake batters and icings used in this store, and that is a very good thing, in the following sense. I recognize the recipes--many of them were passed down to my brothers and me by our forebears on both sides of the family (one set from the south, one from the northeast). The southern recipes in particular are genuinely represented here. Most of the cupcakes are absolutely delicious. After talking to some of the staff, I learned one reason for this: the cupcakes are made fresh each day. The business is so well-organized and so thoroughly patronized that they actually make only enough of any given kind of cupcake to sell on a given day; when that kind is gone, that's it until the next day or so. This means you *never* eat a stale cupcake from this place. The strawberry cupcakes are almost too good. The sour-cream-batter ones are also very fine. I'm not as fond of the chocolate icings or batters, but honestly even these are clearly authentically conceived and prepared, and are simply quite good. Only the red velvet (again very good) is less strong than those I make with my ancestors' recipes (but I have a gift too!). I haven't experienced the cake-ordering side of the business, because I haven't been in Philly enough to use it, but I'm betting it's professionally and artistically handled. In terms of service, once or twice there were specific counter staff who were snooty (one woman in particular) but this seemed to stop, and honestly none of these quibbles were enough to make a chip in my five stars.

text: Note: For those road cyclists who regularly ride the flats in Columbia, IL, this restaurant is located in that strip mall that you park your car in. It's to the right of CVS Pharmacy. I was a bit hesitant to drive all the way to Columbia, IL for Chinese, but I refused to go to my old stand-by Chinese restaurant (Old St. Louis Chop Suey - Chippewa/Kingshighway) due to stale ingredients. If you're curious, I plan to share my thoughts on my Yelp review of that restaurant. But I digress... Anyway, so I was desperate for GOOD, FRESH Chinese food. I was quite impressed with Mr. Chiu's. Here is what I ordered: Crab Rangoon: Dough was fresh! Filling was good, but could have used more. I wish they offered more than six in an order. Egg Rolls: Perfect size, fresh ingredients inside. The cabbage was fresher than any others I have tasted before. Pepper Steak: The green bell peppers were fresh and nicely sized. Sometimes restaurants are in a hurry and leave the pieces too large for human consumption. Onions could have been chopped smaller though. Pork Fried Rice: Holy Cow! This is the BEST fried rice I have ever had. The rice, bean sprouts, pork all seemed tops. Bonus Points: I was surprised to see a small rice container of sweet n' sour sauce provided, as well as hot mustard. I also was given many packets of sweet n' sour sauce upon my request, as well as hot red pepper. AND the packets were clean packets; I hate when it looks like the restaurant has recycled the packets from a previous patron that left them at the table.
label: POS

text: I ate here several months ago (my life, pre-Yelp), and I normally wouldn't review something not totally fresh in my memory, but I have to add my 2 cents in because I feel like after reading others' reviews I must have been to a Pod in an alternate universe. The food. I barely remember it. And thats a real bad thing for a place like Pod. I can remember dishes from restaurants I've eaten at well over a year or more ago. But Pod's food to me was almost completely unmemorable. What I do remember is simply not being happy with my food in general. If I'm paying a higher than average price for my food, you better believe I want an at least somewhat positive semi-memorable meal! What I do very clearly remember was the HORRENDOUS, TERRIBLE, SLOW, and UNFRIENDLY service. Yeah the food was pricier than average, but as far as trendy and/or Starr restaurants go in Philadelphia, you could easily spend much more money at many other restaurants, and on top of that, your money would be much better spent! The decor was funky, I'll give it that. Very cool. I remember while being here constantly having the overwhelming feeling of just wanting to jump out of my seat and run as far away as possible. I did not enjoy my experience very much at all. I could not get out of there fast enough. I was going to give it 3 stars because the food isn't 100% fresh in my memory, but I just can't let myself do that. Overall, I didn't think it was 3 stars good in any way! It would take alot of cajoling to get me to ever return!

text: Kitties everywhere!!! Watch your step! Cuz' seriously, there are cats hanging out all over the store. On the floor, tables, tops of food bags, hanging bins, the register.....24/7 kitty mania! And you know what? It's so adorable I can't stand it. I had to pet every sweet feline in this beautifully elaborate animal shelter. I discovered this place while tagging along on an errand run with a fellow Nashville friend who was visiting from Japan. She wanted to find some specific kind of cat nip and wound up buying enough to keep her Japanese kitten fully occupied for the next 3 years! This place THE end all pet store. Whether you have special cat needs or you just want to spoil your sweet, furry children, you will definitely find it here. The business also runs a dog concentrated pet store next door, and of course, all of the animals are for adoption. They work hand in hand with Petfinders and advertise locally for adoptions. The owner clearly had a vision, and I wish animal shelters were more like this establishment. Be prepared for cute kitty overload!

text: The Natural Cafe!!! No wonder you have such great reviews! I was second guessing my choice when I arrived at the Natural Cafe when I was reading the menu. It seemed a little more naturally adventurous than I originally thought. LOL! Is naturally adventurous even a proper phrase? By that I mean it seemed to be overloaded with vegetables, some I've never had in my sandwiches, and the soups were quite interesting. Lima bean Vegetable soup? Corn bisque? Veggie chili? Lemon herb dressing? I'm not a lemony person I guess you can say. I'm DEFINITELY happy that we decided to stay and eat!!!! Everything was SO good. I'm surprised my body didn't reject all the natural, healthy goodness and instead accepted it quite willingly. We had a half sandwich/salad and a half sandwich/soup which we shared. I'm not a fan of tuna sandwiches generally and it was SO good here! Not over saturated with mayo. There were sprouts and many other veggies in my sandwich. The bread was grainy yet delicious. The lemon herb dressing was FABULOUS too!! Let me tell you about their 500 veggie chili. Okay there aren't 500 veggies but there's a lot in there! Lots of veggies and beans that aren't in "normal" chili and it was SOOOOO yummy especially with their blue corn tortilla chips. The turkey sandwich was good but definitely get the tuna instead! Great meal + water + sparkling apple juice and that's a GREAT LUNCH. If you're ever in SB, definitely check out this place! Also, if Natural Cafe heads down to OC or LA will someone please keep me informed? LOL :)

For a place that's suppose to serve bar food, they're not very good at it. Mac, I think you need to take a look at your joint a little closer. Maybe a flipadelphia will push this to 3 stars. text: There is never a type of store that exemplifies the debate between large stores and small stores like hardware stores. On top of that, the dusty antiquated good you need is super expensive as the four dudes working there need to pay their mortgage. And frankly, the service can be down right creepy and invasive. This place, is neither. I needed a metric screw, nut, and two washer. Not only did they have it but pointed me in the direction. text: I prefer Elicias to Imo's nowadays. WHY? Imo's has become "too known as St Louis Pizza". What I mean by that is, they have stopped to impress upon the food, and now its about the name, Imo's. Their cheese is a mix of mozz/prov, but that is better for me, its not as runny and browns atop nicely. Elicias has other food too, sandwiches which are just ok, and the standard appetizer fare. The other thing they do well here is Wings. I am somewhat a Chicken Wang expert, and can say Elicias is in my Top 5 wing spots in St Louis. (list coming soon, add me :) The tub of wings, which must be 4-5 lbs of wings, is only $18 and the mild sauce is awesome.. Order them "Crispy" for a bit extra crunch. Overall; 4/5 on food (its as good as delivery gets for me) 4/5 on service, fast & friendly. 3/5 on Phone service, sometimes they are rude. text: I went for brunch/lunch within the first week of opening and am pleasantly surprised. Between new staff, new menus, and new everythings with new restaurants, it's difficult to get a clear reading, but Garces has it down at his Trading Co. Staff: Pleasant, knowledgeable, attentive. Many looked a bit nervous, I didn't see too many smiles, but I think it was their anxiety to perform well that showed, rather than a disinterest in being there. Food: I ordered the Minestrone soup to share and the ingredients were super fresh. Portion was good to share & to have as a side for my sandwich. As my main dish I had the Tartine aux Fromage, which was listed under the "sandwich" section of the menu. It was an open face sandwich, not good for the extreme hungry, but very tastey. The brioche was crisp, tomatoes fresh, and vinegar very refreshing. My boyfriend ordered the Moroccan sandwich and liked it (not loved it). Overall the sandwiches are good, but not mind blowing, and not the typical over-sized portion - so if you are hungry, get an app as well. Dessert: I tried the coconut tart which was f-ing great. If you like bits of coconut, and a nice crusty pastry, definitely try this. What others had: I took a look around the restaurant and noticed a delicious pizza that was ordered. The pizza is sizeable, and can feed at least two, if not three to share. Next time I must have this! Why 4 stars: Well, I love brunch. And there is no brunch menu (at the moment they only serve lunch and dinner). Please Mr. Garces, provide me with a breakfast sandwich and I will gladly update my review to 5 stars.

Everyone raves about their mac and cheese, which I haven't tried because I incorporate enough cheese in basically every meal as it is, but the food that I tasted was bland. The meatballs were kind of bland so I didn't particularly enjoy it much, mostly because the cheesy garlic bread was the best part and I could've made that home for free. My ex had the tuna sandwich (I think?) and he also wasn't a fan. I really wanted to like this place when it first opened up, but I just can't. text: This was by far the most perfect meal of my life. My father treated me to dinner here after my college graduation. Of course, I went all out for the grande degustation menu with wine pairings for each course since it was the only event in my life that justified the price tag. If not now, when? I've outlined all the courses I was served below. I don't know shit about wine, I just drink it, so I don't remember what they all were can't really comment on them. If you're curious though, about a half-glass was served with each course, so I was QUITE tipsy by the end of it. The courses were as follows: Amuse Bouche: Tuna Tartare w/ Daikon -Light and a perfect way to start the meal. I love any kind of tartare, and this was no exception. Bread & Butter: Rolls w/ Milk & Chives, Onion French Bread, something else -I only tried the onion but it was very good. The waiters kept bring the tray of bread around and I think my brother had about 10 pieces. Raw Oyster w/ Caviar & Hibiscus Foam -Absolutely perfect. It had been a while since I'd had an oyster and this one did not disappoint. The hibiscus foam was especially interesting - more fruity than I expected. Salmon Tartare w/ Vinegrette & Essence of Lavender -Another tartare! Perfect. The presentation on this was very interesting. The bowl sat on a plate filled with dry ice, then the server poured liquid (the lavender essence, i believe) on it at the table. I actually don't really like the smell of lavender, or anything very floral for that matter, but it didn't detract from the dish. Foie Gras w/ Risotto Chip, Black Sesame, Berry Sauce & Cherries w/ Ice Cream -Possibly the most creative of the dishes. On one side of the plate was the foie gras and risotto chip, and the other side had a scoop of ice cream (possibly kirsch flavored?) with macerated cherries. The sweet components and salty/rich foie gras were the perfect foils for one another. Some Firm White Fish w/ Consomme and Zucchini Blossom -I can't remember what the fish was, but it was cooked perfectly and delicious. Served in a shallow bowl of consomme with a tempura-fried zucchini blossom on top - nice and light. Lamb Tenderloin w/ Crispy Potato -Lamb is one of my favorite meats, so this was an obvious winner for me. The crispy potatoes were like a classy version of that old vending machine standard, Potato Stix - but obviously way more awesome. Taglatelle with Porcini & Truffles -The simplest course, with just a few beautiful ingredients. Pasta, butter, porcini mushrooms, salt, pepper, some generous shavings of truffles... that's it. Melon Sorbet w/ Powder (palate cleanser) -My least favorite course, but I'm biased because I hate all kinds of melons. I tried a bite and then let my dad eat it. Cheese Tray -This was awesome. A server came out with a gorgeous glassed-in cart containing about 10 different cheeses. You're allowed to choose as many as you want, but they recommend about 5 for a nice-sized tray. I told the server I liked soft, strong cheeses, and he made up a beautiful assortment with some grapes and 2 kinds of bread. Dessert: Yogurt Sorbet, Lemon Macaron, & Tomato Confit -The first of quite a few desserts. Served in a parfait glass with a dollop of tomato confit at the bottom, the lemon macaron balanced in the center, and yogurt-flavored sorbet on top. Dessert: Truffles -I was served a platter of 5 truffles: mixed nut, tarragon, saffron, curry, and red beet. The unexpected flavors were all quite good, but the saffron and curry were my favorites. I was also given a cute box of 2 chocolates to take home. Dessert Cart -Yes, the famous dessert cart! It was every bit as wonderful as I had hoped. I asked for a small slice each of the Grand Marnier Souffle, the Flourless Chocolate Cake, and the restaurant's Signature Chocolate cake, which consisted of rum-soaked genoise with rich chocolate buttercream. Unfortunately, by this point I was pretty full, and all the desserts were so rich I could only have a few bites. Finally, we were served a variety of petit fours with the check. This is really extravagance, but for a special occasion it can't be beat. The service is impeccable and treat you like royalty even if it's painfully obvious that you don't belong (like my frugal and tactless grandmother who loudly exclaimed "It looks like a roach!" when the amuse bouche was served). My only complaint is that I will probably never be able to afford a meal like this again.

text: If someone were to ask me why Thai food in St. Louis was less-than-stellar, I would probably list the admiration of the King and I as exhibit A. The stir-fry dish I had here was oily to a fault, and the appetizers (crab rangoon, spring rolls) were mediocre. Forgettable food, service that wasn't endearing, and slightly overpriced. Now I'll list the more fundamental problems I have here that cause me to rate this 2.5 a 2 instead of a 3: -It's named after a Rogers and Hammerstein musical about an English governess who in real life fabricated large parts of her story. They're in Thailand for goodness sakes and there's singing and dancing. And they got a Russian-born actor to play the King. It couldn't be more fake if Jayson Blair wrote an article about Pam Anderson's upper half. As such, it is, to me, a lousy name that suggests the food is fake and caters to Westerners, which probably would be accurate, but I digress. -On the menu, you will find Thai Ravioli, Bangkok casserole, Thai Fajita, and something called Forrest Gump. I'm not making this up. But the owners did, because it's sure as heck not Thai. Maybe the casserole is, I honestly don't know, but if they're going for delicious fusion food, I think they could do better than throwing some meat and curry sauce in a cheap tortilla to attract people who really wanted Mexican but got drug to this place. -Despite boasting of Thai Fajitas on their recommended section (!), they have the audacity to boast of authenticity on numerous parts of their website. Call me what you will, but I'm sorry, if you offer Thai Fajitas and Thai Ravioli, I can't take you seriously. You're a half-step from offering curry burgers, sweet potato fries, and Thai custard milkshakes. Maybe I'm just a stickler, but I don't think you can't have your curry and eat it, too. If you're authentic, be authentic and get the Empress Chicken and the Forrest Gump off the menu. If you want to appeal middle-of-the-road Yankees and pseudo-cultured 20-year-olds who think Pad Thai is hardcore Bangkok cuisine and appreciate things like Thai Fajitas to introduce others to the Thai flavor palate, fine. Frankly, I'd rather have you refine that flavor palate and cut the oil out, but to each his own. I just don't think you can claim to be a true Thai restaurant with such blatant Americanization.

text: Ok, so everybody knows that really good Asian restaurants are hard to come by. Mostly diners are relegated to the Chinese restaurant clones that pepper strip-malls all over the country where the food is plentiful but often mediocre and the commonality of the menu from one restaurant to another brings to mind Chinese conspiracy theories. After reading the overwhelmingly positive reviews here on Yelp and also some feedback from coworkers about how good Veekoo is my brother and I decided to try dinner here last night. So here's my take on this place. The decor in here is what I consider stereotypical eat in Asian restaurant; Panda print cloth on the booth benches, the prerequisite shiny black chairs, faux flowers, etc. It's hardly offensive, it's just not a very original looking layout. We ordered 2 appetizers to share, Szechuan Dumplings in Hot Sauce and Crabmeat and Chinese Wonton. The dumplings were ok but certainly nothing to rave about. The dish was very light on the Szechuan sauce and it wasn't very hot and spicy at all. The wontons were even less impressive and were served with duck sauce and shredded lettuce that was starting to wilt and slightly browning on the sides. I've had much better fried crabmeat wontons from smaller takeout places. For entrees my brother and I got General Tso's Chilean Seabass - seabass fillet sautéed with General Tso's Sauce and Mandarin Fancy - cubed fillet mignon, scallops with fresh shiitake mushrooms and peppers in Kung Pao sauce, respectively. My brother liked his Chilean seabass, though it did have a very fishy taste to it. When seabass is cooked properly this should not be the case, it should have a mild flavor. I was very unimpressed by my dish. The taste was just so-so and there were only 3 medium sized sea scallops in the dish and the cubed filet mignon pieces were VERY small (about the size of a thimble) and there were very few of them, like 5 or 6 pieces. There were also no shiitake mushrooms to be found in my dish which was disappointing. At $18 for the entree I definitely felt shortchanged for such a tiny serving of meat and the missing mushrooms. The service we received from our waiter was very good. He was friendly and quick. In my opinion this place is seriously overpriced for the quality and quantity of food that you get. I don't know, maybe all the hype I heard from others about Veekoo set the expectation bar a bit too high for me but I just wasn't impressed with the food. I've heard that they excel at sushi but I can't comment on something I didn't try. This place isn't horrible but I'm giving it 2 stars because I think any more would be a tad too generous. As I look over the reviews for this place again and I see all the 4 and 5 stars one thing keeps going through my mind.... people, if you think this place is good then try Han Dynasty around the corner. You'll have an Asian food-gasm, you'll get more food and it'll cost you a lot less!

text: For the two of you that don't know yet, Blue Ocean Sushi is the new sushi joint that opened alongside 609; its claim to fame being all you can eat sushi. All you can eat sushi. Basically, there are three "levels" at three different price points (prices go up $5 each, for dinner). You can eat all the sushi you want for as little as $15, and as much as $30 (dinner rate). Well, is the sushi good, Brandon? No, it's not, Yelp. The nigiri was terrible. It was warm, and some of it didn't look very fresh. The rolls were okay, but I was annoyed with how many "unique" rolls they had. I like my sushi old school and simple. No I don't want a "cheeseburger roll," damn it. The reasons I'm giving this two stars is because a.) the service was excellent, b.) I appreciate their attempt to bring something different to the sushi scene in St. Louis (if you want to call it that), and c.) if you can find something you actually enjoy, you could easily crush some sushi at this place. I don't know about the rest of you, but my group easily spends $50-75 a person when we go out for sushi, so if you can find something you like here for $15, well, jackpot for you.

text: I enjoyed my first experience with Froyo. I tried the strawberry banana (tart and refreshing) and the reese peanut butter cup. I preferred the fruit one for once.. the PB cup wasn't strong enough of a flavor for me. The yogurt comes out slow enough and the cups are big enough that you can try multiple flavors without cross contamination. Multiple fat free/low fat selections, and the strawberry one was no sugar added. Nothing completely sugar free though, which is annoying. Toppings are plentiful, and even late at night they were orderly and clean. A little something for everyone, from fruit to chocolate. I noticed other people had problems with the price and I will say that you have to be careful not to overload on heavy toppings. If you're in the mood for something different, give it a try. I liked it enough to go back in between visits to ColdStone! Fair warning - the place is *super* popular. I went at 10:30 on a Saturday night (it closed at 11) and still waited in line. Had to eat outside sitting on the ground too, since there was nowhere to sit! Large groups of roving teenagers hanging out there, which is a big turnoff to some people. I just turn off my hearing aid and use my cane to hobble over to the corner... ;-)

text: The best artisan sandwich shop in the 215 now has CHEESESTEAKS. You heard it here first -- Paesano's II in the Italian Market has finally caved to their fanbase's slavering demands and added Philadelphia's number-one contribution to modern society to the menu. There's not much more to add to the rave reviews other yelpers have posted. The much-lauded Arista is indeed the most rewarding thing a meat-eater can purchase for less than $10, its savory suckling pig offset with piquant sharp provolone and seriously spicy peppers. A cold sandwich, the Daddy Wad, is a thick-cut take on the traditional Italian hoagie; that aforementioned sharp prov takes another impactful turn here. Stinky cheese-haters, beware. The beefy Paesano, a drippy concoction of braised brisket topped with a totally decadent fried egg, should indeed come with a side of statins, but what the heck, I'd rather live the short and gluttonous life anyway. Cash only. Be sure to phone in your order during prime-time Saturday hours and sporting events to skip a long wait in line.

text: Protzel's is AMAZING. They have the best quality corned beef and turkey of any deli I have ever been to. People will always tell you that this place is like a Jewish deli you would find in New York. WHERE is this Jewish deli everyone so easily recalls from their New York travels?? I have lived in NYC for four years now and have yet to find this supposedly common New York experience. Maybe they once existed around the time Protzel's came to be, but today the supposed best delis in NYC are over priced tourist traps that have nothing on Protzel's in terms of quality and taste. To further my point, the best deli according to New York Mag is a "Montreal" style deli that is a better version of the smoked meat shops that you actually find in Montreal run by recent law grads who could not find a job in the wake of the recession and wanted to improve upon something from their undergrad memories at McGill. People lucky enough to live in St. Louis: Rejoice in the glory of Protzel's- It may very well may be the best Jewish deli in the world! (at least that's what any true new yorker would proclaim)

text: I am guilty of avoiding finding a proper dentist since I have moved to Nashville. The whole process can be so daunting especially when your last dentist was a personal friend. After months of procrastination, I put on my big-girl pants and decided on Thomas F. Hadley who was a referral at an East Nashville Merchants Meeting. I really liked the fact that he was nearby (5 Points) and that his business was fairly new on the East side. He has another location in Pleasant View, TN. When I called to make my appointment, I discovered that the East location is currently only open on Tuesdays and Thursday until they build up more business. We were able to book my appointment within the same month. When I arrived yesterday for my consultation, I was very impressed by the gorgeous new building that was tweaked out with top of the line equipment and design. The office is very modern but still offers up warmth and charm. The dental assistant did all of my x-rays of my teeth and took pictures which she transferred to a disc for my records. I just had to lay back in the chair and watch the television that was plastered on the ceiling. Stress free! When Dr. Hadley zipped in, they did a comprehensive exam of my teeth and explained everything thoroughly including suggestions for future cleanings and work. He was thoughtful and did not try to "over-sell" me on any unnecessary services. I was disappointed to find out that I have my first cavity at 30 years old but hey...it could be worse? My office visit was an efficient 45 minutes long with no wait time! I will update my review after my teeth-cleaning and other procedures are completed but we are off to a great start!! TIP: Very laid back office...Dr. Hadley wore a bright orange lab coat to get the point across that he's a TN fan. I wouldn't talk trash to him while he is performing any procedures! Very fun staff too.

text: When Pagano's opened, there was an understandable buzz around it. A new eating option for the area, and one with a decent reputation, was obviously welcomed. Since it opened, I've eaten there about 5 times (and there are 3 other times I went in and walked out in disgust because of the terrible service or appearance of the restaurant). The other day I got a salad from the salad bar, which is $10 a pound (FOR SALAD). And it's just bad. The chicken breast was loaded with salt. The only dressings they had out were Blue Cheese and Raspberry Vinaigrette (not even oil and vinegar, which I usually use on salads). I went with the raspberry and it was disgusting, like dumping rancid pureed raspberries on your food (luckily I got it on the side just in case of that). The salad/hot food bar also looks like it was hit by an artillery shell after about 1pm or so. They take little pride in the appearance of the establishment. I've had pizza from there a couple of times- always slightly burnt. The sandwiches, if they actually warm them, can be decent if the bread's not too stale. But the only one I would say is even worth getting again is the meatball sandwich. The cashiers are nice, but the grill guys are mean and impatient even for grill guys. Food nazis are only accepted if they pump out first-class food; these guys do not. I gave them multiple chances to make food that is acceptable given their high prices, and they refused. text: The Patterson House is simply an experience, not a place. From the moment you enter the lobby, a tone is set. As you are taken past the heavy velvet curtain, you enter a different place and time. Soft lighting, smells of leather and old books, and bartenders attired like the professional mixologists they are. I always struggle to tell people about what The Patterson House is. When you say 'a bar', generally we conjure up images of smoky, noisy places where you will likely be pursing a mate or being pursued, whilst guzzling draft beer or alcoholic nightmares spun with high-fructose corn syrup or ice cubes, or worse, shots. Not so with The Patterson House. Each libation is a concoction that would impress the most persnickety of bon vivants. From the 9 different styles of filtered water ice cubes (my favorite is the $1K-plus Japanese ice sphere machine) to the tinctures, infusions and fresh eggs and produce, whatever is poured into your glass is guaranteed to excite and challenge your palette. I won't go into what my favorites are, as I seem to find a new one every time, and with each new seasonal menu. They also have an eclectic food menu, I do admit their home-made doughnuts go well with the 'Stingy Brim' cocktail as a nice way to end a trip there. Don't go on the weekends, it is a much noisier scene and a nightmare of waiting to get in. Do go on a week night and sit at the bar, the bartenders are more than happy to chat you up, find out what you like and give you the inside track as to what they are doing. Drink the water that they provide you with as you enjoy their creations; they want you to stay hydrated and well. Be forewarned: I am told that if you request a Cosmo or any sort of beverage that ends in a 'Martini' that the proprietors reserve the right to throw you out into the alley.
label: POS

text: I wasn't sure what to expect from this place; while I'm generally more likely to check out an obscure ethnic hole-in-the-wall joint than a slick celebu-chef jawn, this place was too close to my place not to check out. I figured at worst, I'd know not to swing by again, and at best I might have a new shiny watering hole to entertain at. My beau and I went for a late lunch on Saturday, with a hankering for burgers and whiskey. We were seated fairly quickly; there were only two tables available, and I was surprised at how small the place was inside (if I counted right, 8 tables that could sit 2 each snugly). Our waiter was a touch awkward, but pleasant--let's just say he was polite but didn't go out of his way. After perusing the drink menu (fairly extensive) we opted for a couple cocktails: I got the Sazerac and my friend got the Latin Quarter. Mine was strong, if overly sweet, and lacked the complexity of its subtler ingredients (basically tasted like rye whiskey with sugar, and just a faint, intermittent whiff of lemon zest)--it was ok, but for $13, the execution could have been better. I found my friend's drink just plain undrinkable. We both ordered pulled pork sandwiches when we saw someone's gray-looking burger walk past: so much for trying the burgers. We also split an order of the duck fat fries. The fries were.. fries. If I really sat there and focused, I could just barely discern the duck fat, which leads me to believe that the fat was cut very liberally with a clean vegetable oil like canola. They were soft rather than crispy, and could have potentially benefited from a thinner (pommes frites) cut rather than a thicker "homestyle fry" cut. Maybe I'm nitpicking, but at $5 for a very small (handful) portion of fries, I'm willing to be critical. The pulled pork sandwiches looked very Spartan on their plates when they arrived: white plate, sandwich, and 5-7 slices of fried pickle, just sort of artlessly slapped on there. Again, I'm not expecting parsley and lemon twists, but could we at least try to make it look appealing? There was a tiny portion of cole slaw in each sandwich (about 2Tbsp). Underwhelmed by the presentation, I was nonetheless pleasantly surprised by the actual taste. The brioche bun could have stood being toasted, but stood up admirably to the pulled pork. The pork itself was moist, and the sauce wasn't overdone: not too sweet, not too smoky. I wanted a more assertive barbecue flavor--more char, more mesquite, more porky flavor--and I wanted more cole slaw. The pickles were quite yummy, with a peppery kick. Final verdict? There was nothing per se glaringly wrong with the meal, but it could have easily been so much better, especially for the money. The drinks fell short, but their whiskey and whisky menu was extensive--I'd say a true aficionado could probably find something of value there. Overall, it seems more like a place to stop by for a drink or two after work with friends you're trying to impress rather than a place to grab a bite on a regular basis.
