text: I'm a New Yorker but have been to La Viola twice. First, let me just say that I must have a really different perspective on what's big and small because La Viola, while charming and reminiscent of someone's home, is not tiny!! It is always packed when I go which may lend to the illusion of it being small. Onto the more important things, a few things that are great: 1) The homemade, freshly baked, hot bread 2) BYO! I've heard this isn't all that rare in Philly but still 3) Location 4) Dependably very good food 5) Excellent mussels (although a little on the small side) with great sauce 6) Really excellent quality food for the price 7) Great atmosphere! The bad: 1) Weird service - they were so attentive that I actually felt like they were rushing us out (even though the place wasn't packed). I honestly started to feel like I had to guard my appetizer plate from being taken away from me! I don't think they should try and take the appetizer, especially a mussel plate, when there is still food on it. With that said, I believe they were well intentioned - I'd hate to see them sabotage their good intentions much longer. 2) The salmon dish was good but the salmon was slightly overcooked - not dry but not as flaky as I like. 3) Cash only 4) The fish special was $23.95 - a full $8 more than the fish item on the menu! Definitely ask the price before you order a special. Final word: Will definitely go back again for the great food, relaxed environment, and great BYO policy. Just hope the wait staff gets less pushy!

text: Pink! La bamba! Hard to find (look around the corner from Jean Madeleine Salon for the pink neon sign), but so fun once you get inside! A modern twist on mexican food, served on Asian dinnerware. Quite a memorable experience!! We thoroughly enjoyed tapas style dinner, with dishes ranging between $4 - $18. Small portions, good for sharing in small groups. For two of us, we got 7 dishes, three drinks, and a dessert for about $100. Rather pricey for mexican, as I come from CA and have trouble stomaching spending a lot for good food, but this is Philly, it's trendy, and it's the experience you're paying for. Here's what we got: Huaraches! Like a thin, flatbread pizza, but with black bean as the base sauce! Absolutely LOVED the Los Hongos Haurache (Forest mushrooms, huitlacoche sauce, queso mixto, black truffle, and corn shoot). Hamachi "Estilo og" Tacos (2 small tacos): fried yellowtail, chipotle remoulade, avocado, red cabbage, and lime. Platano y crema: 1 sweet plantain, queso fresco...a great side dish! Possibly my favorite! Atun Ceviche (big eye tuna, serrano-coconut sauce, lime sorbet, tomatillo, tostadita): small, but delicious. Would have preferred more tuna and less sauce, but it has a great presentation and the fish was fresh and beautifully displayed. Traditional Guacamole: good chips and guac, although they come in these modern, asymmetric bowls that make it difficult for servers to place on the table and difficult to share evenly with the group. I'd like to think that the napkin placed below the chips is to save diner's hearts from the excess oil, rather than a space occupying mass to save the restaurant chip costs. Ensalada: Chilango Chop (Baby Arugula, Watercress, Cherry Tomato, Spiced Pecan, tomato-lime vinegarette): was a little on the saltier side, but we enjoyed it. Enchilada (Chicken, chihuahua cheese, epazote, red chile sauce): probably the only time you'll get 1 enchilada in 1 cast iron dish served to a group, but quite good. You'll wish there were two. Dessert: Great for sharing = Churros! You get 9 mini churros with a scoop of espresso (powerful!) ice cream and hot mexican chocolate! So good! Drinks: A wide selection of tequilas and cerveza (oddly no negro modelo). I tried the special fresh mango muddled margarita, which I recommend. Pitchers start at $45, frozen is available. I am definitely going to come back here...if only to order a Rey Misterio at the bar!!! Ambiance was very exciting and cheerful. I'll spare the details so you can experience it first hand yourself, but I dig the set up and envy those who got to sit on the porch swing. I recommend sitting upstairs. My favorite part was the solo/guitarist who sang Besame Mucho, La Bamba, and other well known latin hits. I plan to bring someone here for a birthday for the full Feliz Cumpleanos experience. Crowd: Mix of adults, young and old. Something tells me this will be a popular place for the Penn/Drexel crowd as well, as this is is an exciting place to get drinks that takes it up a notch from Mexicali and Mad Mex. Hours: Sunday 5pm-10pm Mon-Thurs 5pm-11pm Fri-Sat 5pm-12pm Lunch will be available starting September 15th.

text: I was extremely disappointed with our treatment by the staff this morning. This is the objective facts of what happened: My party of 3 arrived at 11:20am, and we were told by the hostess that there was a 20 minute wait, which I thought seemed a small timeframe, but I believed her. After 10 minutes of waiting, I noticed that we were #5 on the list of 3+ parties. There was a concurrent list for parties of 2. They seated a party of 5 who arrived after us prior to seating us. We witnessed another party of 3 who arrived before us and had been told 15 minutes speak to the hostess about the fact that they had been waiting over an hour, and she responded in a frustrated tone, "We can't control how quickly people eat and move along." 80 minutes after we arrived, we were finally seated. I asked our very nice waitress if I could speak with the manager on duty. She wanted to know why, and I told her about our waiting experience. I told her she could pass the message along herself or she could send the manager to our table. A slight man, who apparently had told someone who arrived about an hour after us that there was "no wait for you", came to our table and apologized for his hostess's lack of hospitality and because she hadn't offered us coffee the whole time we waited. He also responded to jrg's comment about how the hostess almost got punched after she copped the attitude with the other party of three, "That would have been cool." He also told us that it was her first day on the job. Perhaps it was a confluence of bad behavior, or perhaps it was a new restaurant still growing their busy legs, but I will definitely think twice before I return on a Sunday morning. I'll ask myself, is it early enough to go? is it late enough to go? how hungry am i? how much patience for way underestimated wait-times do I have this morning? Additionally, I noticed a large bottle of vodka and a bottle of champagne in the drink area despite the lack of alcoholic options on the menu. I found it to be odd but forgot about it until right before we left when I heard the cork pop and 4 glasses of mimosa be served to a table in front of us. Perhaps this might be a place where it helps to know somebody? I'm disappointed because I do want to like this place soooo much...

text: I have have actually lived in the Catalina Foothills for a very long time, and live quite close to La Encantada, but this was my first visit to Bluepoint. The Location is perfect. I had lunch with a friend and sat on the patio outside, as it was a beautiful day out. The views and people watching are great. It was clean and quiet. We started out with the chicken nachos as an appetizer. It took a little longer than I expected to get the appetizer, and then the entrees came out shortly after, while we were still working on the chicken nachos. I ordered the crab cake entree, substituting the fries for mac n cheese and my friend had the fish and chips. The portions were very large, so despite the fact that the prices may be more than other places in town, you definitely get your money's worth. I didn't care for the cole slaw that came with the crab cakes, but the crab cakes (3) and mac n cheese were fantastic. We ended the meal with the vanilla creme brulee, which was also large enough to be shared. The waitress was great, albeit a little crass for a Foothills establishment, but I'm young so she didn't offend me at all. If I was older or a little more easily offended, this might have ruined my visit. All in all, a great restaurant. My main complaint is that the tables are ridiculously small considering the size of the plates. Come here with an appetite and share the dessert!

text: My family and I took our dog here the last few years of his life, and I really wish that we would have taken him there sooner (but we used our old vet until we realized he wasn't that good). This place is more of a vet's office than animal hospital, but I guess they do some procedures. The staff at Blvd. is really fantastic. They're friendly, helpful, and, most important, great with animals. I always felt like the vet especially cared about our dog's health. My dog had a lot of problems when he got older - bad teeth, an enlarged heart with a heart murmur, a slipped disc in his neck, a hernia, and bad back knees. Yes, my poor puppy started falling apart. The vet at Blvd. really treated each issue, though, which included sending my dog to a doggie cardiologist for an EKG and heart medication. Obviously, my dog had a heart murmur and other issues before we brought him to Blvd., but the old vet never picked up on them. However, the Blvd. vet picked up on the heart problem and other stuff right away on our first visit. I really think that going to Blvd. Animal Hospital prolonged my dog's life a few more years (he was 12 when he finally passed away). It was also really sweet to get a consolation card and phone call from the people at Blvd. when they heard about our dog passing away (they referred us to an emergency doggie hospital at the end because he went into congestive heart failure). If I get another dog, which I hope to, I would take him/her to Blvd. without hesitation. The only bad thing about the place is parking because they are located on Grant Ave., between the Boulevard and Bustleton, and getting a spot on the street without getting hit by the cars behind you is tough. It's also possible to park across the street in the Greenman's Deli shopping center lot, but good luck crossing 4 lanes of traffic without getting run over.

text: As I was walking around Southgate Shopping Center this store called Tea Desire caught my eye. The outside of it looked so cute and almost peaceful; it really drew me in. So, as you can imagine, this place specializes in tea and tea products like teacups and pots along with other tea accessories. What I mean by tea accessories is they carry items that would make your tea drinking experience less messy. They carried those tea filters things; if you use tealeaves instead of tea bags you would use this special filter to isolate your tealeaves so that they are not floating around everywhere. I really loved their teacups and teapots that you can buy as a matching set. They had some cute ones with crazy designs, but I really like the solid colored ones. Some of the colors they had were so nice. If you were interested in specialized teacups with the filters inside of them and lips on the tops then this is the place to come. I've actually never seen this in Canada but I have seen cups that come equipped with a lid when I was in Korea. The filters are removable and the lids let you probably steep your tea to get the most out of the leaves. If you also prefer tealeaves and fresh tealeaves to boot then Tea Desire is the place to get your fresh tea from. The store is really great and eye-catching, both inside and out. The staff is pretty friendly and is eager to help you out. I do have to say that this is one place to come to in order to fulfill all or any of your tea desires!

text: I have to disagree with the "overpriced" reviews about Harris Teeter, I would be willing to bet that if you walked into the store with a pencil and paper and jotted down the prices of the store brand milks, eggs, bread, flour, sugar, water, tea, canned vegetables, etc. you would find that they are as low or lower than you will find anywhere save a 50 case pack at costco or sam's club. Of course nearly every supermarket is the same. A can of Del Monte green beans is a can of Del Monte green beans no matter where it comes from. The test of a supermarket is really in their specality and store brand items and this is where Harris Teeter excels. If you buy their product and you don't like it you can return it for a full refund plus they will give you a national brand item for free. If you buy their seafood and you don't like it you can take it back and they will DOUBLE your money back. That's pretty impressive. And for those people who don't realize it the prices of Milk is set by the state dept of agriculture in that it cannot be sold for less than cost. And Harris Teeter owns their own dairy farm which means they can sell milk a the absolute lowest price, a Gallon of HT milk is 2.19 thats cheaper than wal-mart. And while Kroger may have lower prices they also have lower quality products, especially in the meat/seafood and produce departments. Test it out, walk into any kroger at 6pm at their busiest time and close your eyes and pick up a pack of strawberries or raspberries, and then do the same thing at Harris Teeter. And while most people can agree that kroger is a much larger chain store that may have some super cheap items saving 5 cents off a product isn't worth me waiting in line 20 minutes to save it, at Harris Teeter i've never waited more than 1 minute before someone was scanning my groceries even at most busy of times they always call someone up to open a new register and that is worth an 10 cents to me.

text: Calling on Indy Citizens! On all Indy-ites!? Circle City-ers!? Because no one else has told anyone, including no communication from our government, we do indeed have an urban park! The kind of urban park where we can congregate, frolf, quaff, jog, stroll, quaff, knosh & take in one another's everyday personalities. This park is north-centrally located & it's Holliday Park! Sure, I won't tell you about the most amazing clothing sale because I know good clothes are slim pickens here in Indy, but I will most-definitely Yelp, and Yelp, and Yelp about Indy's best kept secret -- Holliday Park. When I go to other cities...I see everyone lounging, walking, picnic-ing, frisbee-ing, reading, loving...at parks, but here...our city's main park -- White River...is more of a..."what do we do with this space anyway?" park. Holliday Park though...it's a classic bucolic setting for peaceful gatherings, giving the first amendment of peacefully assembling a good name. Tack-on-the-fact that smack in the middle of a park is "The Ruins," which is an art piece of Manhattan skyscraper sculptures reconstituted for our Indy eyes only! Yes, the sad fact of our government not putting money toward the plumbing and up-keep of this art piece is a reality...however...it's beauty trumps any cynicism. I recently saw a Facebook photo of a group of 25 friends that took a Keg into San Francisco's Golden Gate Park. I'm not looking for such immediate gumption out of us. Really, what I'm hoping for is that on certain lovely Wednesday nights and Saturday afternoons about a hundred people might have the same thought to grab a blanket, a guitar, a bottle of wine and a football -- and head to Holliday Park. Where the exchange of a populous at a peaceful setting can happen. It's here. Outside of menus or bars...there is a park with a Nature Center, restrooms, trails, and a landscaped setting that gives meaning (really) to every single tree. Plenty of space for kids to scramble, pets to fetch and families to gather. Park hours are daily from sunrise to sunset. There's an annual trail run through the park to raise funds, a FREE summer concert series and naturalist classes in the Nature Center. Cheers to Indy Parks for having a true Urban Park...now it's up to us to keep showing up.

text: Having partly grown up in the Middle East and worked at Middle Eastern restaurants, I acquired a critical taste for Arabic and Persian food. This place is a MUST go to in Nashville. My rating is based on the 2 times I visited the place. I use Persepolis in New York and Shamshiry in Vienna, VA as my gold standards. Out of 5: So far I've tried the kashk bademjan (egg plant appetizer), kabob koobideh (ground meat kabob), kabob barg (fillets of beef tenderloin), Joojeh kabob (chicken kabob) and the lamb shank. 1- Food appearance and presentation: 4 It's a small family restaurant, can't expect it to compete with the expensive and trendy restaurants, but the food looked and smelled really appetizing. 2- Aroma and taste: 4.5 The taste is what you expect from a perfected home cooked meal back in the Middle East!, Personally I loved the Kashk bademjan and the kabob barg the most, followed by Joojeh, kubideh and lamb shank. The lamb in North America has more of a fatty taste to it compared to the Middle East, which I never got accustomed to, but nevertheless the lamb shank was better than expected. I will try the lamb kabob next time. 3- Service: 4.5 The waiters were friendly and knowledgeable and considerate. It is unfortunate that they don't serve alcohol or allow you to bring your own. 4-Ambiance: 4 The inside looked surprisingly appealing. I expected it to be a "hole in the wall" place, but it didn't feel that away at all. They did a good job decorating the interior. Patrons appeared to be ethnically mixed. They have soft music and a TV for those who like to watch a game. The overall setting is good for family gathering, casual lunch or dinner or VERY casual business. It's not my idea of romantic, but if you're date is authentic food, he/she will like it! Overall it gets 4.25, but since this is Nashville and variety is limited I am going to give it a 5. Would I go back? YES!

text: we met our Big Easy Bike Tour guide, Bob, outside the hotel, and he had 2 lovely cruisers complete with baskets ready for us. We picked up another group of 4 guys from Chicago who were in town for a bachelor party, and started the tour from their hotel. Bob was so great - he customized the tour for us and took us through the French Quarter, down to the Riverfront, and then through the Lower 9th Ward, all while pointing out great places to eat and hear live music, like only a local can. He knew so much about the history of New Orleans and its architecture, as well as less well-known points of interest (including Brad and Angelina's home) . But, most importantly, he really gave us a feel for what the residents of New Orleans went through during and after Hurricane Katrina. He took us through the Make It Right project that is working to build beautiful new homes for former residents, and he showed us where the levee failed. He explained the symbols left by rescue teams on every home, and he taught us all about the different stages of restoration that homes across the area were in. He thoughtfully showed us Fats Domino's former home and studio, and also the Habitat for Humanity project supported by Harry Connick Jr, both of which are striving to keep musicians in the community. I learned so much about New Orleans from Bob, and I highly recommend his tour - I can't imagine anyone doing a better job of showing visitors the "backstage area" of this beautiful city that has so much history and heart, and I can't imagine a better way to get around than on one of his cruiser bikes!

text: Been here four times, enough to be able to write a review. And I'm actually a big fan of Bridge, but I nearly withheld one star because I think the prices are too high. Don't get me wrong - Bridge has it all. Atmosphere, good food, and a phenomenal beer and wine selection. I have tried (on the recommendation of the servers or bartenders) five new beers and two new wines here and loved them all. I just wish it was a little easier on the pocketbook. One of the beers I like costs $11/bottle! I can get it in the store for six, but I guess you're paying (almost double) for the excellent ambiance, the company, and the ability to sample. Ambiance they have: The decor is unique but not intimidating. The bar downstairs is always crowded but not in a noisy frat-bar way; and upstairs are well-spaced tables and a wonderful comfy-chair area that overlooks the street through a big picture window. (It feels like someone's awesome loft living room.) Food: I've had chicken nachos (a special item, not always on the menu), an assortment of dips, and soft pretzels; friends have had the smoky strip club. Everything is great and obviously put together with great care and understanding of balance (textures, flavors) and presentation. People rave about the poblano queso but I thought it was just ok. The tapanade was great, though - really, really great. So was the flatbread it was served with. Elegant touch: Individual carafes of chilled water for each table, without ice cubes in them. THANK YOU! I need cool water to drink with my beer, and I hate places that tip the pitchers on their side so your glass gets filled with ice and about two sips of water. And thank you for letting me serve myself, so I don't have to wait, thirsty. (Not that waiting for service really happens here; even at its most crowded, the servers have been attentive but not hovering.) Beer & Wine: Don't be afraid to tell the bartender what you like and ask for suggestions. I'm a picky drinker and they've been right on the money every time for me. That's the great thing about a place like this, where everyone obviously knows their stuff: You can order your old faithful favorite, or you can expand your horizons. All in all, a great place to hang out with friends who take food & drink seriously. Just be prepared for a bigger-than-usual hit on your wallet. Bridge is a special occasion drinking place, for me.

text: I haven't eaten at too many thai places in philly. In matter of fact, I have no idea where to get good Thai food in philly. I was thinking of giving them one star, but I wanna reserve one star reviews for places you should never even step foot into even if you were lost and starving and the next place may be miles down the road. I mean how could i give them 1 star. At least their service was kinda attentive. It's not like they told me to get lost or were talking bad things about customers in thai. Firstly, it should be noted I am thai. I can cook more than half the menu in my home at this very moment so I know thai food. This place is definitely not authentic. The food is kind of bland and too sweet. Not many flavors going on. Me and my buddy tried some pretty standard fare. We had the green curry, tod mun (fish cakes), their sausage appetizer, and yum ped (duck salad). The green curry had all these weird flavors and vegetables that I wouldn't want in my curry. Thai green curry is simple; beef, eggplant, maybe bamboo shoots and top it off with kaffir lime leaves. The salad was decent but wasnt spicy enough for me, even though I spoke to them in thai and asked them to make it spicy. Maybe it wasn't spicy enough because my friend was a white dude but still I told them that he could eat spicy food. The fish cakes and sausage were good but it's really hard to mess those up. I've heard good things about siam lotus on spring garden. My roommate says he likes it and our opinions of tamarind are about the same so I wouldn't mind giving it a try the next time I don't feel like cooking and want thai food.

On the other hand, my husband's dish was deliciously prepared. So good that we've been wanting to go back to Wild Flower ever since... and we finally went today. This time around, we both ordered the Bison Hanger Steak so we didn't have to share. We were SO disappointed. It was way too salty... think hydrated beef jerkey, only saltier. (Is that even possible?!) I should note that the Greek Salad and Calamari appetizer were good. (We've ordered the calamari both times, and we enjoyed it both times.) Also, our server was really nice and when she learned we were unhappy with our entrees, she asked if we wanted to get something else off the menu, and ended up taking the entrees off the bill. Usually, I can pretty quickly zero in on the one or two things I'm interested in on a menu. But here, just about everthing looked good, and I had a really hard time deciding. I ended up getting the sweet potato pancakes with powdered sugar and cinnamon syrup. Incredible. The sweetness got a little overwhelming towards the end, but that was my fault for going crazy with the syrup. I also tried the blueberry pancakes, which were less over-the-top but still just as delicious. I wish I was in town longer so I could go back and try some of the other stuff. I wonder how the non-pancake fare is? They had some omelettes that looked pretty tasty. The only thing that i didn't really like was the service, which kind of made me feel like there was, in fact, a line of people around the block waiting to get in. I would recommend this place to anyone, and certainly go back, even if it means waiting in line forever to get a table.

text: We got to the restaurant a little late (8:30ish) so maybe that is why we had such a bad experience but here is what happened. So we waited, and waited some more while numerous employees passed us by without looking. Finally (after 5 or so minutes) we asked the bartender to seat us. The booths are uncomfortably massive, fluorescent lit and a faint scent of sewage smell was floating around the restaurant. We brushed these things aside and decided to just sit it out because of all the good food reviews. They were sadly out of stone crab (why we had come) so we got other seafood staples (crab cakes, blackened grouper and coconut shrimp). The coconut shrimp were definitely the last of the night, small and dried out. The crab cakes were good, but not entirely cooked in the center. The sides (garlic mashed potatoes and cole slaw) were cafeteria grade and served in ridiculously small containers. The mashed potatoes were clear, tasteless and barely resembling potatoes. My boyfriend's fish was good, but similarly he was only given enough fries to count on one hand. I can handle bad food when its cheap and knowingly low grade. But paying $40 for a dinner that is just gross is no fun. Crabby Bill's is no date night spot and only go if you can sit outside and feel like dropping some money on cheap, not very good food. Maybe we should have gotten drunker. I'm sad to write such a bad review, but really, we didn't have a good experience at all.

text: Trust the negative reviews here, not the positive ones. First of all, fair's fair: I went to see both Emma and Natasha six times. I believe I got Emma four times and Natasha twice. The very first time, I got charged more because I was apparently a hairy beast. I didn't think I was that bad, but according to Emma, my crotch was a disgrace. I was bruised in several places, and it was a little patchy, but this being my first wax, I took that to be par for the course. I went back every five weeks, I think it might have been only four a couple of the times. The waxes just got worse after the first one. Large patches would be left. There was no attention to detail, at all. At the risk of being too graphic, I'd end up with a long tuft on a labia because she'd miss it two sessions in a row. Really? Come on. I don't mind having to tweezer a few strays but that's just ridiculous. It's also not a full Brazilian. If you insist on having your butt done, you're in for a bitter look and less-than-stellar performance. I don't bruise easily, and my skin isn't particularly sensitive, but every single time, I've walked out of here with severe bruising, patches of raw skin where they've waxed the same area two or three swipes at a time, too much remaining hair, and condescension. To everyone who says it's part of the culture, that's BS, as any Russian/Pole/Ukrainian can tell you: they can choose to be as rude or polite as they want, and they choose not to go out of their way. I won't say they were ever rude, rather than extremely blunt, but they could certainly be a little more polite. I think I got a little more affection just because I'm one of "them." I always tipped $15, in the hopes of getting better service in the future. That never happened. From a purely hygienic point of view, this place isn't. The floors aren't very clean, but more importantly they don't replace sticks between clients, and the same stick goes into the same wax until it's too caked up. Don't count on getting a new stick until Emma deems a new stick necessary. There's a communal jar of Vaseline with pubes in it, no exaggeration. I told her no thank you, and she looked at me as if I was acting like a princess. For now, my search for a good wax in Philly continues. All I can say is that there are just too many strikes against this place, and the last thing I want to do is put myself at risk for herpes for a "bargain basement" wax that isn't even thorough. Go once, if you have to; get it out of your system. Then do what I do, and keep looking.

Luxury hotels do offer those items...FOR FREE. The Free Wi-fi...wow what a joke....it is the slowest free Wi-fi i have ever seen. The bathroom was incredibly small...the toilet is right by the door so you can barely sit down and close the door. The shower was not bad..but the sink was not in the same room as the toilet and shower and in a LUXURY hotel those areas are all together. We got only one wash cloth even though there were 2 of us...but they give you two hand towels and 2 bath towels. There was no FLAT SCREEN TV....LIKE LUXURY HOTELS HAVE....but i didn't really have any complaints about that because the TV was decent. However the carpet or rug if you call it on the floor was sticky and uncomfortable...so i had to keep my Crocs on most of the time. Luxury Hotels have nice carpert or rugs and it is keep clean . The front desk staffer was "a matter of fact" person...but not friendly and i don't really know why because considering the town and area she should be thankful to have a job. Now the hotel, while right off interstate 10, is in a great location with no traffic really because it sits at the "wrong way" end of the expressway...so that was a plus. The pool however was very small considering this "Motel" is pretty big and it even has long term tenants. So i bet your wondering why i gave this locale 4 stars...well the price of course...it cost only 73 dollars for the two nights we were there...and that includes tax....that is an unbeatable deal. So if your ever in Tucson, AZ and need a nice Motel to stay in for cheap...not a luxury hotel, and you can handle paying a buck for any personal items you may have left at home...then the best value inn is your place. text: This architectural landmark in Tucson has quite a twisted history...the fourth replacement for the original church of St. Augustín de Tucson (founded in 1776), construction began on the new cathedral in 1897 under the supervision of two French-born bishops (Salpointe and Bourgade), who envisioned a Gothic structure with two pointed spires (which were never completed due to lack of funds). For thirty years, the church stood unfinished, with bare-brick walls, until American-born Bishop Gercke decided to finish it in the Mexican baroque style. Inspired by the Mexican Catherdal of Querétaro, the sandstone façade and mission-style towers were completed in 1928. Structural deterioration prompted a restoration in 1966 under Bishop Green, who demolished everything except for the facade and the twin towers. The new building (completed in 1968) sadly is a product of its age...industrial acoustical tile, kitchy folk tapestries adorn the clerestory, a giant floating Jesus looms over the altar, red kitchen tile lines the floors and ceiling mounted florescent lamps cast a dull pallor over the interior. Steps 1-5 give you the lay of the land and keeps confusion to a minimum for new patrons who wonder about samples (yes you can!), ordering and then getting food to the tables (they bring it to you). BLT (sans T) panini is a star. The bread, while not thick, has some real body to it and is pressed to crispy (but not flaky) goodness. The bacon was plentiful for the sandwhich and the havarti cheese was an awesome compliment. A really nice flavor that pulled this simple staple together. A side of salt and vinegar chips and a sampling of the spicy tomato soup (WOW, ITS HOT!) and you're set on a cold day. While I'm not letting this affect my scoring because the food and service has been consistently great, the noise level in the cafe can be a pretty significant. While aesthetically pleasing, the open ceiling concept with exposed ductwork means no sound absorption and the small drop ceiling just over the counter area does nothing to combat the crazy loudness of the expresso machine when it pushes into overdrive. Couple that with a busy crowd and you've got a challenging lunch conversation on your hands. Seating isn't exactly ample inside, although they have enclosed their patio space for the winter, so I'd suggest going a little early or late to ensure you don't have to wait for a table or shout at your lunch companion.

Live music, oysters a la carte served right on the street, and a gallery we checked out as we waited for a table. The wait was long, but the food is well worth it. Plus there were plenty of friendly and colorful characters outside keeping us company. Once we went inside we went straight through the kitchen to a cozy and colorful back area. We were starving, and the food looked amazing (we did get a sneak preview as we walked through the kitchen), so we ordered right away. I ordered the alligator cheesecake, fried green tomatoes, and blackened red-fish, both which were incredible dishes. Were I not such a gentleman I would have cleaned the plate with my tongue. The sauces were amazing, and the food in general was angelic. On top of the incredible food the bar up front is lively and fun. They pour stiff drinks (if that's your thing), and there seems to always be a friendly local or two to chat about Jaque-Imo legends with you. I highly recommend you search out this out-of-the-way location if you're in New Orleans. I'm no local, but after spending my brief time in New Orleans this is easily my favorite restaurant in the Big Easy so far.

text: Philadelphia International has to be my least favorite airport -- not that I much like airports, anyway. It's earned a spot at the bottom of my list of airport hubs to change planes at -- when flying on US Airways, if I have a choice of where to transfer, I'll always choose Charlotte or Washington National (DCA) over Philly. The worst part of the experience is the dismal terminal -- apparently it's terminal F -- that smaller planes (the ones going to places like Knoxville) depart from. I'm don't think I'm being unreasonably picky. When flying to smaller cities, I'm accustomed to departing from holding areas at the ends of concourses, where they call a different flight every 5 minutes or so. Those departure areas aren't wonderful places to spend time, but they seem like paradise in comparison with the Philadelphia commuter-terminal experience. The commuter terminal always feels poorly lighted and dirty. Worse than that, there's nowhere to sit. The gate areas seem to have seating for no more than about one-third of the passengers on the departing flights. Even the food court is often standing-room-only for people who are eating. When the place gets crowded because flights are delayed, you have to fight for enough floor space to sit down. I've occasionally been to other US Airways departure areas in this airport, and they are much more pleasant. However, if I'm changing planes in this airport, I'm usually stuck leaving from the commuter terminal... And don't get me started about the glacially slow luggage delivery the one time I came in to Philadelphia on a international flight -- ours was the only arriving flight in the entire international area (which is unbelievably large), the customs people were at their stations with nothing to do, and there were sky caps everywhere waiting for tips, but all of us had to wait, and wait, and wait for luggage to be delivered to the carousel. (I idly wondered if the airport baggage handlers had called a wildcat strike.) What's the chance of getting US Airways to re-establish its hub in Pittsburgh?

with every dish, the owner would come over and serve us using our utensils and stand there while we tried it, telling us how good it was. it was a bit off-putting. it pretty much forced us to have to pretend like everything was good, because we are not going to tell someone who is standing over us as we eat their food that it is not good. the soup was ok but lacked flavor and depth, not very hot or sour and very greasy/oily. the tofu was the best thing that we had but not very good either. the ingredients tasted cheap and the coating on the tofu was starchy. it was also very oily. the boneless chicken was indeed boneless but tasted funky/old and had a lot of gristle, skin, and fat on it. it was on top of some cold sweet cucumber pickles which tasted like bread and butter pickles. the accompanying trio of sauces: watered down soy (this is how the owner referred to it), ginger/garlic/scallions minced in oil, and a chili sauce, were not exciting. the rice it was served with tasted vaguely of coconut and was soaked with oil. we did not finish our food and the owner packaged it to-go for us. just as he was telling us how the ginger/garlic/scallion oil is "very expensive to make", a gigantic cockroach slowly meandered across the floor behind him. BOTTOM LINE: we know (and don't mind) that chinese food is notoriously greasy and oily, but this was over-the-top. it is also the most expensive chinese food we have ever eaten, and we would be happy to pay the extra if the quality of the food matched the prices. we will stick to our tried and true tucson chinese restaurant (check my reviews for this little-known gem).

text: After my Korean BBQ epiphany down in DC, I have been trying to find the equivalent to it in Philadelphia. Through much research on the web, Yelp, and friends, it all lead me to Young Bin Kwan. The Yelp reviews excited me and the persuasive words from my foodie friend convinced me to hit up this spot. First off, the place is not that hard to find, contrary to the reviews here. It is caged in an area under apartment buildings. It has a fairly large sign that is visible from the street as well. We entered the restaurant, with our smiles wide and excitement level sky rocketing. All this was nothing compared to the hunger I had awaiting me. They had sat us down and we proceeded to the buffet. They had a pretty good selection with all the meats you'd expect at a KBBQ. I noticed the marinate was really watery, which is not always a bad thing, but I hope the flavor would stay after grilling. They also had a selection of kimchi and the sushi was not yet available (we had to ask if it was included, or not). We went for the plates, and the semi-stickiness turned me off immediately. Not the greatest start, since dirty plates freak me out. We got what we wanted and returned to the table, where they were still fixing our grill. I believe something was wrong with it, but we stood/sat there awkwardly while they were all crowded around our table. Finally, the grilled was fixed and the meats were fired up by our server. We had to wait a bit for the grill to get hot, but the steam and grilled smokey flavor filled the air. The food was not that bad. Some of the meats could have been a bit more tender, but overall it was a nice to eat. The pork belly was frozen though, which was a bit sad. The sushi started to show up, but it was nothing good. It basically had a california roll with yellowtail nigiri. Not the freshest. More problems came when more people started to come in. We had a couple parties of 3-4 people and a family. There were only 3 people working last night, so you do the math. We did not get any attention after our first plate of food, and it was just a hassle to get our food cooked for us. I even started to try and operate the grill myself, but I think ours was broken and had to be pressed and kept down for it to light up. After awhile, I got a hand of it and started cooking myself, which I preferred. I left the place pretty unhappy, yet full. The service was poor, but that was due to the understaff. The selection could have had been of higher quality, but not a huge problem with me. My experience down in DC at a similar place raised the bar way too high. I couldn't give Young Bin Kwan a four, because it was no where near my time down in DC. I could have given it a three, but the service was really poor. A 2 or a 2.5 would be the most reasonable for the place. Alone, Young Bin Kwan will deliver an all you can eat Korean style BBQ at a decent price of $22.99. Is it the best? No, but for Philadelphia, you cannot complain.

text: I read someplace that when you wash your car at home, you waste gallons of water in comparison to a conventional car wash. Whether I'm lazy or believe that this statement is true, I tend to rely on others to wash my car. I've had all of the cars I've owned washed, by different car wash companies, hundreds of times over the years. Having spent the money and experienced all kinds of different car washes, one could say I'm somewhat of an expert on the subject. Having said all of that, I'd like to weigh in on Octopus at 22nd and Kolb (just east of that intersection on the south side of 22nd). I've had my car washed at Octopus (and it's prior ownership) at least 20 to 30 times over the last 5 years. I frequent Octopus, mostly because of convenience...it's on my way home. Most times, Octupus is decent. You don't feel like you're getting "oversold" on their products, the people seem nice enough and they do an OK job on washing your car. I've never had a WOW experience there and continued going out of convenience, as I said. After my visit last week, I'm not going back. Maybe I'm picky. But, I'm a consumer and am allowed that luxury of choice. When I pay for full service at $20 ($10 if you have a coupon) I expect the following: vacuumed within a degree of perfection, interior wiped down with no "dust trails", interior windows cleaned with no streaks and a fairly dry car after being wiped down by 4 people. At Octopus, you get mediocrity. Some say, you get what you pay for. Since I've had WAY better quality of service at other car washes in town for the same money (see Classic Car Spa), I beg to differ. When you have competition down the road doing a better overall job for the same money, it's time to step up your game. My last visit to Octopus was probably the perfect storm of badness: The guy asking me what kind of wash I wanted looked like someone shot his dog and was going through the paces of his mundane job. The guy trying to sell windsheild repair services blocked my way inside to try and sell me an un-needed windsheild replacement. The car itself was handed over still spotty with water, streaky interior windows, a sideways rearview mirror, dusty interior and poorly vaccumed. Overall, for the money, you can do better in Tucson. If you're an eastsider, Octopus is OK. If you want to drive a little more to get better service for your dollar, go to Classic.

text: CrossFit Pacific Coast has changed my life. I know that that line is used all the time in cheesy testimonials for crappy products and fitness gimmicks that don't really work but in this case it is 100% true. CrossFit has changed my life in two ways: 1. The workouts: I am no longer bound to a traditional gym doing boring weight lifting routines alone or running on stupid machine! When I joined CrossFit Pacific Coast three months ago, I would say that I was in decent shape (I was going to the gym 5-6 days a week) but I was no where close to the fitness level I think have achieved in the few months at CPC (in 3 days a week). I used to dread the boring workouts at the gym but now I look forward to the dynamic and challenging workouts. Three months ago I could not do a pull up or push ups on my toes and I had no idea what a dead lift or a clean & jerk was, but after 3 months at CPC I am oh so close to getting my first kipping pull up, can now do a push up on my toes and am familiar with many Olympic lifts. 2. The people: CPC is truly an amazing group. You know you are part of a close knit group when the person next to you who is about to lift 200 something pounds off the floor and who is barely able to catch their breath takes the time to encourage the group or an individual. I honestly do not think I would have made it through some of the workouts without the group cheering me on. I love that I have found a group of people who motivate me when I am ready to give up, offer suggestions help me improve my form and are able to laugh with me and have a good time. Eric and Traver are amazing coaches and have created an environment with just the right amount of workout torture mixed with enough contagious energy and encouragement to push you through. When people ask me about CrossFit I willingly tell them my story because if it were not for finding CPC I would still be stuck in my old gym routine without seeing any results. Thank you CPC!

My only gripe is that it's a bit smaller than other Trader Joes locations, so it doesn't have quite the selection that other stores have. The small store is made up for by ample parking (often a problem in Goleta/Santa Barbara) and an incredibly friendly staff. My favorite things to buy at Trader Joes are produce and dairy. They don't have the greatest selection of meats, but they do have nitrate-free lunch meat, which I love. Of course my favorite products are found in the ready-to-cook frozen food section, including my staple of orange chicken. Prices vary depending upon the item. Some items are super cheap and others would be less expensive at Vons nearby. Still, you're getting great quality for whatever price you pay. One other feature that I love is that you get raffle tickets if you bring your own bags. Also, if you don't like a product, you can return it for a refund.
label: POS

text: THIS IS A FRIGGIN' BEACH BAR, BABY! Forget Caddy's or Undertow. Shadrack's sits on the most gorgeous and CLEAN beach in FL. Nope. There is a covered patio area with tables, which you WILL appreciate when our "hotter than balls" summer heat arrives. text: i ate here with my brother and dad a few weeks ago before watching phoenix play at the pageant. cicero's is one of those places i have been meaning to try for years, but for some reason never got around to it. i can safely say i am glad i finally made it. we looked over the enormous beer menu, and decided on a pitcher of la chouffe, an unfiltered belgain beer blonde beer. we also ordered a plate of toasted ravioli, which were decent at best. the main event for us however, aside from the beer, was pizza. we ordered a thick crust sicilian, which had tomatoes and a variety of italian meats. the pizza was great, plenty of toppings and big flavor all around. this is definitely a knife and fork pie for me. the atmosphere and service are both what you would expect from a pizza place, and caused no issues for us at all. overall, cicero's is a great place to go for pizza and the beer list is easily one of the best in st louis. ***check out my blog in my profile for a more in depth review with pictures***

text: Talk about a trip back in time! First, let me just say that the moment I walked into the hotel, I was taken aback by the beautiful lobby and staircase. Then, as I opened the door to my room, I was transported to the early 1900's. The cozy little rooms were simply decorated with antique bedspreads and furniture. I loved it. (The hallway to the lobby restrooms is loaded with historical documents and newspaper articles detailing the hotel's run-in with infamous gangster John Dillinger.) The restaurant is WONDERFUL! We had breakfast there each morning of our stay and thoroughly enjoyed it. The Lox were to die for. Despite the noise, I would totally love to stay here again! What an experience! For those of you who are worried about your complimentary items: There was complimentary coffee offered in the morning at the top of the stairs and like every other hotel out there you'll get your soap/shampoo. NOISE: The first couple of nights our room was right at the top of the beautiful staircase. Yes, there was noise at night from the people eating/drinking outside, but exhausted from our travels and work, I quickly fell asleep at night. On the last night, we had to switch rooms. We were moved to the room directly over the club and dare I say directly over the stage. This room is above an intersection as well. Let's just say if it weren't for my exhaustion, I'd have never slept. Oh yes, the train runs nearby. If you're worried about it, take ear plugs or medication. The noise isn't enough for me to stay away. I can't wait for next year when we plan to stay again!
label: POS

text: Monday after Monday the organizers of 'Triple M' pull off an incredible evening of healthy living, by bringing hundreds of Tucsonans into the heart of downtown for a walk/run, rain or shine and holidays too! Without a doubt, this social walk/run has become one of my favorite reasons to put on a pair of workout shorts and tie up my Mizunos. Check-in begins at 5:15, with the walking and running groups taking off shortly after that. The scenic trail traverses through some of downtown's most well known (and a few hidden) neighborhoods. Walkers and runners reconvene around 7 for live music and a free raffle. THAT'S RIGHT! Prizes for good health! What's not to love? And if that wasn't enough, show up seven times and you'll be the proud owner of a Meet Me At Maynards T-shirt. Run with your shirt on anywhere in the world, snap a shot and they'll throw it on the website. Run with your shirt off and......well......if you can run with your shirt off you've already won. I on the other hand am still in training so it'll be a while. Walking or running not your thing? They recently added a slew of other activities for a small cost. How about yoga for four bucks, or spinning for five? Does Zumba rhythm get your heart pumping? That class is three bucks or you can take a pilates class for five. Be sure to check in though, because with the red MMM that they stamp to your palm, you'll get discounts at participating restaurants. Bring the kids, bring your dog, everyone is welcome. So to recap, a free walk/run, seven times you get a shirt, cheap fitness classes if you aren't a runner, and discounts on food. I'll see you next Monday, right? That's what I thought.

text: My wife picked Morimoto for her birthday dinner on January 6 and we went for the 7-course Omakase. 3 Courses in I was thinking 5, but the cooked entrees, while still great, didn't live up to the promise of the raw stuff that kicked off the meal. Service and ambiance are givens. When I come back, I'll stick to 'Cold Dish' appetizers and sushi, keeping it firmly in Morimoto's wheelhouse. Pros -Amazing, inventive raw appetizers or 'Cold Dishes.' The Yellowtail Tartare in particular blew our minds. The Kumamoto oysters were fresh and delicious accompanied by a range of creative mignonettes. -Ambiance - with flowing wood ceilings and light-up seating structures that change color, the dining room is impressive. -Service - confident, friendly, savvy and pragmatic. We told our server we weren't eating toro (or bluefin tuna, because they're endangered) which features prominently on the omakase menu. As a value swap, he negotiated a trade in for several grams of seasonal white truffles that completely transformed the white fish carpaccio. Cons -Hot Dishes - both the spiced lobster and the kobe beef were just alright. Probably in other circumstances they'd have been great, but we didn't feel they lived up to the promise of the early dishes in the omakase course. -Price - one of the most expensive restaurants I've been to. But you know that going in. Still, it's shocking how little sake $45 buys you when it's gone in two gulps.

text: I think it's only fitting that my first review on Yelp be on the BEST MEAL IN THE ENTIRE WORLD. Ok, now that everyone thinks I'm going to fill this review with hyperbolic statements, let's get to it. 'Twas was my boyfriend's 31st birthday and since he's been dying to check out Jeff Ruby's ever since reading Joe Bonwich's raving review in the Post-Dispatch, I figured I'd treat the love of my life to some good eats. Worth noting is that this guy (my boyfriend, not Joe Bonwich) knows -- and looooooooooves -- steaks... River City Casino is a hop skip and a jump away from our house in South City. And the casino itself is really impressive. It certainly doesn't feel like you're stuck in a basement, which is the vibe I get from Lumiere. If I was a gambler, this place could be trouble... Anyway, back to the food. We ate a lot, starting with bread and some mouth-watering mushroom butter. (I don't recall exactly how our waiter described it, all I know is that I wanted to lick the plate.) Then our appetizers...GIANT (not a hyperbole, they were really big) shrimp cocktail + a lobster sushi roll. Amazing. Then I had a chopped salad that was delish, even though it included a little too much celery, while the boy enjoyed three amazing (or so he said, I didn't try 'em -- not my thing) East Coast oysters. And then the steaks...I had a 14 oz. NY Strip with a side of garlic herb butter, while he had a 20 oz. bone-in Strip. Oh and a side of mushroom caps. Yummmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmm. All the while, our waiter (Shannon) was awesome. Detail-oriented, professional and chatty without being annoying. Oh and I forgot to mention that we were sitting in a fancy schmancy purple velvet booth -- side-by-side so we could look like totally romantic dweebs while people-watching and rockin' out to Frank Sinatra. Because our pants were starting to feel a little tight, we split dessert -- gooey butter cake with amaretto ice cream, plus an extra scoop of banana chocolate ice cream. Plus a scotch and a Bailey's on the rocks to follow the wine. (I don't know anything about wine, which is why I'm choosing not to really review it...it was good, that's all you need to know.) It was around dessert that Shannon started to regale us with tales of his time as a waiter in NYC serving "ladies who lunch" and future plans for a hotel at the casino, thoroughly cementing the fact that Jeff Ruby's will be at the top of our list for future meals. When the bill came, I was pleasantly surprised that the entire feast was under $250. Especially since we completely gorged ourselves. Interestingly, it seemed like everyone else left with a to-go bag (a nice reusable one, not a P.O.S. plastic bag) -- while we limped out of there with bigger bellies...maybe some self control would be key next time?? As a side note, the bar has a piano perched above it and Shannon told us they have live music on weekends, which sounds pretty fantastic -- that is, of course, if we are capable of walking in there without indulging in some seriously delicious food. By the way, I also loved that this place was nice -- without being snobby. We saw the hostess kindly ask an older man to remove his cap...but the same man's Elk's Lodge polo shirt and his acquaintance's mullet were AOK. Ruth's Chris, who?!
label: POS

text: My mother, who has never as much as smoked a cigarette in her life, decided that for her 50th birthday she would throw caution to the wind and do something that she had always wanted to do...get her nose pierced. So, this short, stubby nurse and I went to my favorite spot in town when one gets a hankerin' for a bit of self-mutilation...Cheap Trx. Her piercer was Stan, who had done a number of my piercings and was never anything short of impressive, and on this occasion he did not disappoint. I think he sensed her nervousness, and spent upwards of 45 minutes with us. He explained the details of the nasal structure, what the piercing process would entail and a gave a thorough review of all after care procedures. The piercing was quick and easy (we discovered Mom is a bit of a bleeder), and in less than a week was healed enough that she didn't even notice it. This was not simply a piercing for my mother, it was a symbol that she could overcome her hesitations, that she could do anything. Each time that we visit to pick up a new face bobble, she remarks with amazement how kind they are to her, and how welcome they make her feel. Stan and the staff at Cheap Trx gave me the opportunity to give my Mom a gift of confidence to mark her half-century of existence. And I cannot thank them enough.

text: This is the single best place in Philadelphia. I could leave it at that but I'll go a little deeper. If you are visiting Philly, you have to include Reading Terminal Market. Best to go Wednesday through Saturday when the Pennsylvania Dutch merchants are open. The market is open Sundays but a number of merchants are closed. You might think it is a tourist trap. It is to a degree. However, most of the people there are locals. Tourists can't sustain the meat, fish and produce shops that are there. So no shame, none, ever associated with it. Its not like being a New Yorker and going to Times Square for a meal. The market is closed at 6PM, which is one of the few drawbacks: it has no evening hours. I hope one day that will somehow change. Also, it can be overwhelming. Lunch rush is intense and finding a seat to enjoy that roast pork sandwich can be a challenge. I went there during lunch rush of the week between Christmas and New Year's and I have never seen it that crazy. So that's not the best time to go because hundreds of suburbanites like myself get the same idea to enjoy Reading Terminal with their day off. For breakfast the options are limited. There is the Down Home Diner which is decent but I'm not kvelling about it. Some of the stands do breakfast but I haven't really tried them. I finally tried Profi's Creperie and it is pretty good. My suggestions about food if you're there one time during a Philly visit: If it is Wednesday-Saturday, go to the Hatville Farms deli counter and get a smoked turkey special with iced-tea and potato chips. Hatville Farms is one of the Pennsylvania Dutch merchants and I swear that the smoked turkey special is the best thing in all of Reading Terminal Market. Plus, they have stools at their counter so you don't have to go looking for a seat. If it is Sunday-Tuesday, go to DiNic's Roast Pork and Beef. The line will be long but it moves fairly quick. Get the roast pork Italiano with broccoli rabe and sharp provolone. That's a Philly sandwich! Reading Terminal Market, you are what makes New Yorkers jealous of Philadelphia!

text: God, I love this place. Every time I come down here, I wonder: 1) why I don't come more often and 2) why more people don't come in the summer. Yes, that's right--this rink is open year round. I understand people don't necessarily think to ice skate in the summer, but for real, it's awesome! You can come in out of the heat and get a bit of Christmas-in-July action. Being a pale, northerly type myself, I find that taste of winter most welcome in the sweltering dog days of summer. And I can't be a complete anomaly, since the rink is, after all, doing well enough to remain operative twelve months out of the year. Public skating hours vary seasonally; see the website for a complete schedule. At just $4 for admission and $3 for skate rental for adults (children and seniors pay less), this is one of the cheapest and healthiest thrills money can buy. If you're serious about your winter sports, this is a good one-stop shop for all things icy. They offer figure skating lessons and private ice rental for curling and broomball (whatever that is), and the Pan Am Pro Shop will help you out with equipment purchases or repairs. The Skating Academy is also home to the Circle City Sirens, Indianapolis's oldest women's hockey team. Wicked!! I prefer this rink to the Pepsi Coliseum because the temperature is kept lower--I like a brisk air for my skate. Do with that as you will.

Sure you can go to a museum and see really old furniture, but there they have a little placard with some series of dates and facts, blah blah...not to mention, you can never dream of owning it. Darling, I will soon be leaving to fight with George Washington and the Continental Army. Where is my musket? Did you polish my boot buckles? President Lincoln has been shot, they are almost certain he will die. Have you heard that the worlds fair will be in St. Louis? If that kind of thing is appealing to you in the least bit, then this store is so very worth a visit. I couldn't afford a thing in it - but that didn't even matter. That seemed like a lot. But he seemed like an honest guy, and I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt. So I went for it. He boxed it up in a used cardboard box that another bike had been shipped to him in. Once I'd ridden in Hawaii, I got a shop there to ship the bike home. The folks there only charged me $150 (!?). Once I got home, the Bicycle Revolutions guy started bugging me to return the used box, claiming that it was a special bike box. (It looked like a big cardboard box to me, but I'm no cardboard aficionado.) The Hawaiian shop had returned the bike in a different box, which the airline tore in transit. I told him that, and he started emailing and phoning me, leaning on me to pay him $50 for the used box. As the barrage continued, I decided to just send him a check. I figured, at worst, I'd forestall any more communications. His gratitude for the $50: To glare at me whenever he saw in the neighborhood afterwards. (I lived around the corner from the shop.) In the end, I didn't care about the $50 (though I do still wonder about the $300 vs. $150), but I still can't fathom the treatment, especially after I'd been a regular customer and one of the first people to bring him business after he opened up the shop. So if you're looking for a shop in Philly, try Bicycle Therapy, instead. If my experience is a guide, you'll get much better service and inventory, and the cardboard boxes are a lot cheaper. text: I'm leaving this four stars, but barely. I'm leaning towards three. We arrived on a Tuesday evening when we were literally two of six people in the entire restaurant other than the staff. If it was 'octopus salad' it would have been perfect, but we really wanted to taste a touch of acrid char against that delicious tender octopus. With the Chef in the back, no excuse on this one. The Wonton Taco was the other smash dish that saved the four stars for me. The SUPER crispy airy wonton filled with the perfect blend of shrimp and seasoning was top notch. This dish was so good I could have eaten another portion right away. Five stars on this dish. The suzuki shashimi was tasty, with good size portions of fish, a nice portion of pommelo (a citrus similar to pink grapefruit) and tapioca pearls with various seasonings. It was, however, a pain in the ass to eat. Chopsticks were useless as the citrus was too delicate and tapioca pearls scattered like, well, pearls. Trying to stab it with a fork resulted in similar self-destruction. My guest was annoyed, as the overpowering garlic and seasoning in the pile of tomato salad that covered the lobster pretty much occluded the sweet taste of most of the meat. I agree, and would not order this dish again. The ice cream flavors of the evening were kit-kat and burnt marshmallow. Apparently whoever was in charge of charring and burning things didn't make it in that evening, as my burnt marshmallow tasted like vanilla soft serve, and that was it. I did get the kit-kat in the chocolate offering. These cones are fun, and I'd order them again happily regardless of the flavors. As I wrote this it hit me the inconsistency in the intensity of flavors dish to dish. I've mentioned before how I felt the truffle taste in the edamame dumplings is weak, which echoes the burnt-marshmallow in the cone, yet we are uber-garlicked on the lobster sashimi. The espresso at the end of the meal had that same intensity disconnect. It was very good, and we both LOVE strong espresso, and this was so strong that we were remarking that we could still taste it walking back to my car. It completely cleared away any flavor afterthoughts of the ice creams. So I'm still telling you to go. Try the Bahn MI, absolutely try the wontons, get the ice cream, and yes, get the espresso. text: Best breakfast spot in the city. There, I said it. At first, I was hesitant to go...all the way to South Philly? For breakfast? But what the heck...lets do it. And it was SO worth it. The server, Alexei (sp?), was incredibly warm and inviting, and we were seated with large mugs full of coffee/tea right away. No menu, save for what is on the board...4 choices, I believe. Somehow choosing from 4 dishes is harder than choosing from 40...not sure how that works. Anyway, I went with the omelette. Stuffed with steamed broccoli, onions, goat cheese, and some other tasty tidbits I can't recall (oh yea, it was BIG), it was served alongside potatoes, toast, and lamb sausage. Fresh preserves, too. Simply divine all around. I ate every last bite, and didn't need to eat again for almost 12 hours. This is not a cheap breakfast place (the bill for 2 was slightly north of $30), but worth every penny. Also, as previously noted, the decor is totally unique (and totally South Philly). Hard to describe, other than to say you need to see it for yourself. Won't find this in Center City (or any other city), that is for sure. I hope to return, soon, and dine in the pickup truck parked outside (yep...pickup truck). Lots of friendly conversation will be had (as everyone in the place is within normal talking distance), as well. If you are a picky eater, and/or the sort who always has to tweak something, you might want to think twice about coming here...Carman don't take no guff. But I hope picky eaters don't read Yelp, so this warning will likely be unwarranted. Finally, people, its CarmAn. Not CarmEn. And bring cash.

text: My boyfriend and I went to Luna Bella on Friday night. We were on our way somewhere else, drove by and decided to give it a try. The front desk was very friendly. As the hostess led us to our table she encountered a walkway blocked by a server so, she threaded us in and out of a few tables to get us to ours. In doing this we had to sidle by a table of diners and as I squeezed by, one of the gentlemen went to put down his menu and his elbow came in contact with my leg. It was not a soft bump for either of us and he turned and gave me a very angry look as I apologized. What's my point? The tables are too close together in the main dining room! We were seated in a back room that looks out onto the intersection of Fort Lowell and Swan - well it should look out - all of the plantation shutters were closed up tight - giving the effect of being in a banquet hall- While an intersection isn't the best view - it would have taken some of the emphasis off the inside - which was very "golden girls" retirement community dining hallesque. There was also a very strong smell of fish, cheese or something malodorous. I have to say I am not a big fan of restaurants that use carpet in their dining rooms - hardwood or tile are much more appealing from an odor and hygiene perspective. We also noted they are using scented candles on the tables - while I would prefer glade to old fish - it's still a no no. The menu was not quite as varied as I would have liked but, we settled on the fried artichokes to share, a rib eye for him and pasta bolognese for me. I had a nice glass of Guenoc Pinot Grigio - and we waited for the artichokes. We were served a large portion - which is often not a good sign. The breading was pretty heavy, they weren't warm and the accompanying sauce was a bit bland. I actually enjoyed the undressed mixed veggies on the plate more than the artichokes - yellow peppers, some radishes. I was really looking forward to my pasta -the menu had a paragraph about the chef, Steve Schultz, stating that he had worked and trained in Europe and even more specifically, Switzerland. Having travelled and lived in Europe, I thought this was a good sign that I would get a proper bolognese. What I did get was an enormous bowl - huge -monstrous - of pasta with huge chunks of sausage in it. Bolognese when done right has a very fine mix of veal, pork, beef, carrots - no sausage. There are probably a hundred different variations of bolognese, but I have never had it with sausage. The menu stated "chopped beef & veal" - no sausage. Anyway, it wasn't horrible or inedible but it also wasn't pasta bolognese. It had so much sausage and such big chunks it seemed like some of the pieces were still pink inside eww. I almost forgot to mention, some of the pasta was cooked stuck together and hard - pasta faux pas - not al dente. On to the rib eye - my boyfriend thought it was great - the gorgonzola gummy goo, i mean risotto, it was sitting on was not liked by either of us. Conclusion - would I go back? Not for dinner. They told us they have happy hour in the bar and am a lot less picky when I am getting things at half off.

text: I'm again conflicted about giving this identity crisis Japanese & Korean restaurant only one star, so I'm settling on two STARS. It seems that any time I show up at a Japanese/Korean restaurant, something isn't quite right. See my other review on Daruma in Jersey (see: http://www.yelp.com/biz/I67MQNC8sYjqIjsz-8bwkg#hrid:zpP1pY81x-NmF6YELUMVgQ ). I came here with extremely, high expectations. At Kabuki, I concur with Chris L. and Dave H., service is too slow. On a Sunday night there was only one server and it took almost 30 minutes for us to order after we sat down tonight at 7:00PM. (-2 STARS) I ordered two items: 1) Crunchy Spicy Tuna - nice portion and nice presentation. Excellent fresh flavor. This Spicy Tuna is not pre-made. It seemed made to order and was good quality tuna. The crunch was a nice touch. I would definitely have this again. Oddly enough, a normal spicy tuna roll is $7.00, yet a crunchy spicy tuna is only $6.50. I should have concluded my meal with this item. Unfortunately, I didn't and ordered an entree. The sushi rolls and sashmi all seemed excellent and probably warrant a higher rating. 2) Curry Rice with Chicken : This dish was a BIG disappointment. The only plus was that the Curry was good flavor and nice and spicy. Otherwise, the curry was too watery and runny. The portion was extremely generous with chicken breast meat however it sucks to have huge portions of mediocre food. That's more like a punishment. In addition, this Curry Rice had slices of napa cabbage, red pepper, and way too many sliced onions. I've never seen a curry plate like this before. I'm used to having just potatoes and carrots with Beef in my Curry Rice. Comes with White Rice and even this was poor!!! It was a little too dry and tasted old (ie not fresh) like it was made many hours earlier. The little details matter. The hot entrees come with Miso Soup and a Chilled Salad with a Ginger dressing. I would NOT recommend this dish. (-1 STAR) Final verdict: - Don't go for Korean food, there are no traditional items like Bulgogi, Kalbi, Tofu Soups, or Bi Bim Bop. - Don't go for hot Japanese dishes. - The ONLY safe bet is the fresh and tasty sushi and/or sashimi. + 1 STAR for friendly sushi chef Kenny. pix laters...

text: Formerly Manna House, they've rechristened themselves Korean Restaurant[1], and they're not kidding: they serve Korean food, have Korean staff, and you can watch Korean TV while you eat. We were greeted, seated, brought a pitcher of warm barley tea, then menus. Their menu sports appetizers, a few BBQ meat and seafood options, and a ton of hot soups. Took us some time to deliberate, then we settled on a few choices. Two of us shared an appetizer and two entrees: a plate of kimchi gochoo pajeon (tasty, and surprisingly had huge peppers in the pancake; $12.95), a plate of galbi (delightfully marinated prime ribs; $16.95), and the dependable kimchi jaeyuk bokum (~$14.95). The accompanying banchan plates were good: kimchi, little fish, bean sprouts, thin strips and large chunks of seaweed, and a ginger salad. When we requested more kimchi (free), we also got a plate of kaktugi (radish kimchi, my favorite!). Coupled with miso soup and white rice, the entire meal was more than filling; I'm eating leftovers this week... Pricing is typical for a Korean restaurant, and credit cards are welcome. [1] The Korean characters on their awning is probably their "real" name - unfortunately, transliterating Korean isn't my strong suit. For those not near Blue Bell, there's another Korean Restaurant in Upper Darby, near 69th street.

text: May 2008 Update Recently I dined here for both weekends of Jazz Fest and ate some absolutely splendid food on both occasions. Before they take their usual July vacation (and the quarterly menu change), you must have the escargot with the Chilean Carmenere. It's been a while since I had a such a perfect pairing. Garlicky escargot with prosciutto, garlic confit and smoked mushrooms in creole mustard sauce with a big, flavorful carmenere tthat exhibited firm tannins with a buttery silk finish - the best wine I have had in 2008! Note to self: get the name, then get a case or two. Try the duck duet and the fried soft shell crab with thai green curry. 9/29/07 Update Two words: Duck Cracklin' I had dinner there this weekend and had another great meal. I started off with the smoked duck salad, which was pretty damn good. The duck was tasty but the true star of this salad was the duck cracklin' - fried duck fat! The taste was unbelievably good! So smokey and crunchy, it was friggin' awesome! I wanted to get a bag of that to go! My dinner date had the escargot which was served in a puff pastry with a bacon and garlic bordelaise sauce that kicked butt. Who knew escargot could taste so good? For the entree, my friend had the appetizer sampler with the crawfish and andouille sausage cheecake being my favorite (damn good). For my entree, I tried something new: the entree sampler! It included: Smoked Lamb Chop with Braised Red Cabbage, Pecan Fish with Smoked Corn & Vegetable Capellini Salad, Seared Duck Breast with Southern Greens & Grilled Sea Scallop with Asian Slaw. While you can't go wrong with D n J's duck and lamb chop (the red cabbage was really good), my favorites: the seafood, the pecan crusted redfish and the scallops. The redfish was creamy, saucy, and truly decadent. The scallops had an amazing combo of flavor and seasonings! ----- So I have been waiting for Dick and Jenny's to re-open after their July vacation to go back and sample some tasty treats. I usually go there about 2-3 times a month. I have dined at this place since my post-Katrina return more so than any other restaurant in the city and it has truly become one of my favorite places to go and to bring friends. Time for total disclosure - I know the staff here better than most places and not just from familiarity/frequency of dining. The owners sit a couple of rows behind me at Saints games and I have pre and post game tailgated with them, and even been over to the chef's house for sunday BBQ. But first and foremost comes the food... I am embarrassesd to say that I never got to visit this place pre-K but it was always on my list of places to go. At the time though, I lived in West End/Lakefront area overlooking the marina so going Uptown for dinner was a bit of a drive, but my move to the Garden District made Dick and Jenny's one of those great neighborhood restaurants that are 'down the street'. Now I go there all the time. The restaurant is Uptown on Tchoupitoulas only one block upriver from Tipitina's - how convenient! Think of an old NOLA house converted to a restaurant, with the covered in (and air conditioned) 'patio' area where additional tables and the waiting area are located. The inside isn't the fanciest - in fact there are a bunch of painted 'plates' on the wall - but in this old city, remember fancy does not always equate to mind blowing meals. As previous Yelpers have pointed out, this place takes no reservations, so come early. Now the food - I have never had a bad meal there. Ever. The other night I had the fried oysters with slaw, the mussels and sea scallops in chimichurri broth (I know, chimichurri and seafood, but it was delicious). The oysters (which I get a lot there) were perfectly fried and seasoned and the mussels and scallops were surprisingly tasty with the chimichurri broth. I also stole some of friends portabello mushroom and blue cheese 'cheesacake' , which I have to say, blew me away with how good it was! Not being a blue cheese fan, I was a little skeptical, but it was so damn good, I kept going back for a little taste, even after my dinner date had her leftovers boxed up and was taking a cigarette break outside (sorry Michelle!). The staff here is as friendly as they come. The place is definitely a little folksy, and homey but it only adds to the experience, especially when the food is so good! I normally eat at the bar, since the wait for the bar is usually shorter. The menu changes quarterly, so I will update my review everytime I go back. Zagat's 2007 review gave the place a 27 for food, so that should help convince you that the place is worth visiting. When going say hi to Chef James and Will and Leigh.

text: one of the best seafood restaurants i've been to- a truly uplifting experience where the intricate combination of fresh seafood and colorful pallets will make you drool on your entire napkin. First, kicked off with oysters from Totten Inlet (WA) and Hoods (WA)- while the Totten Inlet oysters carried a fresh, creamy rich texture, the Hoods oysters had a unique lemony, refreshing, juicy bite (both the largest in size among a range of selection). One of the best examples of showcasing distinctive flavors of oysters from different areas in the US. Also had a bite of the first course lobster, where its lightly cooked on the outside, leaving the inside a semi-raw-like texture- amazing combination with sea urchin and oranges. For the entrees, the Skate Wing and Monk Fish rocked my belly. The pan-fried Skate WIng had a rich flavor, partnering with a parmesan broth and truffles on top. The Monk Fish in contrast has a lighter flavor- but this is carefully balanced with the flavorful lamb belly, octopus and artichoke. Finished with the Chocolate Torte and Blueberry Cobble- a simple yet regal ending. the result of the distinctive food combinations will put a smile on your face- and you won't know why until you walk out and begin to drool again. and again. to sum up: -warm, insightful service -cozy atmosphere -wide range and carefully selective seafood -creative touches on every flavor combination -pricey, but worth every penny

text: I am a big rooter for all things East Nashvillean, as many people living in East Nashville tend to be. But I'm not delusional.
