On the other hand, the service was really good -- both of the employees with whom I interacted were incredibly friendly and helpful. They offer you a choice of soup and some sesame bread with every meal, and while the soup was pretty underwhelming, I thought the bread was good. And ultimately, the stir fry was pretty good too (imperfect cooking liquid mixture notwithstanding). My friends seemed to enjoy their meals as well, including a girl who insisted that she wasn't that hungry before we got to the restaurant but finished everything on her plate. One warning I'd offer anyone planning to go there: They give you a choice between one bowl of stir-fry and all-you-can-eat, and the latter is only a little more expensive. In my opinion, the one-bowl option is overpriced considering what it is, and I'd probably go somewhere else rather than come back for that. But given how small of an increase in price gets you the all-you-can-eat option, it seems to me that they're actually offering a pretty good deal on that. So show up hungry! I'm giving this only two stars because I honestly didn't think it was remarkable, and given all the other options in Tucson, I probably wouldn't actively recommend that someone come here. But I wouldn't recommend that someone NOT come either. I'm suspecting that I'll eventually end up going back and trying the all-you-can-eat option; I'll revise my review when that happens. text: If you're looking for a genuinely romantic restaurant to woo your (soon to be) significant other, I highly recommend Violino. It's an Italian restaurant located in the upscale High Street district, in a newly renovated 1913 mansion. Inside, the restaurant is accented with granite and marble walls, and dark wooden panes around the old-fashioned windows. The suede chairs and fireplace on both levels of the restaurant add to its classic yet modern charm. My boyfriend and I recently came here for our anniversary, and I was so glad we picked this place. It's absolutely beautiful, plus I felt like a princess the whole night! The waiter did the whole flapping out the napkin and placing it on your lap thing, which I wasn't expecting. We ordered the antipesto misto for appetizers, and their signature dish, the bistecca alla fiorentina, a 40 oz. sterling silver steak with veggies and gratin potatoes. If you order this, be sure to order it earlier on, because it takes them about half an hour to prepare. Our waiter was really great, and gave impeccable service through the whole night. He suggested that we order the antipesto for one, because the servings are quite large, and we still needed lots of room for our steak. I really appreciated his help on that, because boy was he right! The antipesto misto is basically a platter of cold and hot appetizers, like smoked salmon, mushrooms, artichoke hearts, and prawns and scallops. The smoked salmon was delicious, and I highly doubt I will ever taste salmon as good as that anywhere else. I was disappointed that there was only a single shrimp and one scallop on the entire plate. They were delicious -- tender and juicy -- but we had to cut each in half in order to share them! Sorry, Violino, but you lose one star there. The steak is their signature dish for a reason. They bring it out to you on a cart, and before hand-slicing it for you, they pour some Italian brandy into a ladle and warm this ladle over a flame. Once the flame is really hot and glowing blue, they pour it over the steak, and it all looks like one big blue flame. It's really amazing, to see what you're about to eat engulfed in hot blue fire! The steak was heavenly -- so tender and juicy! It makes the Keg seem like McDonald's! I noticed a few other tables around us ordered the same dish that night too, and afterwards, the guy sitting behind us commented on how good the steak was as he was leaving. Everyone agreed, you can't beat a steak like that. I really wanted dessert, but my stomach urged me not to stuff it anymore, or there would be consequences. Our dinner came to $85 that night, including tip. Expensive, but you really can't expect anything less of this place. And for the excellent quality and service, it's definitely worth it. For your next night of fine dining, consider Violino!

text: I don't know why I do this to myself. I really don't. It's not like there aren't other sub-par chain alternatives out there. I could have done TGI Fridays. Just as repulsive, but a little closer to my house. I could have done The Olive Garden. Again, just as repulsive, but with a little more care taken in the final product. But this meal wasn't for me. It was for two friends whom I hadn't seen in several years. They like the joint and I was just kind of tagging along. I obliged happily, perused the on-line menu before hand, and figured I'd make the best of it. Ruby Tuesday's has gotten a fair amount of press of late for the apparent "upscaling" of its menu. Well you can take the girl out of the trailer, but you can't take the trailer out of the girl. It doesn't matter how much lobster you put into something as homey and mac & cheese. If some basic cooking fundamentals aren't there, then it's still cardboard a la cheese. But I digress. My friends and I gathered on a Saturday night and expected a crowd. Well, perhaps Ruby Tuesday's just ain't the hip thing anymore; the restaurant was only about a quarter full. My friends and I were seated in a too-small booth. Since none of us is terribly large, we think this may have been a two-person booth. We were greeted promptly by a very kind and cheerful young waitress who took our drink orders. We perused the menu and placed our order when she returned. She took our appetizer and main entree orders at the same time. I'm normally reluctant to do this because -- as would be confirmed later -- I find restaurants often rush out the mains after serving the apps just minutes before -- a HUGE no-no in my mind. We each ordered the salad bar with our meals and decided to head up. Honestly, this was the best part of the meal. The vegetables weren't perfect, but they were discernible foodstuffs. And, it was actually a pretty tasty salad. We each agreed this was our favorite part. The waitress brought our appetizer -- guacamole -- and I gave it one look and knew it wasn't going to be good. There were big chunks of all sorts of stuff in there. Tomato, jalapeno, onion. This was definitely not a "normal" guacamole. Also not normal was the excessive amount of heat provided by the jalapenos. The avocado had little -- if any -- flavor and I almost wonder how Ruby Tuesday's prepares this dish and if it's even real avocado. The presentation was messy, as well. Sorry, but serving something goopy like guacamole in a lettuce leaf is unacceptable. A good deep bowl is what's called for when it comes to guac! The chips and accompanying salsa were no good, as well. The salsa, in particular, lacked flavor and a good bit of salt. Disappointingly, a few minutes after receiving the guac, our entrees arrived. Simply put: How annoying! Ugh...but whatever. This meal wasn't designed to impress. For my main, I ordered the turkey burger minis. Instead of fries, I opted for a side of broccoli. What a disappointment. The burgers were lifeless and flavorless. I swear the only reason I didn't put down the burgers was because my body required a good amount of protein after a workout an hour earlier. I literally needed to shove those burgers down my throat so I would get the protein I so richly needed. The broccoli I substituted wasn't necessarily bad -- it's just it looked a mess! There were about five tiny florets scattered messily around the plate as if no one in the kitchen had taken any care with presentation. My friend ordered the 7-oz. sirloin medium well. It looked like it came out medium. She also ordered the mashed potatoes and broccoli. After one bite of the potatoes, she could eat no more. I tasted them and something was definitely off. Almost like they poured a whole canister of MSG in them -- there was definitely a taste about them. My other friend ordered some wings and mashed cauliflower. The mashed cauliflower went uneaten after one bite; the wings were greedily devoured. Unimpressed, we decided against ordering dessert; we went out into the mall and walked a bit to the nearby gelato stand in the food court and had a decent bowl of that Italian delicacy. Can't say I'll ever be returning to a Ruby Tuesday's. The generic, uninspired Americana cuisine they're serving doesn't make me proud to be an American at all!

text: So, I enjoy a good dive bar/restaurant/dumpster as much as the next guy, but there's not a lot of bright spots on the horizon here at Cap'n Cat's. The front of the restaurant is their frozen food display and take out area. This should be your clue to what's inside. You pass the shop area into a wooden paneled restaurant decorated with various nautical items.You are seated by a waitress at a table stocked with both large round and small soup style oyster crackers and a nicely spicy cocktail sauce. I should note I usually come for lunch, and I've never had a problem getting a seat. WXTU Redneck Radio plays on a sad little stereo in the corner of the restaurant that has been there for the ten years I've been coming. Pricing is certainly not bad, but then again, there are very few items that are not pre-prepared and right out of the freezer. Oysters are tasteless and bland, unremarkable in species, and when I asked the server what type of oysters they were, she replied 'raw'. Yep, silly me, I should have known that. Thank you. The raw clams are pretty much chowder clams. They are so big and tough at one point I was not sure who was eating whom. My guest could not deal with clams this big, so I slathered them up with cocktail sauce and dispatched them. Thank G-d we only ordered half a dozen. Clams casino were undercooked and had too much green pepper. You could barely taste the clam, which appeared to have been minced up. Snapper soup was watery. The stuffed clams (think deviled clams) were a hit. I'd get them again any time and just wish they were bigger, versus the cherrystone version they serve here. Worcestershire sauce and sherry accompaniments (for the soup) were provided pleasantly and in great quantity when requested. You pretty much get a half shot of sherry. Prost! I ordered the three crab special, which came perfectly cooked. Except for the dungeness crab, which was black and smelled like ammonia. Seriously. You think someone would have caught that, but nope, so back it went to be taken off the tab. Shrimp cocktail was good and my companion had the broiled seafood combo, which he enjoyed very much. Our waitress was attentive and pleasant, provided all the sauces and refills we needed, as well as plenty of napkins, so no complaints about the service. She was not a teen, nor were there any teens there today, but I know what Brian means in his review. Overall, it's not bad, and it's a guilty pleasure for my friend and I, but don't expect to be dazzled. It's cheap, frozen seafood heated up and served to you. You could do the same thing at home with the same results. Probably better in some cases. Definitely better in others.

text: I went to Midas to replace a bent exhaust pipe and fix an exhaust leak under the hood. The fumes penetrate the firewall and get into the passenger cabin. An exhaust leak can actually kill you if you leave the windows up and run the engine for too long with no ventilation. I didn't actually confirm the exhaust leak had come back until my regular mechanic noticed it weeks later, and then I called them up to fix the problem. They said that they were booked for the day. I got upset and explained to them that their work had put me at risk, and I expected them to fix the problem immediately. They told me that they only warranted their work for 30 days, but grudgingly agreed to replace the seal again. After waiting for hours, the seal was replaced. However, it was still not airtight and now I'm in the same boat again. I suspect that they didn't secure the new exhaust line properly, which is causing it to break the seal in the engine compartment. However, at this point I won't be going back to Midas.

First, the beer. Any of the beer. All of the beer. It's all great. Our most favorite of what is a truly awe inspiring selection has to be The Chili Beso, The Lemon Wheat, The Jackpot Porter, The Old Fitz Stout, the Wheeler Peak Wheat, the Ichthyosaur Pale Ale, the Wild Horse Ale and, oh, heck, whatever else they are pouring that day. But our two absolute most drop dead favorites are the Rosemary Rye Patch and the Harvest Ale. It was because of the Harvest Ale we were last at GB, as you can see from the photos I uploaded. We were there to help shell pinenuts for the Harvest Ale - for every glass you filled with shelled nuts, you got a free beer. Now, if you've ever shelled a pine nut, you know how difficult it is. But let me tell you, it was worth every bit of that hour's worth of work to get a free beer. And we have been back to taste the resultant batch, and ahhh! Heaven! It tickles me a lovely amber hue to know we "helped make" that great beer, even if it was only in a teeny tiny fashion. On to the food. Just try anything. It's all great. The stand out appetizer for us is the Jalapeno Won Tons. But be warned: they are amazingly addictive. I also have a weakness for their Willy Dillys; beer battered and fried dill pickle spears, they are outstanding with any of the beer. Other menu standouts: The Sausage Platter, the Shepherds Pie, the Fish & Chips, the Bruben, the Black & Blue Burger, the Garden Burger, The Shroom Burger, and the Pizza (any pizza). Try the pizza with macaroni & cheese and bacon. (See photos) Trust me on this one. I know it sounds crazy but you'll bite into it and you'll think you hear angels weeping, it's so good, but that will just be you and your companions, sobbing with sheer delight at your great fortune to be enjoying such soul-satisfying beer and food on a Friday night. Another thing I love about Great Basin: they've got terrific community spirit. (Thus, the pinenut shelling event!) They support all local Reno events and groups and give generously back to the community that loves them. Even though I have never been a Reno local, going into either Great Basin location always makes me feel like I am. I sit there with a beer in one hand, a pickle spear in the other, and sigh happily, thinking, "Man, it sure is great to be home."

text: I was excited about a new place opening up and expanding the choices in the Reno/Sparks area. I was let down with every aspect of the dining experience. First, trying to find the place. At the time I went the website did not have the address or a map to locate (only indicated in was in the Legends Mall). I called the restaurant to ask directions and the girl who answered the phone replied with "uhhh, I don't know the address or how to get here" Okay, that wasn't very helpful. I asked a few people in the parking lot if they knew and they directed me to a construction fence on the side of Scheels. There was a placemat sized printed sign that indicated the restaurant was past this fence. (it's in the same building as Scheels, in the back). The restaurant space feels very chain/franchise (I realize it is, but since it was a smaller chain I thought it might have more character). It's filled with New Orleans/jazz memorabilia, but the piped in music was top 40 (some jazz would have been nice), and they had several large flat panel tvs showing sports. The ceiling is really high so the restaurant is extremely loud, even though we were only one of maybe 6 tables seated. The waitress brought our party of 6 a bread basket with 4 tiny slices of bread. She brought 3 of us our drink orders immediately, but the rest of our party had to wait until after the food came out. The menu looked appealing and seemed reasonably priced. They offer 2 portion sizes on most entrees (full and "not full"), which I liked a lot. We shared an order of fried pickles and popcorn shrimp for appetizers. The 3 pickle spears were really salty and had erratic clumps of breading stuck on about half of it. It was in need of a dipping sauce. The popcorn shrimp tasted like it was frozen and reheated. well seasoned, but lacking shrimp. It was more like fried clusters of dense cornmeal based batter with a fishy fragrance. I ordered the blackened chicken breast diane (garlic mushroom butter sauce). I decided to order a fll size portion and take half home for lunch the next day as the price difference is only a few dollars. The waitress did not ask what size, so I indicated I wanted the full size. When she brought my plate it was so small that I asked her if this was a half portion and she looked panicked and said it was the full size. It was a small plate, maybe about 9 inches across (perhaps I'm used the the trend of monster sized platters) with food spilling grossly over the edges. Entrees come with Veggie Medley, New Potatoes and Dirty Rice. The veggies were soggy and greasy and sort of mixed into the dirty rice which was served underneath the chicken and one golfball sized potato was plopped on top of this mess. The chicken breast was perhaps 3 oz and covered in a thick brown gravy with mushrooms. The "garlic butter sauce" did not taste of garlic or butter, it tasted like brown gravy. None of my dining companions were happy with what they ordered. Two particular complaints were the Shrimp fettucine (was served on the same small plate as the chicken, could have benefited from a shallow bowl perhaps as it was messy overflowed the plate. there was about 4 very small shrimp) and one of the kids ordered Mac and Cheese (we were expecting a creamy southern style dish, it was a congealed dry pile of mac and cheese that appeared to be Kraft mac and cheese made with water instead of milk). We ordered a side of hushpuppies and cheese grits to be shared that never arrived on the table. The waitress made no attempt to refill our beverages or stop to check on us. We successfully flagged her down after 3 polite attempts, we requested water refill and some more bread. We did not get either until after we requested our check. We also ordered dessert, even though the meal was unsatisfactory we were too tempted by the beignets. I've had delicious beignets at Commander's Palace and even some lovely ones made from a box mix. fluffy, light, crisp, and chewy morsels. Jazz offers stuffed beignets that sounded interesting, they offer a choice of two fillings per order ( I think the choices were chocolate, strawberry, peach, and blueberry?). I asked the waitress how many come in an order, she said 2. We got one large calzone looking thing. It was dark brown and like a very thick cracker with a hot strawberries in syrup filling. gross. The kids enjoyed the little rosette of whipped cream that came in a small dixie cup though. It wasn't expensive (the chicken and the pasta were indeed both "not full" sized orders afterall), but I'm doubtful we'll ever return. So sad as we were so excited. p.s. A co-worker of mine who's from Louisiana said he wasn't impressed but would come back to try a couple staples before making a judgement. He updated and said his two visits did not convince him to return.

text: "THE MOST RELIABLE SIGN YOU CAN FIND AS YOU TRAVEL..." Once upon a time, in a land called 1960, conveniently located just off the interstate, there was a Holiday Inn. Beneath the conspicuous flashing starburst and the green and yellow display of neon and tidy, slanted script, there was a drive-thru portico sheltering various two-toned, two-tonned hunks of Detroit steel with elaborate fins and chrome trim. Inside, across the lobby from the front desk, beyond the Danish modern seating area, was the entrance to the restaurant and lounge. Jones IS the restaurant and lounge at the Holiday Inn of 1960. It is refreshing for the weary wanderer to dine at Jones - a wonderland of flagcrete (formed into columns, planters, a bar, and a fireplace), vegetation, cozy booths, cradling chairs, soothing air conditioning, and vibrant yet restrained colors that won't tire your eyes. The two times I have visited Jones, it was to briefly escape some unpleasant reality. (Much like the people at the Holiday Inn in 1960, I imagine.) I succeeded both times. From other reviews on Yelp, it is clear that the food isn't quite pretentious enough for a lot of the people who visit this establishment. FLASH: If you're going to Jones expecting haute cuisine, you are going to completely miss the point of this restaurant, and you would do well to explore other eateries. For everybody else, the food is reliable, hearty, and plentiful, as it is in your mother's kitchen. After a day of desired and undesired new sights and sounds, sometimes you simply want something familiar, even if it is only a meal. For entrees, I can personally recommend the fried chicken basket. The Thankgiving dinner is also delicious. My dinner companion enjoys the meatloaf at Jones, and, on our latest escape, was presented with an extremely generous Cobb salad. You will not leave hungry, and even if it's not the best food you've ever had, it probably won't be the worst, and it will certainly take you back to someplace pleasant that you know and love. Thoughts of your home... away from home. Our waitress was extremely attentive and pleasant. The music is decidedly not of the Holiday Inn 1960, but was very bearably modern. I actually heard a couple favorites (Nada Surf's "Blonde On Blonde," Rogue Wave's "Lake Michigan," etc.). For the sake of comfort, give Jones a try.

I had the beet salad to start, a geometrically designed plate featuring two small piles of layered beet, goat cheese and black truffle goodness with small streaks of a raspberry and Dijon vinaigrette. Then I had a Peking style duck breast with cabbage, black beans and snap peas. The flavors all worked quite nicely together, none of which overpowered the others. The one problem I had was the portions. The mini salad and the huge entree seemed like a pretty drastic contrast. While my dining partners decided to to take the light fare route by getting apps for both courses, they agreed. They were also a but put off by the trendiness of the space. Yes, all the beautiful people were stationed at the bar, and the bulkiness of the aluminum menus kept knocking over the glassware on the way-to-small table. And the last small inconvenience was the service, which was adequate but a bit clumsy and unpolished. But those little things did not diminish the over all experience though. The dining room is beautiful, with polished wood and arching, spider-like chandeliers over the bar and lounge. Everyone from the hosts to the service staff were knowledgeable and friendly. Yes it's trendy and yes you will pay for it when the check is dropped, but don't let that stop you, the food will keep you coming back for more.

text: One of the best things about Middle TN is the history. And Franklin is ripe with Civil War history so it only stands to reason that I would take the BF to experience a bit of it at the Carter House. So you pay in the front building and they tell you what time to meet on the Carter House front porch to start your tour. Then you are free to tour the museum while you wait. I found the museum interesting - personal articles of clothing, letters written home from Civil War soldiers, pictures of soldiers that died there including the Carter family member that was fighting on the Confederate side (even though the father was a Union supporter!), muskets, coffins, etc. Really fascinating! Then you can walk the grounds and see the smokehouse, the office with all the bullet holes in the back of it, and the kitchen building. I thought it was cute how they had Carter house cats too - the one had extra paws that made him look like he had opposable thumbs. Maybe he could open the door at my house like my cat always tries to do! You meet your tour guide and he starts telling you the story. The one we had definitely had a flair for drama and told everything like a story starting with lead up describing the Carter family and how the armies came to be there in Franklin. Very interesting. You get to go in the master bedroom and also the parlor area that was specially decorated for entertaining guests. Check out the molding around the bottom of the room that was painted to look like marble! Check out the rocking chair with a bullet hole through it! And then they take you out on the grounds to show you where the battle was taking place. Then you go back in to see the basement where the Carter family hid while the battle waged on around them. You also go in another bedroom too where the middle Carter son died a day after the battle from his wounds. The entire tour takes about an hour and the guides are all knowledgeable. As I said, our tour guide had a flair for the dramatic and I liked it all up until the end when it sounded like I had transformed from a tour of the house to church where they were about to beg for $$. He didn't and it wasn't like that, but I had that same weird uncomfortable feeling. Maybe I was just hungover and things struck me as weird. But he was still kickass in all other ways. Speaking of hungover, the musty smell in some of the rooms kind of stifled me and made me feel sick to my stomach so if you have a sensitive stomach or drink too much just be aware. Also, we didn't get to go anywhere upstairs. I thought that you used to be able to go up there on the tour? I might be mistaken, but when I came as a kid for field trips I thought we did. Definitely go to the Carter house if you are in town and want to learn a bit more about the Battle of Franklin, the Civil War, and history in general.

text: I've had a lot of experiences with car salesmen, but this takes the cake. My father (a 63 year old business owner, just for some back up - the guy has experience in car purchasing/haggling and sales) was going to help me buy a new car. I had a car accident recently that had totaled my car, so I intended on paying for a car with cash (including my insurance check). We had looked around at a number of vehicles, and decided to check out what kind of deal we could get on a Honda Fit. We had driven around the front and back lots and saw that there were about 20 (including 10 black Fits) on the lot. We headed into the show room and asked for a salesperson. An older man, John, came up and politely introduced himself. But, that was as far as the politeness went. My father mentioned that we were interested in seeing what we could work out on a Fit. John proceeded to tell us that there was no "overhead" on the Fit and that negotiations were out of the picture. My father said "Come on, do we still have to go through this negotiation stuff? Even with the economy the way it is?" John said "How about I give you $500 off," we said no, and stated that we'd like to talk further about it. John said "no deal," and shook his head. He told us that we'd have no chance in getting a deal on a Fit, and practically shooed us out the door. He had no clue that we'd pay cash, he had no clue that we were ready to walk out with a car that very moment. We left completely insulted. He was rude, inconsiderate and seemed like he had more things on his mind (like his newspaper) then to try to sell us a car. My father even mentioned to him "You have 10 black Fit's out back, about 25 on the lot!" and John proceeded to say "no deal." We didn't even get a chance to haggle! UGH! Yes, there is a stereotype of rude salespeople when it comes to cars, and we expect to go through the whole song and dance thing, but, that doesn't mean we expected to be treated this poorly. I advise that you take your Honda business elsewhere. I am even a previous Penske customer (two Chevys) and had never felt this degraded by a sales person there. So, this delays me buying a car another day. I'm really disappointed and we both left so pissed off at the staff that I shot off an email when I got home to Penske. Rudeness = FAIL.

text: I went to Toscana 52 for the first time last night with my boyfriend...every time we drive by this place it has been packed, but after last night's dining experience, I'm not sure why! We went in after the dinner rush, waited about 5 minutes for a hostess to seat us. While she was getting us menus, one of the owners came over, spoke to her with his back to us, and then proceeded to explain to us that "she's new, just give her a week and she'll be up to par". um...ew After we were seated, we waited about 15 minutes for a waiter to greet us, then another 10 for our waters. The decor is very pretty, very homey & comfortable atmosphere, but I agree with the comment from Lily that "beauty is only skin deep". The menu had a slight "diner" feel to them...plastic coverings. It is obviously practical but did not fit the portrayed "upscale" theme. We ordered the mussels for an appetizer, portion size was good, they were OK but bland. We never add salt to our meals when we go out, but everything we ordered we added salt & pepper to. Something I read in many other comments was that the silverware was cleared and then replaced. The only silverware that was replaced was my fork, which I purposely left on my appetizer plate. Our server did not replace any other silverware. Also, we were sitting at a four top, and the other place settings were not cleared away, even though there were only two of us. The bread was a disappointment, it had obviously been sitting for some time. And I was surprised/disappointed/appalled to receive bread sticks that I could have bought from the grocery store--still wrapped in the plastic and presented alongside the bread. My boyfriend had the ravioli, which was flavorless--and the ravioli themselves were flattened down with hardly any filling. I had the gnocchi with the Gorgonzola crema & walnuts. The gnocchi was quite doughy, too large of a portion size and my dish was flooded with the crema. The sauce was good, there was simply too much of it!! We also ordered a side of broccoli rabe, which is hard to screw up, but it was slightly tough. The broccoli rabe was the only thing that actually had flavor to it. The second side we ordered was the risotto cake--it was horrible. It was FRIED!!! When we tasted the risotto, all we tasted was cheese. It was overcooked, there was no nuttiness to the grains at all, it in fact tasted like long grain white rice! Overcooked and no flavor to it besides the cheese. I cannot believe they fried it. YUCK!! Wine selection was nothing special, mainly wines you see in the state stores and they up the price dramatically. You can get Luna di Luna for about $12 in the state stores and the price was $27 at Toscana. At least order good wines from a distributor that you don't see everyday! We ordered Robert Mondavi, because you can't go wrong with that! The waiter we had, Vic, was probably the best part of the meal. He seemed like he cared about his meal, gave us time to decide what we wanted for our entrees and did not rush us at the end of the meal. For dessert, we shared the creme brulee pie, good but it had to have been previously frozen & then microwaved, because half of it was warm & half was frozen! We were not offered coffee. Didn't want it anyway, but it still wasn't offered. At the end of the meal, another server/busser came over and cleared everything away...noisily. I might try Toscana 52 again, and if I do, I'd like to go during the dinner rush to see what the differences are at that time. I recommend spending your money elsewhere!!
label: NEG

text: We decided to try Wang Gang because of a group coupon special. When we entered the mildly crowded establishment, we weren't exactly sure what to expect. The cash registers and large flat panel TV made us think this was more of a fast food type of establishment, and we were right. After a slightly longer than average acknowledgement from waiting in the "Please wait to be seated" zone, we were sat down and introduced to our friendly waitress. She took our drink orders as well as our appetizer orders; Tom Kha Kai soup and Spring Rolls. After the waitress came back a few minutes later to take our main course order, she had remembered that she'd forgotten our drinks, no big deal, but she did mention that she was a novice and just began working as a waitress. Hmmm...Friday night, busy with lots of people...waitress on her 2nd expedition into the restaurant world. :/ We received the appetizers after 10 minutes. The spring rolls were very large although awkwardly prepared and unusually shaped. The taste was bland because the roll was mostly lettuce and had little sprout and carrot. The dipping sauce was overly tart and had a sharp after taste to it. The soup was served acceptingly hot, but not steaming. It had a rich mushroom creaminess but lacked some other ingredients one would expect from a spicy thai soup. My partner wasn't too hungry and simply ordered a fried rice for an entree, but since the expediter didn't bring it out even though we mentioned it was missing, she never got it. The waitress was very busy with other tables (full of other relatively not too happy customers) so by the time she came around, it was too late to re-order it. One thing I'd like to encourage the mgmt. there is to teach the staff to never say "the Mexicans in the back don't speak any English and that's why your fried rice did not make it to the table". :/ The other entree that did make it (called #88, $10) was described as a "classic black pepper dish with vegetables and a 3 pepper soy sauce." Since I am a huge fan of the Thai style pepper dishes, I was looking forward to a zesty chicken dish, but was served something that reminded me of take-out Chinese bucket food. The meat was sub-par and had the rubbery consistency of a take out dinner meat. To top things off and what ultimately went down from a two star review to a one star was the music. I do not want to hear country music, and pop rock music while trying to enjoy Asian fusion.
label: NEG

text: For members of two world religions, it is profoundly offensive to be offered ham. Last night I and my sisters went to Los Arcos for a bite to eat. We happily munched on chips while we waited for fish dinner. We distinctly made sure to order only dishes that had no mention of meat in the description. Everything was okay until my sister inspected closely and saw that her fish dish was laddered with pink and fleshy ham. No big deal. We'll just send it back but order something else. But here's where the problem starts. I called the owner/manager and explained that for religion reasons we cannot eat ham. I asked him kindly to take it back and bring us something else. He refused. He argues with us, "What am I going to do with this food. I cannot waste this food." He refuses to take it back even after I told him that I will pay for the dish even if we are not eating it. We asked for our checked and paid and left without eating anything. He didn't offer a replacement dish. Not even a measly salad. Worst service I received ever. My sisters are distinctly religious looking as they wear religious clothes. He owner/manager should have known that Jews and Muslim don't eat pork. Instead of being reasonable, he said he'll pick the pork out of the dish and suggested that my sister continues eat the meal. While we were leaving, the guy didn't even apologize a single time. He stood there and took our money even though we didn't eat our meal. The owner/manager also treated us in a condescending way. Before we discovered the whole pork fiasco, he rubbed his belly and asked if the food was "yum yum?" What the hell? We are adults in our twenties, not little kids. I think he thought since we are immigrants-looking we must not be able to speak English and he had to use baby-talk with us. This was funny and ironical since all of us grew up around English and are quite educated. As if this wasn't bad enough, the tables were extremely sticky. I wonder if they ever wash it with anything except remove the food. The tables also moved back and forth with slightest of force, which was very annoying. The few bites of food that I ate were not anything amazing or horrible either. Perhaps with a little bit more cleanliness and a better attitude, this place can be a visit-able place again. For now, never again! Stay as far away as possible unless you like being treated badly and like a child for average food.

text: Why, Mi Lah? Why? Why must your vegan brunch menu sound so deliciously amazing and be such an oversell and misrepresentation of the food that you actually produce? I wanted to like this place. Mi Lah is like that boy I dated who was cute and smart and funny and sweet and had two cute dogs and loved the beach and also voted for GW the second time. I just couldn't get past it to make it work with him and I just couldn't get past the disappointment to make it work with Mi Lah. I have been looking forward to trying Mi Lah's vegan brunch for a while now, reading the menu as I pass and salivating as I consider all of the delicious possibilities that are so eloquently described on their menu. My friends and I sampled the pancakes, which should not be hard to make a delicious vegan version of something so simple (relative to meat, right?). They were bland and boring. More upsetting, though, was that they were supposed to come with "blueberry butter", which had all of our imaginations going and turned out was just some kind of blueberry sauce and not buttery at all. The vegan sausage and avocado on a biscuit with (1 tbsp of) gravy was the group favorite. Again, it *sounded* amazing, but by favorite I mean that it was the most palatable of our 3 dishes. The vegan bacon was visually disturbing. My PTSD from that experience prevents my going into further detail. And the tofu omelet just left me disappointed with it's sad little half-toast points looking anemic on the side. Another issue we all had was that there was no salt and pepper on the table. Vegan food sometimes requires one to sauce it up a bit, which was certainly the case on this visit. Regarding service, the one server seemed sweet but was unfortunately spacey and ineffectual.

text: I'd love to give Slate 1.5 stars, but I think it's closer to 2 than 1 so I'll err on the side of generosity. Had brunch at Slate today 'cause the wait at Day by Day was too insane. Satisfactory; not worth traveling for (there's totally somewhere just as good in your neighborhood; I live in the culinary dead zone of the inner Main Line and Slate doesn't improve upon the local "meh" restaurants out here). Among tus we had a frittata (meh & an awfully dainty serving), eggs benedict (good, although the muffins weren't toasted so everything cooled down quickly - that's even after we sent back the first benedict that came out stone cold), the short rib mac & cheese (didn't taste it but it got rave reviews from a friend). Jam was the plain Smucker's packets you get at diners. Charging $2 for a side of Wonder Bread is pretty criminal. Service is where we ran into trouble. Three of our four meals came out at one time; the eggs benedict came out five minutes later. The waitress had forgotten our toast orders (after an extensive conversation about options - do you have rye? She wasn't sure; turned out no. What kind of jam do you have? She didn't think they had jam at all. etc.) entirely - and then took over 10 minutes to bring it out (how long does it take to make toast?). Forgot a friend's side order of home fries; those didn't come out until he'd finished his mac & cheese. It took us five minutes to flag down a busboy to send back the benedict; our waitress was nowhere to be found. All in all, Slate's brunch just didn't add up into being worth the bother. There are way too many terrific brunches to be had to spend any time or money on this one.

text: It's been a while since I dined at Chef Yoshi Chubachi's Wildflower Grill, but my fond memories of my experience have not yet escaped my grasp. First thing you'll notice is the restaurant's snazzy decor. The flower theme is repeated throughout the establishment. We were seated by friendly wait-staff, and the restaurant had great atmosphere, a buzz of excitement could be felt inthe dining room. But onwards with the food! Amuse Bouche: What an unexpected and pleasant surprise! Our amuse of the day was a poached salmon with white balsamic. The fish was tender and moist; balanced well as the vinegar perched atop gave it a nice light kick. Bread: Surprise #2. Wildflower's baked brioche came with goat and cow butter. Their brioche was hot, fresh, and steamy. When pulled open, gave off a beautiful eggy aroma. I enjoyed the goat butter the most as it's goat-y tanginess went well with the rich bread. After our bread, chef Chubachi made his rounds around the restaurant to greet his patrons and asked us how we were enjoying our meal. It was a pleasure to see the interaction and to connect with the chef behind the food. Appetizer: Hot Potato & Leek Vichyssoise - with roast corn, butternut squash and lobster The soup was garnished with basil and red pepper oils; their flavours were subtle but added deeper, fuller tones to the dish. Creamy and tasted of autumn and thanksgiving. Cockles were warmed. Crab cake - with atlantic blue crab,spicy togarashi mayo, orange and avocado salad Absolutely moist and tasted of the sea. Unlike most "cakes" you get at other places, you can actually identify clearly chunks and pieces of fresh crab. Lightly battered and fried, the exterior was nice and crisp; did I mention the wonderfully moist interior? The spicy mayo was alright, the crab cakes would have been perfect, as Guy Fieri would say, eaten with a flip-flop. Entree: Citrus Semolina Crusted Sea Bass - with northern Bay scallops, prawns, chorizo, saffron broth and a side of potato gnocchi with sweet pea and serrano ham Mmmm! Perfectly cooked and moist seafood that sat on a very flavourful broth that packed a ton of body for it's deceivingly light appearance. Gnocchi was light and chewy, lightened with sparks of green peas and balanced with the salty ham. Grilled 'Kurobuta' Pork Loin - sugar chilli cured served with creamy polenta 'dauphine', a white bean cassoulet, scampi provencal, and roasted pepper & sweet corn reduction This was a life-changing dish. I was never a fan of pork but this dish set me straight and now look to try it everywhere. I have yet to find a dish that impresses me more than this. I have never had anything so moist, tender, juicy, and flavourful. My first bite of the pork and I couldn't keep the big smile off my face. The sugar chilli marinade was a match made by Eros himself, the sweet and spicy - perfect. On top of the pork were two pieces of shrimp which were out of this world. It would have won the supporting actor oscar. Were it not for the pork, the shrimp could have easily been the tastiest thing I have eaten. Despite it's diminuative size, these little jewels of goodness packed so much shrimp flavour, I was thinking it was lobster. The beans and polenta were great too, as was the duo of very tasty sauces that went with the pork. But man oh man, I would have been happy with just that piece of loin and shrimp. I am having fond memories as I type this. Dessert: White Chocolate Blackberry Creme Brule - with gianduja chocolate ganache and fruit confit and bushberry sorbet Great end to a great meal. Citrusy fruit and cold sorbet paired with rich chocolate and my girlfriend's favourite, creme brulee, delish. But wait, there's more! Upon receiving our bill, we were given two more morsels to tantalize our tastebuds. From what I remember the white chocolate truffle was flavoured with coconut and the dark chocolate with some sort of rum. But regardless, they were very delectable and pleasant surprise (there were many of those on the night) to end a most memorable meal. What I would describe as the ultimate dining experience punctuated with many bits of unexpected goodness interspersed throughout. Every dish was very thoughtful and one could appreciate the consideration that went into each aspect, every part coming together to be greater than the whole. As a customer you definitely feel like your wishes and needs were catered to personally. I can't help compare Wildflower to the Blue Pear which I dined at recently. As perfect, memorable, and well considered Wildflower was, leaving our minds and tastebuds yearning for more to this day, it was contrasted by The Blue Pear, a poorly thought out and executed menu, a restaurant that clearly doesn't have its customers in mind that left us with a sour experience. To Wildflower - Bravo

text: One-star rating for abysmal service, compounded by the management. My husband and I saw this on the way to this week's client site, and snarked about Thai/Sushi as a restaurant theme. Based on John H.'s 'not bad' review above, we decided to give it a chance. The menu looked interesting - intriguing in some parts, and odd-to-scary in others. (Mind you, this is coming from people who have knowingly eaten "frog fat" (harsmar) - what we mean by "scary" is stuff like cheddar and strawberries on sushi. We didn't try those - maybe we should have; it would have been a more interesting experience.) The "Thai" iced coffee is okay - a decent coffee with milk, not the speedball in a glass caffeine/sugar/fat sua da (Vietnamese iced coffee) that you get in lots of other places. They offer a "Thai tea" which I can't find a description of, and "cha yen" which is the usual Thai iced tea. Sukhothai's version is watery, but it took me far longer to find out than it should have. When I ordered it, the waitress asked me, "do you want the one with cream?" I clearly told her yes, the one with cream - she still brought me the non-creamed variety, and then blamed me for the error. By the time she returned with my drink, my husband had finished his, and he wasn't drinking quickly. Meanwhile, she hadn't taken our food order in all this time. If my husband hadn't been as hungry as he was, we would probably have walked out at this point. We ordered the Kanom Jeep (steamed pork dumpling with ginger and garlic sauce) - at $7.95 for 5 dumplings in a sauce that had no discernible garlic component, badly overpriced. They were bland and unmemorable. They also were very long in arriving. The rest of our order was the Chirashi ($26.50) and #67 Mu Sarwan ($12.75). The chirashi came with miso soup and a salad, and all of these came out while we were still eating our dumplings. After the earlier delays, it was annoying to have the main courses dumped on us. The Mu Sarwan (stir-fried pork with red curry topped with fried eggplant ) was tasty, although my first piece of eggplant was too oily for my taste. Not bad for the price, though. The chirashi was overflowing with a "flower" of yellowtail, and slabs of tuna, salmon, conch, cucumbers, and octopus over tobiko and sushi rice. They draped a tightly curled tentacle over the side of the box - cute. They buried the wasabi in the corner, and I think the box was far too small for the portion - you really had to dig for the rice. The slices of sashimi were irregular - ragged edges and uneven thickness (within each slice, not just between slices!). The lighting was too dim for me to be sure, but I did wonder if it was carbon monoxide infused tuna. Fish quality over all was okay, not great. The rice was really cold, and nearly flavorless. All of this would have merely been slightly annoying, and chalked up to "inexperienced waitress", except that while we were still eating our entrees, she came by to ask us if we wanted anything else. Boxes, for instance. ?!?! Boxes? While we were still eating? And then "did we want to order anything else". She seemed to be so concerned about getting us to order more if we wanted anything that I asked her if the problem was that the kitchen was closing soon. She asked me, "well, do you know what time it 'is?" Surprisingly, considering how sluggish her service had been I hadn't been keeping an eye on the clock so I had no idea. She went back to the kitchen, announced that we had 10 minutes, and pressed again for an order. Given that we really had just started on our entrees, I begged off. She came back about 5 minutes later to ask again. Now, we'd originally been intrigued by some of the desserts (the black sticky rice with caramel), but we were sufficiently put off by her service that we demurred, and told her the only other thing we'd need was the check. She brought us the check promptly (mind you, we're still eating at this point) and then came back to see if we'd paid yet. WHILE WE WERE STILL EATING. The manager visited several other tables around us, but never came to see our table. If he had, perhaps this could all have been dealt with better. As it was, I went out of the floor-seating area to get him to come to our table, and then outlined the service summary I've written above. He apologized, told us she was wrong to rush us, she was indeed new, and promised to talk to her and to her trainer. He suggested comping us dessert or additional drinks, neither of which we wanted. No offer to comp us for anything we'd already ordered. At this point, they never came back to the table again, and we packed up the kiddo and walked out to the register, paid the bill and left without tipping. The worst service experience we've had in a long time, and absolutely the worst service ever in a Thai restaurant. The Thai culture is renowned for gracious service, but Sukhothai might better be renamed "sucky Thai". I hope they improve.
label: NEG

text: When Citygarden first appeared last summer, I was a bit surprised and not sure what to make of it. I work nearby and walk around this area a lot and was pretty stunned to all of a sudden see children playing in fountains, a random head sculpture, and a lot of random people milling about in the middle of downtown. And it is just what downtown needed. A public green space, centrally located, where downtown visitors can just hang out. You can get a good view of the arch, the old courthouse, the civil courts building, and you are only a few blocks from Busch Stadium, Scottrade Center, and Washington Ave. Not to mention how amazing the landscaping and sculptures. For the uninformed, Citygarden is a part of St. Louis' gateway mall, which is a long mostly green corridor that extends from Kiener Plaza to Union Station. Eventually there will be even wider sidewalks, with an LED illuminated walkway all the way down. That's the plan, anyway. I highly recommend everyone check Citygarden out, and it should be on any downtown must-see list.

text: Wow, where to begin? This place is probably the biggest damn hotel I have ever seen--I mean, it is so big that they have had to divide it into several different "modules," all with with their own football stadium sized winter garden attached. If you are checking in, you better get some help with your luggage, because you may have to walk a mile to your room. The gardens are quite impressive. It would be wonderful to visit in the dead of winter because it would be like a tropical vacation. There are a whole bunch of restaurants in the complex. I suspect none of them are very good, from checking out the menus (and from our experience eating in one of them). Check-in was friendly and fairly efficient--but again, I caution you to make sure you know where you're going when you head for your room. If you don't, you may end up walking for days. Our rooms were not up to par, for a place that charges as much as this place does. We had four rooms among us, and one had an inoperable TV and a toilet that seemed to have an automatic flush--except it would flush whenever it wanted to, rather than whenever it was needed. Two of our rooms had burned out or flickering light bulbs. The way the bathrooms are configured makes it very awkward for more than a single person to use at a time, despite the fact that there are two sinks in the rooms. We were there during what must have been prom weekend, since the place was full of groups of dressed up high school age kids, some of whom were obnoxiously drunk. Parking is $18 a day, which is most assuredly a ripoff. $18 a day to park in suburban Nashville, TN? I don't think so. And the final insult: when you check out, you're slapped with a "Resort Fee." As is usually the case with these types of fees, the hotel doesn't want to use the correct title: "Extra Unearned and Undeserved Cost to You that Doesn't Have to be Included in our Rate Quote so that it Makes our Hotel Appear to be Less Expensive than it Really is Fee." So: altogether, not a great experience.

We only sampled 3 items (and missed the much-cited BBQ platter) but were uniformly blown away by the quality and quantity. -Price - big bang for your bucks. -Atmosphere - not divey in the least - considering the China Town location this is refreshing. -Good beers - Singha and a Vietnamese Lager called '33' did the trick in countering the good greasy of the Vietnamese cuisine. text: If I were cool I would wear my sunglasses inside at night, in a crowded bar while listening to bad house jams. No really, thats what I would do . . . Psych Honestly, I'm pretty surprised to see how many gave the g spot a relatively solid review. Well to each his own, and if you are one of the members of the elite class of boozehounds who loves this spot, far be it for me to judge. Here are the highlights as I see 'em. Philly has a lot to offer in the realm of dive bars and shadowy gin joints. Some are cool, some are not. What this city's night life scene seems to lack is a great lounge and G tries to fill that gap. Albeit I'm new here, I call it like I see it. Lets be honest, sometimes we all like to go out and spend it like we got it . . . or at least I do, maybe that makes me weird, but hey, thats what I'm into. The problem with G lounge is that it has all the pretentiousness of a SOHO banger with none of the class. There is VIP bottle service. Its overpriced. There is a dress code. It makes the crowd seem somewhat contrived, as if just crammed into their latest swag simply to fit the part. Frankly, you shouldn't have to force people to look slick. Your spot should do that for you. I also got a good chuckle out of the fact that just throwing on a untucked collared shirt counts a classing-it-up for the evening. I will say the girls, many of whom spent some quality time dancing on top of one table or another, were consistently smoking. Dimes, top of the line, cute face, little waist and a big behind. However, I'm a sucker for skin tight dresses and high heel shoes. Who isn't right? But I digress . . . There is a DJ. I've been there a handful of times now and the MC has never put the place on its feet, there are far better places in this City for a party. The decor is fine. The doormen are quite content to make let you stand outside for a while, only to arrive indoors to find the club relatively empty - I suspect this is just a trick to make passer-bys see the line and go "Whoa, that place must be cool." Bottom line, go for the ladies, but not the scene. I'll be elsewhere.

text: From the reviews on here you would think this was a Mobil 4 star or something. We too were looking forward to eating here, but wouldn't go back. Was the food bad? No. Was it really good , NO. If La Virtu is a 10 for pasta then this is a 5, at best. Shrimp cocktail was fresh and decent size, and my Caesar was ok. Would have been better if the Romaine was chilled and not luke warm, but overall not bad. Bologonese was decent, although the entrees came out about 2 minutes after they took away the starters. My Osso Bucco, which was touted by the waiter was tough. To me , a great Italian restaurant serves Osso Bucco that falls off the bone, not a dish that you need to use a knife to cut the meat. Rice and veggies that came with the dish were ok. Dessert tray appeared as soon as the entrees were cleared. Didn't see anything we liked so we passed. Now, heres the worst part of the meal. Waiter was around all the time before we ordered. Once we started the meal there were people constantly checking to see when our plates were clear to whisk them away. I really hate to be rushed when out to dinner, after all this isnt supposed to be Olive Garden. Ok, so they like to move people in and out. Once I said we didn't care for coffee or dessert we sat, and sat, and sat until finally got a busboy to try and find the waiter. Never saw the waiter after the entrees arrived, very odd. In fact the guy that briings the dessert tray around brought the check back. Wines by the glass are really limited. When I asked for a list the waiter said...what do you want? He said they had Merlot, Chianti and 2 others. When I asked again if they had a list he said no, but I would like what they had. At that point I knew this wasn't going to be what I had hoped for, so I ordered the Merlot. When i asked what kind it was he said he would check, but he never did come back with an answer. Another thing, every glass had wine spilled around the bottom AND it was served that way. We had to constantly wipe off excess wine that was dripping from the base of the glass. I think that will tell you something about how much care if taken in their presentation. This is not my idea of a really good Italian restaurant. text: I was in New Orleans for my second time on a business trip about two weeks ago. Expensing meals is always a great perk when traveling for work--especially in New Orleans, which touts so many great places to dine. Problem is, travel budgets have been slashed since the recession so I had to keep it reasonable. For anyone on a budget in New Orleans, The Napoleon House truly delivers. And actually, for anyone who wants some true New Orleans flavor, whether traveling on a dime or not, I would suggest this place in a heartbeat. The decor is original, and when I say original, I mean early 1800s original! Despite 200 years worth of peeling wallpaper, which by the way adds a perfect touch of New Orleans mystique, a visitor can understand why this place was destined for Napoleon Bonaparte. The prices, however, don't scream nobility. We started with a charcuterie of paté, andouille sausage and foie gras, which was was only 6 bucks! And to stick with the New Orleans theme, I had a muffaletta and a pimm's cup. Both were ridiculously cheap but ridiculously good. Beyond the prices and the quality fare, the Napoleon House is a must because of its location. It's only steps away from Bourbon Street, but those few steps are just enough to remove a person from all of the debauchery on Bourbon Street. It has the type of relaxed environment that allows a person to go there wearing jeans or if the mood strikes them, to dress up, as well. Whatever your pleasure, the Napoleon House is a quintessential New Orleans establishment.

text: Mother's Day dinner at Chez Bryce. Sunday night, relatively few people and we got a great table outside. Check. Menu comes... lots of options but probably 70% of everything has meat in it. For the most part, a very 90s menu. But, wait, apparently he cures his own pork and makes his own terrine for the charcuterie plate. Kudos for that and, well, 1.5 of the 2.0 stars are simply because, if indeed he does his own charcuterie, he clearly cares enough to be running a restaurant. But... Service was an absolute disaster. Our waiter was nice enough, but he just wasn't a competent server. It felt like he was more comfortable swapping out transmissions than waiting tables. There really were very few tables, but after 90 minutes, we had only received our appetizers (I did order the charcuterie and it was simple and good). C'mon, one and a half hours for a half-full restaurant to get appetizers to us. Our waiter didn't really acknowledge the slow service until I started getting pissy, but this really didn't hurry things along. Waiting for our mains, I ordered wines by the glass from a reasonably thoughtful list. Not super-impressive, but it did show that, again, someone did care about what they were doing. However, the pours were consistently miserly - removing any sense of generosity that makes you like a restaurant... as if you can hear the manager going over and over with the servers to pour exactly 5 ounces. Main courses arrive at nearly 1 hour 45 minutes into the ordeal. I ordered duck breast "rare" expecting that they would generally overcook it. Well, screw me, I got a duck breast that was thrown in a pan for 2 minutes with a very slightly browned skin that was soft, no rendering of fat and pretty much room temperature and uncooked (not rare, seriously uncooked) duck meat. I didn't send it back because I had no faith that the cook knew how to cook a duck breast and we just wanted to get out of there by then. Duck came with an onion tart that tasted good but the tart shell was ridiculously hard and challenging to eat (make them smaller or use puff pastry). I ate the ends of the duck but ultimately asked a random server to pack it up for the dog. Mom had a couple of appetizers, brother had a hanger steak - ordered med-rare, cooked very rare... but a mediocre piece of meat. I'd much rather see a couple dollars added and use meat that doesn't taste like you bought it from Meat For Less. Passed on desert. Was charged for the wrong appetizer. Notified server and 10 minutes later he came back and said he just took it off for having such a long wait. Frankly, that action was the only thing that got him a tip. I have only stiffed 2 waiters in my life, and this was about to be the 3rd. Monsieur Bryce, not that you asked for them, but here are my thoughts: * Hire/train competent servers. Teach people how to handle customers who have to wait a long time (apologies, jokes, and if necessary, a free glass of wine or something) * Pare down your menu. Your kitchen clearly can't cope with so many things and you just don't need that many dishes. Honestly, you could probably remove 40% of the menu and customers would be happier and you would execute much better * If necessary, bump up your prices a dollar or two. I think you have room for that. * Add an extra ounce to the wine by the glass. Your cost is probably $0.50 and it'll be appreciated. * Keep fighting the good fight. I certainly appreciate you trying to provide a fine dining experience and you clearly care about what you're doing... maybe just do a bit less with stronger staff and I wish you the best of luck.

text: What a shame, is all I can say. But, let's start with the positive. The Columbus Inn has been renovated beautifully. The drink menu is great. The chef is fantastic. Unfortunately, that's where it ends. The poor management, lack of leadership and terrible customer service will be this restaurant's downfall. Here's what went down. My family and I went to the Columbus Inn last night for drinks and dinner. We had apps at the bar - a nice cheese plate and the blue cheese stuffed olives. They were delicious. The service was terribly slow - probably because all three waitresses were chatting in the corner instead of waiting tables. We were having a great time though and wanted to try the restaurant so we moved outside for dinner. Big mistake. We were seated outside. It was just like old times! We probably ate at the old Columbus Inn once a week and it was one of our favorite places to bring clients, so we were excited to be back. Unfortunately, however, there was a couple sitting to our left a tier lower that was unbelievably loud (I mean, cue Fran Drescher loud). The were shouting to a table of 4 next to them, a table of two behind them and a table of 6 right next to our table. It was like they had rented out the patio for a personal party, only they didn't and other customers had to suffer through it. Management was no where to be found and the waitresses didn't have the experience to mitigate the problem. We kindly asked them to keep it down and they quieted for about 5 minutes before it started again. At one point, one of their friends leaned over my Dad to continue a conversation. My Dad asked her to please quiet down and stop leaning over our table. That's when the couple stood up and started cursing at as - at one point asking my Dad if he wanted to fight in the parking lot. Outrageous. Still no management around. And, here's the kicker. It turns out that the four top table they were shouting with was Mr. Capano's table, who is the owner of the restaurant. We found this out after we asked several times for a manager and he finally spoke up (he didn't even want to admit he was the owner). He apologized once, went back to his meal and let his cronies try to handle the rest. We were told that if we wanted to have a quiet dinner, we shouldn't sit outside and that we were probably just breezing through town, so they didn't care about our patronage anyway. Well, not that it should make a difference, but we've lived here 20 years and go out to eat about three times a week because of work schedules. The manager finally came out - he was hiding in the kitchen - but did nothing to compensate us for our ruined evening. The only thing that made us feel better was that three couples came up to us on our way out and thanked us for saying something - they had been just as annoyed at the loud couple, but didn't know what to do. We paid our bill and left and will never, ever go back. So, folks, the lesson here is, unless you are part of the Capano family, or one of their friends, don't expect to be treated like the valued customer you are. There are far too many good restaurants in the area - Sovana, Brandywine Prime, Toscana, Deep Blue, Bistro on the Brandywine, etc. - to waste your time and money here.
label: NEG

text: If you're like me and have a hundred-plus year old home - or if you simply appreciate things that were made without an obsolesence date in mind - this should be the first stop on your Saturday afternoon home improvement tour. Linda (the owner) is a genuinely nice, knowledgable person with an eye for both bargains and exceptional pieces. The prices are beyond fair, and the items are well sorted. These are the unique fixtures and the furniture pieces that make a home truly special; six-panel doors, cast iron bath pieces, hand-hammered front door sets in solid bronze. I could go on and on. No Toll Brothers, drywall-supported condo garbage. No cute little knick-knacks to pollute your daily life. This stuff's all been carefully eyeballed and has made the cut for a reason. Every week you could find something truly different and unique - but only if you visit often. The really wonderful stuff can move fast. The fact that all the things in this place have already been loved and are just waiting to be reloved - along with the fact that they sometimes require a bit of elbow grease and know-how to reclaim completely - makes them just that much more rewarding to own. I'm not going to even mention the environmental responsibility inherent in an architectural exchange. It'd sound disingenuous from a guy who drives to work every day alone in a V8 Dodge. So I'll just say this: These are the original looks that Restoration Hardware has so cynically repackaged and outrageously priced for their portly, middle-aged-big-box-in-denial-metrosexual customers. They're here, in all their original, handmade, unpackaged glory. For the few; the brave; the irrationally, suicidally stubborn; the modern misfits capable of more than just using the tool that came in the box or calling customer service. For the lonely souls who still cling to a bit of patience, quality and pride in a lardass, pushbutton world, there's Restore.

text: I have a confession...I'm a menu reader. If I am walking past a spot where a menu is posted in the window, I have to stop and scour it, recording a quick mental notation of "would eats" and "nah, not for consumption". So, during a brief stint in my vegetarian life when I WENT TEMPORARILY INSANE WITH FOOD BOREDOM and was eating meat, I saw the Rachael's menu and found "fat free chicken stew". Score! I thought to myself as I vowed to have that very thing the next day for lunch. And it was cheap to boot for a nice portion. The restaurant is always pretty packed, so I had little doubts as to their acclaim. I ordered my stew during a very busy weekday lunch, and I waited a few minutes for them to scoop stew into a 16 oz. to go container. I looked around, read the captions on all of the pictures on the walls, went to the restroom, and had a conversation with a fellow diner. SCOOP STEW. zip zap. Apparently at Rachael's it's some kind of a mastered art. And it takes awhile. But I was excited to try something new, was salivating at the thought of something meaty, and intended to take my little stew into Rittenhouse Square to sit on my sweater and eat in the grass. And I did. I sat and smiled as the sun hit my face, opened my bag, submerged my spoon into a hearty looking feast, and almost lost my lunch before I ate it, then I got a little verklempt. You know when chicken is 2 days old and then reheated in a microwave? That taste? Yeah, that's the one. OK, it's stew. But don't treat it like "meatloaf surprise" or "chef's special casserole". That's not what you do with the leftovers. I'm all about not wasting food, but when you can tell the food isn't fresh, then the jig is up. I didn't go back to complain - usually I would, but they were still busy and I was too angry. But I haven't gone back since. I'd be open to trying their breakfast - hard to screw that up - but I won't be there of my own accord. Rachael failed me. Oye Vay.

text: I used to love this place when it was Big Guys Pizza. I knew the management had changed and I thought I would give it a try. My fiance and I usually get either a cheese or salami pizza when we are checking out a new place so we placed our order right away- a large salami pizza. We sat down and waited (what felt to be an unusually long time for a single pizza) and when it arrived the waitress almost burned us putting it on the table. The pizza was terrible - by far the worst either of us had ever had. There was waaay too much cheap cheese on the pizza and they were a little overzealous with the italian seasoning sprinkled on top. The salami tasted like pre-sliced grocery store salami and there was barely a piece of salami for each slice of pizza. The crust was thick, spongy, and had zero flavor. We each barely finished two pieces (significantly less than we usually do) and got the rest in an undersized to-go box. We thought that maybe it would improve after a night in the fridge and we could finish it for breakfast in the morning. We were wrong! text: As you may or may not know, Copia had a fire back in 2008 and they've finally reopened. Thank goodness they have because my initial reaction is "freaking awesome." The beautiful wife and I trekked here for lunch this afternoon. I'll start of saying that it was delicious, but that I wish we had come here for dinner (more on that later). The interior (normally something I don't care about) is really nice, very "fashionable upscale" -- not snooty, but rather there was a lot of thought put into it. And there are those cascading water panes of glass separating the bar area from the main dinning room. It's pretty cool, but admittedly, if you focus on them, you go might into a trance. We perused the wine list. Here's the great thing about having a restaurant connected to a wine shop -- the prices are LOW. Freaking wonderful low. Now, they do charge a corkage fee ($8), but eve with that, you're still great a pretty decent value. So, if you're a person that enjoy more than a glass or two, this is the spot. Admittedly, I didn't know about the corkage fee initially -- maybe it was mentioned on the wine list and I skipped over it, but our server explained this after we got the bill. On to the food. I had the prime rib French dip with housemade chips. This wasn't Sunday crappy buffet prime rib -- it was all meat and barely any fat. Delicious. And they put the horseradish in a condiment cup on the side, so you can heat to your own desire. I'll let the beautiful wife do a recap of her dish (the pulled pork sandwich), but I tasted it and its accompanying sides and thought it was tasty. Now, why did I wish we had gone there for dinner? While the lunch menu was very "Downtown business lunch" the dinner menu was "rival your favorite spot" interesting. Unfortunately, they don't have a web site up, but there were a number of dishes that sounded excellent. Note that while the average lunch offering was around $9-12, dinner is in the $25-30 range. Service was friendly and efficient (though admittedly, there was only two other people eating). But I got that nice feeling that our server was happy he was working there. They're still getting things in order on the wine shop side of things, but they should be offering a lot of different bottles. I can't wait to go back here for dinner, though I'll have to clean up a little bit. Not sure about things like wine flights, but that may develop as things settle down.

text: What could I possibly say about the Garfield Park Conservatory and Sunken Gardens that would do it justice? I think I can safely say that it is a big, fat jewel in the crown of my city's Indy Parks department. It is a place of Zen. This place has 136 acres and is located on the near southeast side. (Am I thrilled that this place is near my new home...? Why, yes!) Their facilities are open to the public for workshops, gardening demonstrations and they invite guests to lecture on horticulture and landscaping. The conservatory itself is a truly magnificent place to see, smell and hear. Despite the fact our conservatory is smaller in comparison, I am super proud to say that this place gives the DC Conservatory a run for it's money. (I've been there twice, for several hours - both instances I lost track of the time!) There was a horticulturalist working the day I went in and he had me climbing up on rocks near the waterfall because he insisted that I smell this particular orchid! It was a wonderful interactive experience and all the while the sounds of birds and ambient music filled the air. At the other end of the conservatory is a gorgeous koi pond and waterfall with chairs for sitting and watching them swim or just to relax and read for a spell. Outside the conservatory are the sunken gardens, which are nothing short of eye candy. There are rules here about taking photographs, particularly wedding or professional shots so you do want to call in advance before planning a shoot here. They don't mind pictures for your own enjoyment, of course! The gardens are formal - European and absolutely gorgeous. There is an insane amount of information on their website about it's history, so do check it out! I sat down in a great little bench on the far end of the gardens under a pine and proceeded to take my shoes off and read for awhile. A little slice of heaven is there if you are looking for it. I will miss this place when the cold weather comes...but hey, wait, I can go into the humid conservatory and hang out with the orchids and the koi! OM... Winter hours for the Sunken Gardens are 10 am to 5 pm / locked during inclement weather Dogs are welcome here only on a controlled leash within the park. Also see: www.indyparks.org
label: POS

text: We had a great time at the Cardinals game last week, and we weren't quite ready to go back to our hotel. We asked a moderately drunk (yet surprisingly friendly) Cardinals fan for his advice regarding a fun bar in the area, and he suggested "Paddy O's." It took us a few minutes to figure out whether he meant "Patio's," "Patty O's" or "Paddy O's." Thanks to a couple of friendly Cardinals fans and NO thanks to our useless iPhones, we found ourselves in front of Paddy O's. Literally hundreds of people congregated around the giant outdoor bar, watching the highlights from the game that had just ended. A couple of auxiliary beer carts were selling $6 Buds and Bud Lights like they were going out of style. The crowd could only be described as a typical post-game crowd. Most patrons were sporting red Cardinals gear, and some of the more radical ones wore green Pujols t-shirts. There were a few women who were clearly overdressed, but the atmosphere was very relaxed. The music was not too loud (my friends in radio would describe it as "the best mix of the '90s and today"), and, despite the crowd, the atmosphere was conducive to conversation. Standing outside on a warm St. Louis night with a 16 oz can of Bud Light (sorry, didn't mean to make it rhyme) . . . ahh, what a feeling. It made me think of my college days and our annual Spring Training trips to Phoenix, AZ; both very pleasant memories.
label: POS

text: Pho is what I get at closeby restaurants back home when I feel like a quick satisfying meal. A huge bowl full of noodles, rare slices of steak that's tender and cooked in the hot broth, the little extras that I throw into the bowl (along with Sriracha and hoisin sauce) - it always adds up to a pleasurable dining experience - no frills needed. That being said, this place really didn't live up to expectations. First off, for a place called Pho Nouveau, it was really odd to see only two pho options (one of which being chicken pho). I suppose the owners were afraid of exposing Boise natives to such exotic options as tendon and tripe. It's a shame because those are often the best pieces of meat within the pho! There were plenty of other options, though including Bun and rice plates. The place used to be a bar - so it was quite odd to come into it to see no alcohol and the bar area still intact. The restaurant felt cramped and it didn't help that the table where I sat (located next to the bar) was a bottleneck for the waittresses. Remove the table and you'll probably feel like you have more room. But if you decide to keep it, get taller high chairs. It's difficult to eat when you feel shorter than the table... For lunch I got the pho (obviously). Overall, it was so-so at best. The broth felt like it was missing... something. Disappointing was the amount of meat (barely 10 slices), but worst of all was the fact that the meat tasted over-cooked as if they were boiled to well done and then placed again into the broth. No bueno =/ I paid $10 for the bowl that was barely the size of a medium (with the contents of a small) and that I could've gotten at home for about $6 after tax AND tip. =/ Also, the water had a strange after taste that I can only describe as... plasticky. The service was also, to borrow another Yelper's description, "rough." When I walked in, it took the owner about 5 minutes to notice I was standing there before she told me to seat myself. if the place were busy, I'd understand, but there were barely 4 tables seated at the time I walked in. I usually think of pho as a fast and good meal - unfortunately, it took about 10 minutes to get my check and change. Apparently it takes 3 waittresses to figure out how to make change for a $20. Prepared? I guess not - the owner had to reach into her own pocketbook to get my change... Not sure if I'll be back again... nice try, though...

text: Tasty pints and good times. I popped in here for an early dinner and a few pints last week.
