The service was very friendly, and the place had a cozy and comfortable vibe like a proper pub (not some knock-off, wannabe attempt like you get at other so-called pubs). Regulars and newbies, alike, filled the place with warm, but not overly loud chatter while soccer (er football) played on multiple flat screens. In addition to a couple of pints of London's Pride, I opted for the haggis, which was a good, Americanized version of the Scottish treat (the S.A. uses ground lamb sausage). If I had been more hungry, I would've wanted to started with some Scottish Eggs, which came highly recommended from my friend, but I opted to use that stomach space for more beer. text: Fabulous BYOB just off South Street. The chef cooks with influences from Hungary, Austria, Greece, and Turkey. The result is delicious. The restaurant is small but comfortable, with craftsman touches in the lighting and decor. The Serbian chef/owner and his wife were gracious and friendly. There were eight of us, and we all had something different. We tried several appetizers. The sausages were wonderful--they said that people often decide the quality of a restaurant by those sausages. The smoked meat had a lot of other pickled things (sauerkraut, mushrooms, and more) that were interesting. There was a pork dish that translated means "hanging meat," which had three types of pork and was excellent. Sarma, a stuffed cabbage dish, was tasty. The bean casserole was good as well. We finished the meal with Turkish coffees which came with a piece of Turkish delight on the side. The meals were presented well, and the evening felt elegant. The prices are moderate, about $12-15 per entree. Please visit this restaurant ASAP! I can't wait to return. UPDATE: I've gone back several times, and it's still fabulous. The sausages, Cevipcici, are made fresh by the owner and are NOT to be missed. The vegetable stew was delicious. Just remember that it is a cash-only establishment. At the end of the meal, they might offer you a shot of their own homemade plum brandy, a Serbian tradition. After all that food, you won't get drunk from it, but you'll definitely feel it going down!
label: POS

She seemed smart, well trained and open to answering questions. About 4 feet from this exhibit, we were able to see just about every other exhibit, as there is NO ROOM BETWEEN ANY OF THE ANIMALS. Minute 10: We arrived at the Elephants...I was hoping to see a large area for the elephants to roam free. The only reason I was hoping this unfortunately is because I hadn't seen the rest of the exhibits. Both of the extremely depressed elephants were standing still and looked like giant versions of Eeyore except sadder and hotter. SEE Eeyore photo: http://images.pictureshunt.com/pics/e/eeyore_cartoon-4820.jpg Minute 15: We arrived at what may have once been the Lion Den, but is now a glass cage the size of a child's bedroom, right next to what may have once been some sort of make shift lagoon that could at least seem like something out of Africa, but only when there is water in it. Both of the lions were passed out and hiding from the kids knocking on the glass, trying to wake them from their dreams (which I'm sure are self induced states of unconsciousness so as to feel they are in actual nature where they belong.) Minute 20: The Giraffes!!!! Very pretty designs on these animals. And what's even better, they can see the highway from their own safar--i mean sand box (also equipped with fancy, empty water hole to make us feel like we are really watching giraffes move in loose herds on the open woodlands and grasslands of the African Savannah.) Minute 30: Can we bear seeing what the "snow leopard" is forced to sit in. Or even the Gorilla? No. So we left. Unfortunately not before seeing HUGE GREEN GRASSY AREAS FILLED WITH NOBODY. Perhaps on the 4th of July or Memorial day, these areas are filled with happy children and families picnicking. Not today. My question is this, why don't they extend some of the animal exhibits so they can walk more than 10 feet in each direction, and reduce some of the "natural parks" in the zoo. I would have asked a zookeeper but I guess they fired all of them.

text: First Impressions: Note this was my first and last visit to the Cheesecake Factory. When you first pull up to this Cheesecake Factory you are greeted by an enormous gold stucco building with a lot of windows. It over shadowed the Ruby Tuesday's a few doors down. There is a nice sized patio with heat lamps and street lamp lighting. Upon walking through the doors you first notice the high vaulted ceilings. It took everything I had not to scream Hello, just so I could hear my echo. One reviewer said they were 30 feet high. The next claimed them to be 40 feet high. I am going to jump out on a limb and say they were 52 and 1/2 feet high. The floors are of limestone and the upholstered cherry wood high booths claim some privacy. The lighting is very contemporary with amber shades on the walls and tapestry skylights. Huge columns are scattered about with amber shades of light glowing. To the right is a massive sized, glass encased counter with more cheesecake than one could ever dream about. Straight in front of you is the hostess desk. To your left is the large open dining room and the very small, yet decorative bar. Get there early to secure a stool. The lounge area has high top tables with stools. A little Cheesecake Factory History: There are over 161 Restaurants with over 50 kinds of cheesecakes. The Grand Lux Cafe is a subsidiary of theirs. The CCF was the first restaurant chain to reach a billion dollars in revenues with fewer than 100 restaurants in operation. The first CCF was opened in Beverly Hills, Ca. in 1978. Evelyn Overton sold her first Cheesecake in 1949. She baked them in her basement for restaurants and her husband Oscar handled the sales. They then opened a small shop in their home town of Detroit, Michigan. After her children were grown and gone, she and her husband moved to Los Angeles. The rest is history. Our Experience: BYOF Our server was very friendly and informative and greeted us almost immediately. Since there are over 200 items on this menu, It was like reading a textbook. She was patient with my needing to read every item. With all to choose from, we probably ordered all wrong. I started with the Baked Potato Soup. It was loaded with veggies, cheese and bacon. It was on the brownish side and tasted old and burned. We shared Fried Zucchini as an appetizer. They were your typical frozen and fried zucchini, nothing special. The ranch dressing that was served with it was unbelievably sweet. It did not compliment the zucchini at all. Hubby had a Cheese Burger, $10.95 and said wow when he first got it. He was not thrilled once he started eating it. The patties were preformed and frozen prior to cooking. With the burger came a large amount of ice cold shoestring fries. I ordered a MR Filet. It took so long, I knew it would be over cooked and hubby and I both think the server knew too. I cut into it and it was MW. Goofy looking Filet too, flat and almost as big as the plate?! She took it back and brought me the MR. I must say it was flavorful and tender. I opted for Mac & Cheese as my side. I know, I am so silly. The Mac & Cheese was one step up from Kraft. When she presented the check, she had taken the Filet off. Portions are large, prices are as high as their ceiling. The Filet was $34.95 and I am not at Ruths' Chris! We took our piece of Key Lime Cheesecake and Carrot Cake home. The desserts are very good and I would consider using take out for desserts only. They also ship Cheesecakes via Federal Express. Three managers sat together at a high top table in the Lounge. One young attractive server entertained them the entire time of our visit. Not once did I see a manager get up to greet or check on a table. All three were very young and I am sure there for the easy paycheck. If and when I ever receive $50.00 in Gift Cards for the CCF again, I will order Cheesecakes to go. That is how they started. That is what they specialize in and they do know how to do it right. As for the 200 menu items, it is a chain, what did you expect? Come on Toni, come and say " I told you so! " ;+} My Dipping sauce for Fried Zucchini, Onion Rings, Fried Mushrooms: 1 part mayo, to 1 part sour cream, to 1/2 part horse-radish.

text: This was my first apartment in Tucson. I didn't know any better then. There are a lot of car break-ins, but I never had any problems, possibly because I was driving such a beater at the time. I lived in a tiny studio with a bedroom area separated from the living area by a huge cabinet sort of thing that came with the apartment. Next to me was the guy who I could hear having sex at least three times per month (I would hope that he got more action than that though) and then bang on the wall when I played the stereo during the day, the other side was a creepy drunk redneck who would always try to talk to me, and below was a college kid who would have 100+ people parties spilling out of his 400sf apartment. Fun times at that Promontory! The managers were possibly the biggest jerks I've ever encountered in renting. I once turned in my rent check on the morning of the 2nd and was given a late charge of $35. I would complain about things and would mostly be ignored. The grounds are immaculately kept, likely in order to deceive you into thinking that this is actually a good place to live. There are tennis courts, pools (usually frequented by creepy guys) and on-site laundry, the latter of which is overpriced. It's nice that it's on a little street behind a strip mall and in a desert area, but there were always issues with getting out of there. For one, there was a traffic light at Stone and River that you could use, but people turning left from Stone onto River would always ignore the fact that you were there and there were quite few accidents as a result. The city finally changed the light to create a delay on the signal from Stone and that has alleviated the problem. Not sure if things have changed since I've lived there, but I really doubt it. I went up there about a year later to help a random son of a friend of a friend and tried to talk him out of it, but he said it was okay (but he also knew everything about anything, which was pretty amazing), and it actually looked a little worse. More shopping carts, more abandoned cars and people still flying through the ridiculously large parking lot. It's just better not to rent at a larger complex in Tucson unless you're absolutely sure that it's a good place. This one is definitely not one of those good places, and remains the second worst apartment complex I've lived in.

text: My first time eating one of their wraps was late last week. But I made the foolish mistake of thinking that a pita-based place might be good for traditional pita wraps, namely the gyro ($7). It was disappointing. I should have gone for more typical sandwich fillings, I've heard the caesar salad wrap and the BLT wrap are good. A co-worker got a grilled chicken wrap, and her extra sauces ended up in my order. Also, she said she felt "a little gross" afterwards, so both of us weren't overly pleased. In defense of the delivery, I'm sure the bulk arrangement was confusing and stressful to the Pit person, so I'm not knocking them for a little switcheroo action in some orders. Also, I should note that a third co-worker had a lot of trouble navigating the website ordering system, especially backing out and trying to adjust his order. So, whether you find the online system user friendly or not is quite subjective. But, I'm not crazy about the food, and the convenience of ordering/delivery cannot compensate for that. text: I really hate to give a bad review to a local East Nashville business. Being an East Nashvillian myself I do appreciate the idea of a Vietnamese place on this side of town and was very happy to find it existed. So tonight was my first visit, and sadly my last. I will preface by saying that I have traveled to Vietnam recently and ate some spectacular food there, and also have lived in Atlanta where I basically spent all weekend on Buford Highway easting various Vietnamese standards. I will also point out that Far East is not true Vietnamese but more of a fusion and that is cool with me. The unfortunate side of this is that they fail at all attempts. My party ordered 1 appetizer and 2 entrees. We started with the cold shrimp wraps and they were par for the course, but the rice wraps were a bit chewy, which sometimes can happen anywhere. The real upset was the Shakey Beef (Bo Luc Lac) or properly call Shaken beef due to the method in which it is cooked; super high heat with rapid shaking of the wok. Their version was unfortunately very bland, meat was rather tough, and overall just sucked, oh and lastly if there was 3 ounces of cubed beef I would have been surprised. On a scale of 1 to 3, its gets a 0. The second entree ordered was Bun (rice noodles) with Tofu, generally bun is filled with various herbs, cucumber, bean sprouts, and other goodies. This version did include these item, but minimally and overall just fell short of any decent Bun out there. The flavors again were bland and the rice noodles which were served cold seemed a bit old. Interestingly, while we were there, almost every table was sat but I am certain everyone left hungry. Even more disappointing was the fact that the desserts they were serving didn't match the cuisine at all. I will give the 1 star for having the proper Pho condiments on the table and Tiger Beer. I think if the owners of this establishment bring it back to the roots and basics of Vietnamese cuisine they can really bring some unique bits to East Nashville. However, what they are dishing out now is a poor representation of the real tastes of Vietnam.
label: NEG

The plus was that we were there to celebrate a birthday, and they had a man playing guitar and serenading guests - we requested he sing Happy Birthday at our table and that did the job of embarrassing the guest of honor as intended. text: What a waste. I love playing golf, and will play any opportunity I get, but some times it just a waste of time and money. The guy at the register also has problems ringing people out, it shouldn't take five minutes for a solo to purchase 3 balls, and pay for greens fees. There is people out there, and another guy is hitting his driver right at them, and since the driving range area is not fenced, even when you are playing a round you still have to be cautious of stray balls. text: Danger!! Keep away!! You'll be killed then BLAMED for your own death. Do not get your flat tire or anything else repaired here on a Sunday in late October. Better yet, never go near a Canadian Tire service centre at all. While on her way to Lloydminster from Calgary, my daughter Claire went here in desperation on a Sunday afternoon, Hallowe'en actually. After a long wait the Canadian Tire boys finally took a look at her leaking Michelin tire on a 2007 Pontiac Torrent, patched it and sent her down the road. Within 30 minutes of leaving Canadian Tire the low tire pressure alarm sounded. It's a good thing she has TPM (tire pressure monitoring) on that vehicle. Claire managed get back to the Fort Road Canadian Tire to have the tire fixed properly and what does she hear? "It's too close to closing time to do anything? Sorry miss?" That was the story but they did remove the tire to perform a quick soap bubble test, declaring the tire to have 5 separate leaks now. Oh no! Panic! Got to go to work Monday in Lloyd. "Too bad chica, we're punching out." So they put the tire back on the Torrent without doing further repairs and sent Claire on her way... to DOOM. Within blocks Claire decided something was wrong and luckily stopped. It turned out the Canadian Tire boys had re-installed her wheel using only one wheel nut. That's one of the 5 wheel nuts they had just removed. Question: If she survives, what's a young working girl supposed to do in Edmonton on a cold dark Hallowe'en Sunday evening with one leaky tire, 4 missing wheel nuts, stranded at the side of the road 2 1/2 hours drive from home? Oh right! Call your dad in Calgary, he'll know what to do. I wanted to choke someone when I heard what had happened. In desperation we decided to borrow one nut from each of the other three wheels, then jack up the problem wheel and install the 3 borrowed nuts. I cleared this solution with my BIL (brother in law) Terry in St. Albert, a mechanical engineer. On the phone, Claire told me she hadn't thought to inspect her RR wheel before leaving CT; before driving off. How tragic. Here is a young girl thinking she is somewaht to blame for the negligence of CT. I wonder how many drivers think they should inspect the work of their car mechanic. It cannot be many, or wouldn't we be doing our own auto repairs? So, was this criminal NEGLIGENCE? Maybe some lawyer out there could say, but I know one thing, it's GROSS INCOMPETENCE. It shows a complete lack of concern for the safety of the public. Next day, still in Edmonton, now missing a day of work, Claire went downtown to Central Tire and had the tire expertly repaired by real tire people. They assessed the patch by Canadian Tire as AWFUL and professionally repaired 2 punctures, not 5. No further problems. Oh yeah, earlier in the day Claire went back to the Fort Road Canadian Tire, and when informed they had failed to properly reinstall and torque up the RR wheel nuts they REFUSED TO ACKNOWLEDGE THEIR GROSS ERROR. Hypocritically, they suggested my daughter must have removed the wheel nuts herself. WOW!!! A new LOW benchmark for personal and professional ethics is established. I like Canadian Tire for their merchandise but for goodness sake, any enterprise with TIRE in their name has to be better with TIRES. This dreadful performance could easily have turned tragic. I wonder, what will it take to get the management of Canadian Tire to wake up? YELP maybe?
label: NEG

Then, after waiting for another 20 minutes, our entrée's were served. We asked about the salad course and the waitress said "Oh Shit" and rushed to the kitchen to serve them at the same time as the entrée. We checked the entrées - pheasant breast, salmon wellington and rack of lamb - they were all stone cold and inedible. I asked to see the manager and again waited 5 minutes. I told the hostess that if a manager didn't appear in 5 minutes we were leaving. No manager so we left; and were chased down the street by a manager who had suddenly materialized. I said I would pay for the drinks we had but nothing else. He was surly and very un-apologetic but said OK. After getting the check, I found he had added one of the entrée's ($50) and threatened to call the police if I didn't pay. Since I had 2 young children who were hungry and upset, I paid and left to try to find another restaurant who could serve us. I intend to contact my credit card company to recover the cost of the manager's extortion. This may be an OK restaurant for tourists who probably won't return but everyone else should steer well clear.

text: Though I've never experienced bad "service" here, the food has never been quite what I expected. The salsa is SO good, you get Pico De Gallo that has a little bit of a smoked taste to it, and a salsa verde which is equally as good. The chips are salty. But so good. I have found bones in my chicken burrito on two separate occasions here. I've had crunchy rice in my burrito. I've had a brisket that was 99% fat. I know brisket comes with some fat on it, but this was the fattiest brisket I've ever had. It was not good. Texas toast tasted like it had been microwaved instead of grilled. Taco salad had awesome toppings but the dressing was too tangy for my liking. My boyfriend got the nachos, which were AMAZING. I would definitely recommend the nachos. They're huge. They could easily feed two people (which they did, considering my food was so bad). They have an OKAY beer list....and the Texas Tea is great. To be honest, if you want really great mexican food, just walk two blocks down to Dos Segundos. ....Maybe El Camino is better for their Tex than their Mex?

text: Too many bad reviews of this place and wanted to do one from our experience last night. Read the reviews and took a chance because could not find an easy to find buffet that had crab on a Wednesday night and was craving it. Anyway...if you are out of town, this place is a little bit off of the beaten path, but is well worth the drive considering the casino buffets you are looking at 1-1.5hr wait and double the price. For what we paid, they had crab, oysters, nothing special sushi, sashimi, pretty much everything typical of a Japanese buffet. We were there for all you can eat sashimi and crab so we had no problems. The hot table had the usual fare and I didn't give it much thought as you can get standard stuff (Beef and Brocolli, Sweet and sour pork, fried rice, etcetc) at any chinese restaurant. It is similar to #1 Buffet or Kawa in Sacramento but smaller scale and way better service! Staff was nice..our waiter tended to us regularly. Everything was clean, tidy, and modern (by buffet standards that is). We were there around 5:00 and were a little concerned that there were only a few families in the restaurant. Around 6 it seems the locals start rolling in so don't be afraid if you don't see anyone there, you just might be earlier than most. With that said, the food was good but not the greatest. Nothing horrible...everything was just as it should be. C'mon...its a buffet! 3 stars for the food. Extra star for no waiting in line, staff, and service! Lastly...some of the reviews refer to this place as a chinese restaurant??? Not sure if they know what a real chinese restaurant is like (and I'm not talking about Panda Express...those dont count)..but this is not a chinese restaurant! Its a Japanese buffet! We're from out of town and we'll definitely stop by here on our next trip.
label: POS

text: I went here with a gift certificate and oh my goodness wow. They had such a variety of fondue that the knowledgeable server had to go over the entire menu with us and explain. Then a mixture of meat, shrimp, veggies, and pasta pouches to dip in coq au vin, the dip that we chose. Then dessert, a mouthwatering medley of pound cake, brownie, strawberry, banana, rice crispy treats, and odd marshmallow dippers. They also brought out cheese cake with a cherry on top. (I got extra cherries upon request!) We were stuffed to the gills and had to roll out. All in all a pleasant experience, helpful staff, clean eatery, gorgeous bathrooms, (I went twice just to use the mouthwash!) and cozy seating. The prices are high, about $40+ per person but so so worth it.

text: FOR NOW this market only gets 4 stars from me JUST because it's still new and GROWING. That said, the one farm that's there so far is GREAT. The Amish farming family running it is lovely. We have also tried several of their baked goods + watermelons, plums, grapes, and cantaloupes. All have been VERY fresh and super-DELICIOUS. We think the locally made Swiss cheese is SUPERB too. They're open every Friday from 3-7pm. It's also really wonderful to see how this market has brought out the community. Julian Abele Park is still growing and the market has only been open since June 25th 2010, yet already there has been an impromptu blue grass jam session there to celebrate Farmers Market Week last week. Folks just brought out their guitars, voices, etc. and it was really heart-warming.

text: My partner and I ordered from Phoebe's for the first time. Delivery. We both had combo platters and ordered a side sampler just to know what the sides taste like. Overall it was okay. We debated on whether or not to keep the menu. I ordered beef brisket and pork ribs. Mine wasn't even correct. They have an unoriginal method of writing the orders, so PR (pork ribs) looks a lot like PP (pulled pork) when poorly handwritten. However, the pulled pork was really good, and the brisket was terribly disappointing and fatty. The mashed potatoes were great, the greens between bad and okay. My partner ordered beef brisket and pulled pork. His order actually arrived as ordered. He liked both meats. His brisket looked totally different than mine, good and meaty. He thought the pulled pork was great but believes he can make better. He found the cole slaw and candied yams bland and boring. The side sampler contained BBQ beans, potato salad, and roasted vegetables. The best way to describe it all is nondescript! They all tasted as they were named. Nothing special. We both found the "cornbread" to be more like cake. I didn't grow up eating sweet cornbread, so I know that makes a difference. But there's sweet cornbread and then there's cake... I gotta call that cake. My partner still liked it even though it was so different. I'd like to actually try the ribs that were supposed to be there. The BBQ sauces were good. More on the vinegar side which I prefer. The hot one wasn't so hot that we couldn't enjoy the spice and flavor. In the end we decided to keep the menu.

text: My date and I shared a very enjoyable meal here last night. We ordered the Foie Gras (a nightly special), the grilled Kobe New York steak and the Blood Orange & Mint-marinated Chargrilled Rack of Lamb. The food at Bouchon is not about inventive preparations or exotic ingredients, rather, it is accessible and flawlessly executed. The space includes both indoor and outdoor seating. We sat inside, though both areas seem very comfortable. The service was friendly and inviting, especially the owner, who greeted us and decanted our wine. The reason I'm not giving Bouchon five stars is their wine list. I understand and expect some wine markup at any restaurant, but many of the bottles at Bouchon are marked up well over two and a half times their retail price. Luckily, I reviewed the list before we went and brought a bottle with me. None-the-less, their $25 corkage fee is an embarrassment, unfortunately tainting an otherwise splendid dining experience. (An aside: Buchon's butter, Plugrá, is great, though a staff member told us it's Italian. Plugrá is made by Keller's Creamery, in America.)

text: Rating c 2 stars out of 5 Everyone has to eat sooner or later, so we might as well talk about it. Agree or disagree, your replies are valued. Please allow me to preface this review with 2 comments: 1) The ambiance and feel of Bella Luna, was for me, awkward and more than a little bit dated. 2) It pains me to give any restaurant with heart a negative review. Their hearts are in the right place, the food and service? Not so much on the night we visited. It was a Friday, and we met the in-laws for a birthday celebration. We had reservations for 7pm and it was a "dark and stormy evening" in Tucson (not something we get to say very often). We arrived on time and had taken a moment in the car to read some of the evenings' specials on-line. My better half commented on the special menu seeming a bit heavy. Little did she know how prophetic that observation would turn out to be. I don't know if any of you recall Pee Wee Herman's Saturday morning kids show with the secret word? Every time someone said the secret word of the day, everyone screamed and the secret word would drop from the ceiling dangling on a piece of string. The secret word for this restaurant: HEAVY. We walked into what I can only describe now as one of those awful Vegas-styled Holiday Inn lounge act duos performing in the bar area. You know the kind, he plays an electronic keyboard that doubles as a karaoke machine and she sings along. I asked to be seated as far away as possible. I want to be clear here. Put him at a real piano and her singing some jazz standards with an occasional cool cover song and drop the quasi Karaoke and I would have loved them. They did not suck; their show did. One other issue I had on arrival. When I place a reservation at your fine dining establishment, I like for you to not be apparently stunned when I actually show up. I wasn't sure if it was that they were stunned I personally showed up, or if it was they are generally stunned when anyone shows up for a reservation. We stood for fifteen minutes while the hostess scrambled to turn a table for four into a table for four and then sat the five of us at it. The Service? A clearly overwhelmed, under-trained and under-supported staff did their very best to accommodate us. I'd like to also say that our waitress deserved the 20% she received. Some hints for Bella Luna Owners and managers: Asking about getting a table drinks at a fine dining establishment without having provided the table with your wine list in advance is an amateur mistake and is indicative of a lack of training and support. It's really stupid to not give me a list of things for me to spend money on. In most restaurants those are called the main, wine, and dessert menus. Not having enough staff to help out or even wait on your reserved tables means you aren't in the game to win. You failed your staff miserably and if I were them, I would ditch you. One of the ways to placate customers that are waiting too long for a table is to ask them to please have a seat at the bar while you "make arrangements". It takes the heat off of you and us, plus I am a lot more fun, generous, and hungry after a couple of drinks. Since you had no bartender behind the bar I think it might also be the reason you have no patrons at your bar. Zip, nadda, not a soul at the bar. Again, my experience in the hospitality industry tells me that bars are only effective at generating income when you have a bartender standing there ready to take an order and then the cash. While we are on the subject of alcohol. When you bring wine to the table, there is no excuse for not having "red wine" glasses available. Of course, on a camping trip I will drink wine straight from the bottle, but we weren't on a camping trip, were we? Now lets discuss two more things that should never occur in a dining establishment that wants to get more than $20 per plate. 1) It is not OK to seat one table so close to another that your wait staff has to yell at us to be heard and has to do a complicated contortionist act in order to be able to place items on the table. 2) When it comes time to serve dessert it is not OK to plunk down a handful of silverware in the middle of the table for us to scrap over and then scurry off. On this night, management was entirely missing. No one in charge was marshaling or supporting anyone. I had the rest of this posted at my website and Yelp made me take down the link, sorry.

text: Franklin Square, home to Franklin's famous kite experiment holds a very special place in my heart. Growing up in Chinatown meant staring at blacktop. There was no picnic area or even a chance to walk barefoot in the grass, let alone play catch or toss a football until one day, my friends and I wandered outside of our "play area" as most children do and discovered a park full of green. This was our escape! No longer did we, did I go without the smell of morning dew, the mushy feel of leaves underneath my feet and the field that would be my diamond. It was far from perfect.. Broken concrete, a weathered and rusty jungle gym and dry grass. But we didn't care. It was our park!! Then lo and behold, Once Upon a Nation transformed the park to what it is today- a restored green space complete with astroturf and playground equipment for all ages including infants, a carousel where one of the horses is named Smarty Jones and a 18 hole mini golf course that includes ringing the Liberty Bell with a hole in one. With this face lift, I can't even imagine how many more children will create their own adventures here and claim this park to be their own. So no matter what your age, join in on the fun! Oh, the places you'll go!

text: "Dirty Country" Crusted meats: ok. Crusted cheeses: sure. Crusted placemats? Welcome to Carman's, where country and cleanliness are but two forks in a filthy wood. Cream for your coffee? Let it flow briskly from a breast-shaped pitcher complete with mother's crusting 'round the nip. Time to order? No need to commit to sweet or savory, because with lush fillings like goat cheese (or was it ricotta?) blended with cinnamon and red peppers, you get it all. Visual diversions while you wait? So many to choose from! Say, for example, the bold ceramic penis cup broken at the base, then reglued for - perhaps - another round at the rodeo. Or, the terrifying, tiny Venetian glitter mask, placed dead center on the main wall. In a horror movie its eye sockets would be threaded with fishing line, and like the blackest flesh-tearing raven, it would swoop toward you until your mouth wobbles open to a Sissy Spacek scream. BUT DON'T LOOK DOWN. Because your food has just arrived, and that's the scariest thing of all. In an homage to a post-Katrina world, it's an overweight mass of thick, tomato-strewn egg, submerged in bilge water. The extra water splashed up from the dish sink over the counter and onto your plate is entirely complementary. Feeling ill? Perhaps you'd like a moment alone, say in the bathroom. Or perhaps you'd prefer the kitchen. Good news - no need to choose! Because sanitary sakes alive, they're more or less the same room. Next time I want dirty country I'll skip Carman's and ... actually, I'm too much of a lady to tell.
label: NEG

text: I was really looking forward to trying this place out. Unfortunately, I came away disappointed. My wife and I went on Sunday the 5th of July around 7:00 PM. When we walked in the bar was full, we ordered two Warsteiner Pils and attempted to stand behind the seated customers at the bar, however there is not enough room to stand there and still allow the staff to pass by. We decided to get a table. The hostess sat us right away and the server followed on her heals. He gave us menu's and walked away...only to return one minute later, asking if we were ready to order. We said no and asked for a few minutes. Another minute later he was back again, we quickly picked two apps. Potato pancakes and the smoked fish plate. They came out quickly enough. The potato pancakes were very good except for the very center, which was not completely cooked. The smoked fish plate came with rye bread that was an hour from being stale, smoked salmon, which was pretty good if not expertly sliced. The other two fishes were a bit of a mystery to our server, he thought that it was cod but said that he was not sure (never a thought to go ask!) One was trout and the other was most likely sable or other similar white fish. While there was plenty of Salmon the others fish was served in tiny little itty bitty pieces that were dried out almost past the point of being able to identify as fish. They really should put some sort of "lube" on the plate, sour cream, creme fresh, something to help the dried out fish on dry bread go down! Beer turned out to be the only substitute readily available. The applesauce (w/ potato pancakes) was great! as were the pickled onions (w/ the smoked fish). As soon as the apps arrived our waiter returned to take our entree orders. My wife said that she still needed a minute and that I knew what I wanted. The waiter turned to me and asked "well what do you want?" I ordered the Wiener Schnitzel with braised red cabbage and Spatzle. Feeling very rushed, my wife decided just to have a house salad. The food arrived. My pork cutlet (Men's size 6 1/2) featured very bland breading and the scars of a long hard life spent in the fryer. I loved the braised red cabbage! The spatzel was decent to pretty good. My wife's salad was very good except for the fact that most of the Romaine and spring mix had brown edges, it must have been prepped in the morning. Our waiter returned and seeing that my wife's beer was empty, offered another, she declined instead asking for a glass of water. He left without inquiring about the mounting pile of brown edged lettuce being assembled on an as yet to be cleared B&B plate. This would be his second longest departure of the meal. Five or six minutes latter he re-appears and notices that my wife has no bev glass in front of her asks if she would like a glass of water? He returned just as I was finishing my meal, my wife was already done. He cleared her plate and stood there while I finished my last few bites of the red cabbage. As I was chewing the last of my dinner my plate was whisked away, along with our request for the check, which he dropped promptly. My wife gave it a quick scan and put a credit card in the check holder with the edge protruding and placed it on the edge of our table. Just our luck that Speedy Gonzales decided that was the perfect moment to take a siesta. We do not see him for close to 15 minutes. I hope that the food issues are just teething pains but I'm not holding my breath. There is no excuse for such a poorly trained staff member. If you go and have a server with a name that rhymes with Knave, change tables! We will wait a few weeks and give the place one more shot. As I said I was really looking forward to this place.

text: I am still trying to process exactly what happened last night, the first time I ever practiced bikram yoga at Bikram's Yoga College of India. Let me start out by saying that I am experienced with yoga, having been practicing almost daily for more than a year. I had never tried bikram yoga before and was intrigued by the concept of stretching in a hot, hot room. Needless to say, I did not read up on the history of bikram until this morning, after my experience with it. Had I known that the practice is rooted in the 1970s United States, I might have given it more thought, or perhaps not gone at all. The reason I say this is because to me, being in Sandy's 5:30 class was like being in boot camp. Which is not why I do yoga. Her shrill, repeated commands seemed to juxtapose the calming, yet firm, voices of my previous instructors. There was absolutely no zen in this place. My class was 41 people, most in tiny spandex shorts and sports bras. It was a little intimidating, not even going to lie. I walked in to the large studio and was greeted by people lying down in a restorative position. The room was dark and warm. I put my mat down in the back of the class, as I was instructed by Sandy not to block anybody. People at the studio seemed to be in their own worlds, not so much mindful of those around them but really concerned with the reflection in the wall mirror. The class itself was 90 minutes. The last third was probably the worst. I felt like I could keep up with what we were doing, and was not afraid to let myself breathe and go into child's pose in between rough patches. While Sandy said at times that we had to be honest with ourselves and our limits, there was a tone that we also had to push ourselves past our limits. The class was very fast-paced, abrupt, harsh. At the end of the class, to add insult to injury, Sandy told the class to congratulate the new folks. Naively expecting a unified "Namaste," to my own dismay, everyone started clapping. For some reason, it felt so wrong to be congratulated like that for doing yoga... But I think that that is what this practice, based out of Hollywood, California, is rooted in: cultivating and celebrating one's physical prowess and physique to an excess - marked by the heated sauna you practice in. My sense from attending just one class is that bikram yoga is more of an exercise in vanity than the spiritual, holistic, and emotional healing that I find so powerful in other forms of yoga. Now that I have slammed it, I would like to (try to) be fair and say that it is not as if I did not *enjoy* doing bikram to some extent. It felt really nice to feel my body sweat, to feel my muscles get seemingly more pliable in the heat, to take myself to a limit I do not encounter every day. I did find it useful to encounter the force of heat and realize that yes, I can withstand this discomfort. Sandy is well-rehearsed and even in a class of 41, she provided one-on-one attention as she saw fit (pun unintended). All in all, I will be back for my intro week - and will perhaps amend this review after experiencing more - but for now, these are my first impressions.

text: While planning my trip to New Orleans I know I had to hit one culinary hot-spot. Craving Cajun/Creole fusion I though NOLA would be a perfect fit. I read the menu and researched reviews and thought it sounded perfect. The night of our dinner we arrived and were promptly seated. Overall the decor was a bit drab in my opinion. Orange walls, brown tables, yawn. My whole view from my chair was of a wall. I am a firm believer that every seat in a restaurant should be the best and one should avoid seating customers by bathrooms, busing stations, etc. I was not overjoyed to be staring at an empty orange wall all night. Our waiter was suave and confident, a bit too suave and confident in fact. He read the menu to us as though we were 5 years old. We asked for recommendations of other places to see in the city, he announced to us since we looked the "the kind of girls who only want to shop, we should check out magazine street". We came to New Orleans for the history, architecture, culture, and food, not the malls thank you. The bread selection was a let down to start. The jalapeno cornbread was just nasty, the flavors did not marry well. The onion loaf tasted stale. For appetizers I had the brie cream mac and cheese and my date had a salad with pistachio crusted goat cheese. The salad was good, but, forgettable. The mac n cheese was very sub-par, I had to keep loading it up with salt just so it could have some flavor. We both ordered the roasted duck with honey caramel sauce, it was awful. The duck itself was amazingly cooked, so moist and tender you didn't even need a knife. But, it tasted like it had been cooked over a campfire. It was so smokey, I actually coughed after my first bite. The smoke flavor was so overwhelming you couldn't even taste the honey caramel sauce. The veggies that accompanied it were so undercooked, they tasted raw. To top it all off the "bananas foster bread pudding" was the worst bread pudding I have ever had. There was nothing "bananas foster" about it, I don't even think there was one banana on the plate! The pudding was hard, not warm, and had not interesting flavor or texture. Overall it was a very disappointing dinner and I am sad I wasted my little time in New Orleans there. I paid a hefty price for a meal I hardly enjoyed and we got out of there so fast, it was such a forgettable evening. Where was the BAM?
label: NEG

text: the look and feel of Dish is much more overwhelming than the actual dishes. i love the concept: small, few tables, limited crowd... the menu sounds unbelievable - but the food doesn't follow up. i will say that the fried lobster tail appetizer and the roasted pork appetizer were great. i highly recommend getting some wine and picking at the apps all night. we ordered the cornmeal dusted fried oysters and they were bad - they were either old or not fresh AT ALL. we each ate half an oyster and no more. we told the server that they weren't fresh and shouldn't be served - he still charged us for it (and actually asked if we wanted to leave them to "nibble on"). sucks for his tip... my brother had the osso bucco, and it tasted like smoke. the dish seemed like it was steeped in liquid smoke b/c that's all you tasted. it could have been chicken osso bucco and you couldn't have told the difference. the veal was completely lost in the overflavoring of the dish. i had the halibut that was nothing special. it was very bland and the dish needed to be drowned in the sauce, of which i only seemed to get a ladle's worth. i wouldn't order it again. overall, i might give dish another shot, probably when they change the menu up. the oyster ordeal sort of put me out with the whole idea of how a fine dining experience SHOULD be, and that's why i don't think you really get one at Dish.

text: Come on, people, show PHL some love! This place has improved exponentially over the years. I've seen it grow over my three and half decades of life. As a child, my dad was an airline pilot, so I got to explore the place, way back when security was quite different. I knew the place well, yet it always seemed, for what seemed like nearly 20 years, to be in a constant state of construction. But now, construction is complete, and thanks to the terrible state of our nation's airlines, it's a good thing. Delays and cancellations are inevitable, and not due to the airport itself. So PHL has entertainment! First, they have a great rule that all vendors and stores must sell items and food at the current 'street rate' in the Delaware Valley. So no overpriced food unless it is overpriced everywhere. You won't get gouged just because you are in the airport. A beer won't cost $10--hooray! There are rocking chairs in which to sit. The food court is clean and has local chains like Bassetts, not just McDonalds. There are souvenir shops to keep you occupied while the rain delays your trip. The concourse has an entire shopping mall to satisfy our need to shop and consume. Best of all, there is art! Pick up a map and tour the terminals. (You don't have to stay in your airline's terminal, you know.) Get some exercise in, and check out the exhibitions. I am always impressed by their curator's choices. Exciting local art mixed with some folks from far away. In March 2008, there was art made from the old trees from Logan Square that had reached the end of their life cycle. An earlier exhibit of felted sculpture was so gorgeous I called a friend to tell her to learn more about the artist. (Did I mention the wifi so that you could even Google the artist right there if you had a laptop?) You can catch a train right to Center City from Bag Claim. (Though don't get me started on SEPTA's removal of ticket machines. Grr) There are TVs everywhere to entertain you. There's even a spa for massages, pedicures, and facials! So complain if you will. But I think that most complaints are the result of the sad state of our airlines and air travel in general, not the airport. PHL does a great job of making it a little less miserable.

The potatoes are truly home fries, slices crispy, slices softer, cooked with onions and a touch of rosemary. There was a mound of them on the plate-I could never have finished everything and took home about 1/2 to enjoy later. Everyone working was eager to please, thoughtful and helpful. As you know this is an order at the counter, pay and then be seated place. You generally serve your own beverages, refills, etc. And they now have a large selection of expresso drinks in addition to the regular menu items. We got to sample some fresh out of the oven granola and I think it was fabulous, a taste of halvah led me to believe there are toasted sesame seeds plus the coconut flakes and other ingredients. Maybe my experience was an anomaly - after all, there are plenty of other people who love Roberto Cafe. The lighting was a tad dim, but it would have been perfect if I"d been there with a significant other. I ordered the burger with fries and an Arnold Palmer. The Arnold Palmer came out pretty fast. It wasn't quite as sweet as I expected it, but it still was refreshing. The burger and fries came out next. The fries were pretty crispy and tasty. My only gripe was that the salt shaker seemed to be plugged up and so I looked like a salt maniac as I shook the shaker repeatedly trying to get a couple of grains of salt out, even after cleaning the dispenser head. The burger was really hot when it first came out so I let it cool. The big slab of cheddar looked very appetizing, yet it wasn't that tasty upon eating it. The burger itself was disappointing. I ordered a medium burger. What I got was charred on the outside, pretty pink on the inside. The carmelized onions were few and far between, which was a disappointment since I'm a big fan of them. The burger bun was also unremarkable. Service was very good however. As soon as I entered the door the beautiful hostess(think a shorter version of Lulu in a purple cocktail dress and heels) approached me and led me to a table. I barely sat down and I had a waitress come in and fill a glass of water for me. She was pretty quick in bringing out the food and came back fairly often to fill my water glass and to check up on me. I'm not sure I'd eat here again, but the bar looked promising and had a pretty good variety of beers there. And I'd like to see that hostess again.......

text: I ate at Distrito on Saturday night for my friend's birthday party. First of all, I love the decor because it's extra girly! Sean, our waiter, was pretty attentive. I ordered a Strawberry Boing, which was ok, nothing spectacular though. Now on to the food. The food at Distrito is *sigh* GLORIOUS! I ordered the Queso Fundido, which is like this duck and cheese bake. They give you these mini tortillas and you can either spoon the QF out and put it on the tortillas or just eat it directly from the baker. Keep in mind, they serve tapas, so the portions are small. I also ordered the Platano y Crema (sweet fried plantain with cheese), which doesn't sound all that hot, but it tastes ABSOLUTELY delicious! My friend ordered the Esquites, which is like this sweet corn, cheese and lime parfait - again doesn't sound too appetizing, but I tasted it and it was fabulous! We also shared the Encarnacion nachos which were also really good. It's rare that you go to a restaurant with a large group and EVERYONE enjoys their food. Seriously though, I could go back to Distrito to-night! So for glorious food and fun decor, Distrito gets 5 stars!

Beans are beans, and no one will ever get me to eat them, so I stayed away from their version of baked beans, but I did notice a nice hunk of bacon floating around my dinner partner's portion of BBQ baked beans. text: Jason's Deli is set up such that you have to encounter as many people as possible before you get your food. While this isn't necessarily bad in theory, I know they're going for an old-school deli feel but every single staff person at Jason's was rude, abrupt and generally treated me like I was an inconvenience. The greeter regarded me with a cold irritation when I interrupted her conversation with a co-worker to ask for a menu. The woman who took my order rushed me through the process of creating my sandwich and literally scolded me for asking for things out of order on the menu. The cashier wouldn't even look me in the eyes as she wordlessly rung up my ticket, though finally spoke when she thrust my ticket at me and commanded "Put that on a red tray." and scurried off. This made me concerned that I had maybe developed leprosy or some horrible disfigurement since leaving my office for lunch. When my sandwich arrived, the server dropped the plate in front me and shouted "There ya go" over his shoulder as he walked away. At this point, though I was upset with the quality (or lack thereof) of the service I had received, I knew a tasty sammich was just moments away from a contented digestion. Jason's food never disappoints...until today. Apparently, the kitchen had run out of those long wooden picks with the frilly bit on the end and had opted to use a regular toothpick in its place to secure my bread, cheese and veggie tower. "Now, Nickzilla." you might be saying "that sounds an awful lot like nitpicking at this point. I mean seriously, toothpicks?" "Super seriously," I would reply to you, dear reader. Normally I wouldn't even consider such a thing to be a problem unless the kitchen had buried the tiny sliver of birch so far within the sandwich that it couldn't be seen (which they did). Upon my first bite, my lower incisors caught the bottom of the toothpick and forced the other ice-pick sharp end up into my gums. This made it difficult to enjoy the rest of my food since I was now BLEEDING FROM MY MOUTH. Shit-tastic service and assault with a deadly sandwich gives Jason's Deli a one-star rating that even free ice cream can't redeem. I won't be back.

text: 2ND UPDATE Sept. 2011 I was wondering if this place was still around. I went on their Facebook site, and the owner said it's been closed since April 2011, although he's implying that he'll try to come back. It turns out a lien was claimed against him that month. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Completely forgot about this place. It got good publicity in the Statesman and Channel 7 after it opened, and I went there not too long after. After seeing the first review I decided to see if anything had changed. Nope. Basically nothing had changed. And that's not a good thing. Those knowledgeable of Tommy's Burgers in So Cal and Vegas should know that the burgers here are closest in spirit to Tommy's: mustard, chili, tomato, pickles and onions. I was dearly hoping for this place to replicate my Tommy's fix, but that won't be the case. Their single with cheese that comes in at a little over $4 isn't good value for what you get in my opinion, especially compared to the better burger places in town. The meat patties, which are somewhat thicker than Tommy's, have nearly no taste to them. They need to change whatever meat supplier they have. The slice of cheese I got was melted and seemed to be the equivalent of half a slice. And the amount of chili put on the burger is a joke. You get this tiny little lump. I talked to the guy making the burgers the first time I was there, and after I mentioned the puny amount he told me that's the way people were liking it. I didn't know whether or not to believe the guy, but if he's telling the truth I'm wondering what's in the water here for people to prefer a chili burger with barely any chili on it. This also makes the point of having tortilla chips to scoop up the chili wholly irrelevant. Basically you eat the burger with little or no chili residue and have some somewhat stale chips left over to snack on (they were stale on both visits). The chili has more consistency than Tommy's, but I can't say if it's any better or worse because I barely got any to form an opinion! The lack of french fries speaks for itself. I don't think Tommy's is a holy grail of burger joints, but they offer something a little different than the norm and do it cheaply and reasonably effectively. Boobies does it neither cheaply nor effectively, although I am giving them an extra star for basically trying to offer something different. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- UPDATE Like Beauford, I also got a passive-aggressive message from "Patty", alternately berating me for giving a bad review while trying to give me reasons to go back there. Whether or not Patty is truly one of the owners/employees (and it seems plausible given the amount of inside information in the message to Beauford), that's a wacky way of trying to get us to go back. Suffice it to say I won't be returning, especially given the allegations I've since found out regarding one of the owners scamming a nursing-home resident out of her house. Read this article and then tell me if you'd ever want to patronize this place again (UPDATE: The Statesman article is no longer online. text: I worked at Penn as a health economist for almost two years, and lived here the whole time. On an upper floor, I felt privileged to enjoy the best view in West Philadelphia (outside of the UPenn high rises, but... seriously? No comparison). The boy chose the apartment before I arrived. When I first saw it, the "industrial" look of bare concrete made me cringe a little, but the floors were smooth, shiny, and nice... it grew on me. We paid $1500 a month for a 2-bedroom apartment on the 7th floor, facing East. Huge, floor-to-ceiling windows made the corner bedroom drafty in the winter, but it was so worth it. The view was amazing and the sunlight therapy made me happy, streaming in during the morning hours and warming me when I got up. You also pay for the security: the door security codes are changed fairly regularly, the cameras in and outside of the building are monitored, and there's almost always an Allied security guard or two wandering around outside on the corner of 40th and Chestnut. Everything is well-lit, and the one time I remember seeing that the building was tagged, the offending spray paint was removed within hours. (Of course, since there are cameras aimed at every corner of the building, only a moron would tag it... but whatever.) The Hub is a bit pricier than living in one of the dilapidated old West Philly houses, but it was worth it. The majority of individuals our floor and nearby were adults--young professionals, families, Penn faculty and staff, etc. Since the Hub is so close to so many college campuses, you pay a premium to live in a building with other adults who don't blast Kanye loudly on work nights and ralph in the halls. I didn't think I'd turn into a fuddy-duddy so soon, but after a run-in with a set of alcoholic undergrads who objected in very obvious, annoying ways to the fact that my fiancee and I have an interracial relationship, I bit the bullet re: the rent in the hope that I could avoid living in close proximity to fratboys. That said, the building is new, nice, and well-maintained. I never saw ants, bugs, or mice/rats (and those of you in West Philly know how rare that is). One of the benefits of living in a concrete building, I guess. The location couldn't be beat--a block from the FreshGrocer, gym, and UPenn, within a few short city blocks of a dozen yummy restaurants, the Aveda Salon, the Science Center, Drexel, and subways to everything not otherwise in the vicinity. In addition, each apartment had a washer/ dryer unit and dishwasher, which made me SO HAPPY. The management was also good--Rob as the building superintendent, and Nicole in the office--both of them legitimately good people and with whom I've kept in touch since I left my beloved apartment (and the state) to start a PhD program in CA. If something malfunctioned, it was fixed ASAP. If there was a concern, it was addressed right away. Rob even offered to take care of my apt when I was away and water my plants. Overall, a good experience. I was sad to leave and am not nearly as fond of my new apartment in California.

text: I dragged my friend Elena out to play so I could get my first experience of Tampa nightlife. When it comes to going out, I like to stick to goth clubs, gay bars, and places that have a wide variety of music and a "come as you are" feel. None of the pretentious BS and I don't have to hear that one song about the Apple bottom jeans and the boots with the fur. So Castle it was. We noticed almost no one was dancing (one dude was stompin around alone and there was a kid with glowsticks). I'm paranoid about looking like a jackass so I wait until things get a little busier. I like to people watch so all is good. 95% of the clientele that night fit into the two categories: "I'm 16 but I have a fake ID and shop exclusively at hot topic. I'm so rebellious and gawthic! Look at my Tripp pants, fishnet shirt, and trench-coat with buckles!" and older people hanging at the bar drinking alone, not talking to other people. The remaining 5% accounts for people who wandered in mistakenly and didn't fit in. I like the "goth" music scene - industrial, synth pop, whatever. Some of it is kind of -eh- but that's how all genres go. I've gone to goth/alt clubs in south Florida and loved everything the DJs played. Whoever was DJing the night I went sucked for 80% of the music choices and lineup (really fast tempo to slooow to slooow to mid tempo). I can understand music that is more in tune with interpretive dance (i.e. super slow chillout-esque) being played in a lounge type place, but there's a huge dancefloor! Play stuff that you can at least dance to (or stomp to or the leaf waving in the wind thing that super skinny goth girls do- you know, the generic goth girl dancing crap). After an agreement with my friend of "if he doesn't play something good in the next 5 songs, we're leaving," we left. The people were dull and weren't into dancing or socializing (something that was ALWAYS big at the goth places I have been to). I'm used to friendly goths that at least make eye contact and don't live in their little clique. I saw more people txting on their cells by themselves or running around trying to "look cool" than anything. Where are the corsetted geishas, non-mainstream goths, and attractive (and fashionable!) gogo/burlesque girls that I miss so much? Not at castle. And then it hit me. I've never been to a goth club where people under 21 were a main portion of the clientele, let alone even allowed in (soFL is notorious for most places being 21+ just based on local laws). It felt like I was babysitting or something, so many kids running around. And I'm only 22! I wish the morgue in Miami still existed, but I'll survive with an occasional trip to Respectable's in West Palm. Not sure I'll ever stop by castle again, to be honest. text: As far as road trip breakfast options go, few places compare to Bob Evans. I must have been to this particular Bob Evans location at least 20 times. The food is always fresh, the service is always friendly and the place is always clean. For those of you on the West Coast who are not familiar with Bob Evans, let me introduce you. Bob Evans is a couple of steps above Denny's and Waffle House, a step above Marie Callender's and on par with Cracker Barrel. In fact, in my twisted pancake-and-syrup dreams, I like to imagine that Bob Evans is married to Marie Callender, because they're kind of similar in many ways. Denny's could be their son, and they could all live in a Waffle House down the street . . . Are you still reading, or have I lost you completely? Bob Evans markets simple, down-to-earth country fresh food. I recommend Bob Evans for breakfast. I tried it for lunch once, and I wasn't impressed. Eggs, bacon and pancakes are kind of difficult to mess up. I always opt for Farmer's Choice breakfast, which includes 2 pancakes, 3 strips of bacon, 2 eggs and some home fries for only $8.59 (prices and participation may vary). Add a cup of weak coffee, and you're looking at $10 + tip. It's fast, easy, convenient and, most importantly, fresh. Bob Evans' pancakes are very good, but their specialty is biscuits 'n' gravy. 2 biscuits and a bowl of rich, creamy gravy is a great unhealthy way to complement your great unhealthy meal. Strongly recommended. It's a chain, so the decor is consistent across all Bob Evans locations (and I'm not ashamed to say I've visited many of them from Indiana to Maryland and from Michigan to Florida). The decor is that of a mass-produced generic country house with light wood accents, rusty cans, Mason jars and checkered curtains. It doesn't make you feel at home, but it does make you feel welcome. When I embark on a road trip, I always plan to have breakfast at a Bob Evans or a Cracker Barrel. They offer way better options and way better service than most other roadside establishments.

text: Sunday morning, 7:15 AM. No one should be anywhere at this hour, but I get dropped off in front of Beyond Bread, where my plan is to inhale something while waiting for Bookmans to open. I had looked over the menu online the night before, and had an idea of what I wanted. I'm from out of town, never been here before, don't know how things work, serving time at a minimum-security forced labor camp and had the morning off for good behavior. I'm barely awake and approach the counter in a fog with my belt unbuckled and my fly in an indeterminate state. I tell the guy that I'd like the breakfast sandwich thing. He asks me how I would like it. Not able to process the question, I say: "Can I have it with everything?" He says no, but would I like to start with the choice of bread? I ask what they have, not able to focus on the racks of bread immediately behind him. He gestures to the clearly labeled racks that now seem embarrassingly apparent. In my only truly decisive move of the ordering process, I ask for Rye. Odorous, deep, dark, rich Rye with hair on it. No effeminate marble rye for me. Now a cheese. I don't care. I go for Provolone. How about tomatoes, onions or jalapenos? Now I ask again: "Can I have everything of those?" He says yes. Thank goodness. "And coffee please." I mutter. "Would you like a paper cup or a mug?" I ask for a mug, as I plan on sitting around for a while. But then it occurred to me that maybe I was actually buying the mug itself with the coffee. I don't know. I'm not from around here and just escaped from a mental institution in Seattle where you can actually be forced to buy a mug. What do I know? I ask the guy if I am buying the mug itself, and he says no with a puzzled look. I want to tell him that I am from this planet, but he already seems dubious. I roll the bill on my credit card but didn't notice the candlestick-looking thing with a sign on it that was placed in front of me. As I start walking away with my receipt, he reminds me gently to take this with me to my table. I get it. Someone will bring the order to my table. I self-serve some coffee from a pump-thermos thingy and sheepishly head off to a corner where I unsheathe my book and try to disappear. The coffee is gooood. Much better than the coffee served across the street by the contemptible Seattle pushers of coffee-flavored milk beverages. My order arrives in a few minutes. Thick slabs of rye with chewy crusts. In between are a nicely cooked template-formed omelet and the tomato, cheese, onion and jalapenos, along with the potatoes. An excellent, substantial breakfast at a reasonable price. I'll have to try lunch sometime when I can get work release. Clean bathrooms. The Pima County Health Department has consistently given this place the top E for Excellent rating since 2005.

Perfectly cut, seared, seasoned, and cooked, it was a masterpiece. The huge glob of compound button on top helped a little too, but the crust on that thing was to die for. It's almost impossible to get such a perfectly crusty crust on a piece of meat while keeping it moist, tender, and delicious. The meat itself was cooked perfectly and I was literally gnawing at the bone to get every last meaty fiber. I would drive to Santa Barbara in an instant just to have that pork chop again. After that pork, nothing really mattered anymore. http://www.yelp.com/biz_photos/oktohqIGhMQxOP7h5ugHlg?select=0ohVTBOBGFtqQK1vDqE93Q Lamb: The wife's lamb was damn good, but not as good as my pork chop. http://www.yelp.com/biz_photos/oktohqIGhMQxOP7h5ugHlg?select=w-X6D_g0uoPQX1AigGGmnA Pork Belly: Jenni's pork belly was good but the skin was almost too caramelized and stuck to our teeth. But I just want pork chop! http://www.yelp.com/biz_photos/oktohqIGhMQxOP7h5ugHlg?select=1MErcqOhKAHSH_pRhBVdpw Fired Chicken: Squirrel's chicken was nice and crisp but a little on the bland side. text: Rain, mud, beer, blues, more rain, more mud, jazz, gospel, famous musicians, local musicians, more rain, more mud, piles of crawfish, bowls of gumbo, and more beer - even wine now. What a great time! April/May in New Orleans is a rainy season. So plan to get wet. Wear shoes you can throw away before flying home, bring rain ponchos, old clothes, and rags or towels to clean off seats. Sound terrible? Go read the list of performers on their website. It's like nothing else in the world. Two weekends+ of every jazz/blues/zydeco/gospel musician in the world, with half a dozen different performances going at the same time all day every day. (Not quite all day - they end early in the evening.) Jazz Fest is held at a giant fairground, last weekend of April and first weekend of May. It's easiest to take a special bus (reserve in advance) from downtown or the Quarter to get there. They typically have two main stages, where Jazz Fest regulars settle in, stake their areas (the dry ones go first), set up lawn chairs, and settle in to see the headliners. Spread around the fairgrounds, each just out of hearing distance of the other, are the major tents, like the Gospel Tent and the Jazz Tent. You'll want to get a schedule in advance and plan your day, based on who you want to hear, how far it is between the tents/venues you want to see, and how much mud is between them. No tickets once you're in the grounds, just walk into a venue, grab a seat (mostly folding chairs, a few bleachers) or stand (up front at the main stages), move on when you want. Listen to the Dirty Dozen Brass Band, then Nathan and the Zydeco Cha-Chas, then the Leviticus Gospel Singers, then Aaron Neville's new gospel group. Grab another beer and some Cajun food, then catch half an hour of Bobby McFerrin and Chick Corea performing together, then slip over to hear Diana Krall. (That was part of one of our days at Jazz Fest in 2008.) There are food and craft booths everywhere (hence the "heritage" line in the title). I don't believe there are any repeat performances, so it's different musicians every day. The Nevilles may appear in different combinations, but you only get Diana Krall once, Irma Thomas once, Dr. John once, Dave Matthews once, Bon Jovi once, Joe Crocker once, Earth Wind and Fire once, Trombone Shorty once, and on and on. Life is tough. Since each day wraps up by mid-evening, there's no late night problems getting back to your hotel from this less-than-impressive neighborhood. And that way you can still do the French Quarter in the evening, get to a good restaurant for dinner, and start early again the next day. They want you to have a good time, but they also want you spending money in the French Quarter. Shutting down Jazz Fest early also means many of the performers are playing elsewhere in town at night. Add the French Quarter to Jazz Fest and it's the ultimate party. Just a muddy one.
label: POS

text: Oh, how I really wanted to like Restaurant August. Really, who doesn't like Chef John Besh? Handsome and a native to Louisiana, I was looking forward to visiting one of his restaurants ever since we made ressies months ago. But....I realized that Restaurant August is kinda like a fancy Disney of the NOLA restaurant scene. We started with a complimentary Amuse Bouche of a Truffle Sabayon. It was quite tasty with a rich creaminess and a subtle truffle flavor. I ordered the Organic Green Salad with Pumpkin Brittle, Bleu Cheese and Pumpkin Seed Oil Vinaigrette for my starter. And it was the best part of the meal. A bit over-dressed, it was a great combination of sweetness in the Vin and savory in the Greens. The Pumpkin Brittle itself was amazing, but it was quite a large hunk to start off the meal. I ordered off one of the tasting menus for my entree and had the Sablefish in Puff Pastry. It was average. The fish was unusually, well, fishy, and the Puff Pastry really added nothing to the dish. I was disappointed and did not finish my meal. So here's the thing. This place was ultra fancy. But a few things were just....off. We were seated around the corner from the kitchen, which was not a bad thing. Until we kept hearing cheering and clapping every few minutes. We discussed it at the table and figured maybe they were watching a basketball game in the kitchen. No biggie. And we were excited when one of our servers offered us a tour of the kitchen after dinner....we kinda felt like rock stars! Until we realized that all the cheering and clapping coming from the kitchen was all of the other tables getting a tour of the kitchen before us. Great in concept, but it really took the special-ness out of the evening. Also, our front server pretty much disappeared....after I ordered one of the lesser expensive wines. I would say that the service was ruined except for the back server who was personable and really took time with our table. I'm glad I tried Restaurant August, but I'll never go back. There's way too much great food in NOLA to waste a night at this overly priced restaurant.
label: NEG

text: It was a night that would have had Noah running for his toolset and I swear I saw a few animals running 2 by 2 up Chestnut. It ended up costing me about $25 but considering the fun I had, and the people I met, it was worth it. A smart man would have brought his umbrella, but my bent-up olive green piece of crap that I got for free with some horrible cologne wasnt cool enough. I liken it to High School when I walked to school sans hat in sub zero tempatures because, apparently, warmth is nerdy. By the time I walked the 2 blocks to Mahogany, I was soaked to the core in my grey hooded sweatshirt. I guess looking like Id just swum a few laps is cooler than walking in with an umbrella. To their credit, they didnt shoo me out like a vagrant and were very welcoming. To be fair, this could have been a tin outhouse with no heat or ventillation and it would get 5 stars. Its true what many say about the company you keep elevating any experience. I was meeting friends new and old and these people turned out to be the perfect combination for a perfect evening no matter what the venue. To also be fair, Mahogany was the complete opposite of a tin outhouse. Roomy yet cozy, high class but not stuffy. Someone mentioned Wayne Manor and I cant come up with a better description. The servers were friendly and reliable. Im not sure how they kept things organized as we all needed separate tabs and kept playing musical chairs. Didnt seem to phase them in the slightest, and I was impressed. I didnt really eat here but what i saw looked very good. Im not a smoker (but I tried one) and I wasnt overwhelmed by smoke. Id still say that I was out of my league here, but I was not made to feel it. I was able to pretend that I, too, was a classy ind-.......wait did I flash people upon my arrival???!!!! That sounds more like me.

Upon entering the new Peppermill, they were more like a nightclub than an actual Casino with all that special lighting. Their new decor was certainly impressive. However, I do believe this updated decor is more for the younger crowd and not necessarily as impressive for an older age group.... But let's talk about the food at Saucy's since this is a review for them and not neccesarily for Peppermill Hotel and Casino.... I actually did like the food quite a bit and was really soaking in the atmosphere as well. The prices were very fair and I would certainly come back to try more of their menu if I was to visit Peppermill again. We tried their Pork Ribs, Pulled Pork and Brisket. I felt like the Ribs were the best and then the Pulled Pork takes the Silver and for the Brisket, I felt it was a little too fatty to my liking.... As for their sides, we were able to try the Creamed Corn, Chili and Beans, Baked Beans and the Mac and Cheese. All of them were pretty flavorful and no complaints whatsoever... All in all, a quality meal at a more than decent price for BBQ... However..... Kinder's is still king for their ribs as the Kinder's edition's texture is second to none so if I had a choice, I'd still choose Kinder's first but of course, since I have only been to Kinder's once and Saucy's once, my return visits will tell me best which is better as consistency also plays a big role in determining a restaurant's true rating....

We had gone before and didn't get a great impression but it is super convenient and thought maybe it was a fluke. I must add that we are the EASIEST people to deal with. First, when you walk in it is somewhat confusing as to where to go to be seated. We had this problem the first time we went. FInally we saw the sign where to wait to be seated and noone came for about 5 min. What looked like the manager (man in suit) came over and asked if we had a reservation. We didn't so he said it would be a couple minutes and we could wait at the bar. That was fine, we didn't mind waiting. Since we were going to order a bottle of wine at our table, I just ordered an iced tea at the bar. The bartender seemed very displeased by this and took away our napkins. After about 5 min he brought the drink and without saying one word he put it in front of me . We did find it somewhat odd that a whole room was empty and there were other empty tables throughout the other rooms. Not to mention there isn't anyone under the age of 65 with the exception of 3 people. My boyfriend, myself, and a boy that looked to be about 11. He was standing at the bar watching the phillies game. The bartender yelled at him to get away. I am not exaggerating when I say yelled. When he asked if he could stand by the bar the bartender said "did you not hear what I just said, I just told you no. You can't be anywhere around the bar. You can sit against the wall." A bit unnecessary. That made our final decision. We left and will never go again.

text: I really dig this thrift store. I'd go so far as to say that it's my favorite around. It generally has a good assortment of furniture (mostly dressers and tables, some chairs) and lots of odds and ends and household items. It has the biggest and nicest selection of furniture that I've seen around (the Sally Army may have more sofas, etc but the quality isn't as good). It's not all antique stuff either. The prices are reasonable and they always have half off items every day - check out the colored tags as you walk in the door to know what's half off. Their women's clothing selection on the top floor is really great. Bigger than most of the other second hand stores. The only have one dressing room (apparently made for multiple people...?) so that's a bummer. They accept credit cards and that's awesome. I have walked out of there many times with happy little surprises.
