Treating it as a fee... means you're obviously not doing your job well enough for people to WANT to TIP you. Wanna B's has a big, high stage (optimal for taking funny karaoke photos), a full bar and there isn't a bad seat in the house (great mix of tall and low tables and a big rectangle bar that's easy to get to. It's location, right in the heart of Broadway, is ideal and it gets crowded, but never TOO crowded like Lonnie's, Ms. Kelli's or Buck Wild. Overall... I like Wanna B's a lot. It was the first karaoke bar I went to in Nashville and it's probably the nicest one of the 4 or so downtown... with a new KJ and some kind of "we're open", call to attention, hey look at us promotions/signage/etc... they'd probably be the best by a long shot (the place ALWAYS looks closed). text: Went here for lunch on a Thursday and was really impressed. I think of all the places we ate at in New Orleans, I would rank only Lilette higher than Herbsaint. The oysters were delicious. I'd recommend it, unless you want to be more daring. Herbsaint, Tomato and Shrimp Bisque - Making good bisque requires substantial skill, as it needs to have subtle flavor without being either too heavy or light. I thought the shrimp flavor in this one really shines through. Louisiana Shrimp and Grits with Tasso and Okra - Okay, I now acknowledge that grits actually can be on a level with polenta. This is very savory and does a great job of combining several "Louisiana flavors". Housemade Spaghetti with Pancetta and Fried-Poached Egg - Sometimes a dish just doesn't leap off the menu at you, as this one certainly didn't. But WOW is it good. Whoever thought to fry a poached egg? Dunno, but it works. The pasta is in a fantastic cream sauce that the pancetta does wonders with. This may have been my single favorite dish in a 5-day jaunt through great NOLA restaurants. Order it! text: Me momsie and I just did a craftie weekend in Tucson and this was one of our first stops. It didn't take me long to decide she needed to come inside, too. Laraine, who works there, is brash and fun and quickly told us they were the "best knitting store in Tucson". When we told her of our plans for the weekend, she told us we would go to the other ones but we would find "we're the best". Skeptical though I was at first, she just may be right. Their stock is of the highest quality compared to other stores in Tucson. Kiwi is pretty close up there, but Purls has too much crap yarn, and Tucson Yarn only carries the best. I wasn't sure of the vibe when I walked in because Laraine is so over-the-top. I asked if they carried Misti Alpaca Super Chunky (I'm short a skein for a project - I ask wherever I go...sigh...) and got a quick, brusque "never heard of it". Fine, there are TONS of yarns out there, I don't expect you to know every single one... If you go on Tucson Yarn's website (as I did today) it will warn you: "Make no mistake about it. Laraine is NOT a Knit Doctor - not even a Knit Paramedic. Laraine is a relatively new knitter who will be happy to show you around the shop, ring up a sale, register you for a class or wind your yarn." Okay, I get it now. Anyway, they have lots of Cascade, gorgeous Sublime yarns and patterns, Berroco, some Rowan, lots of Debbie Bliss... all great stuff. The ironic thing is I DIDN'T BUY ANY YARN!!! I bought a pattern book and a needle I needed, but Laraine was RIGHT - I should have gone there last - I didn't want to blow my wad at the very first stop of my weekend! I have that problem when I go to a really nice store with a superior inventory - I want EVERYTHING and so I can't pick ONE THING. Boohoo. But I will definitely be back. Gorgeous products. Our waiter resurfaced at the end of the meal to ask how things were, we told him we were finished, and no less than 20 minutes later he returned to again ask how we were doing. Check please? He wandered off not to be seen again for 10 minutes, and we entertained ourselves watching the hostess wander from her post then sprint back across the restaurant every time the phone rang. Professional. Really. Add some bizarre, disjointed decor and the overall atmosphere almost ruined my food. I've eaten at a few other Besh restaurants and have never been disappointed until now. text: Every single time I visit a new city outside of the Bay Area, I need to do at least three things. 1) See the sights. 2) Try a signature dish or food item from that particular city. 3) Karaoke. Well, I had spent the day sighting seeing in Philadelphia with my dad and uncle. I tried an authentic Philly Cheesesteak sandwich (and the Yelp review is coming soon). After a few Patron shots and some delicious beers; I had the itch to karaoke, so I jumped on my Blackberry and found this place listed for Sunday night karaoke. At this point, I definitely know I need KA (Karaoke-holics Anonymous). This place is a total dive bar. It's small, cramped, and dirty. This joint has a mixed crowd. Some people were watching the Eagles game, some were just drinking at the bar, but most were enjoying karaoke. The bartenders offer very strong drinks at low prices. A Patron on the rocks was $7. Nice. The karaoke song selection was very extensive and had all of my favorite karaoke songs. I signed up for a couple songs and waited for my turn. The karaoke crowd was small, but extremely lively. Everyone sang along to the chorus of each song and clapped at the end of the performance. These were karaoke diehards with manners. No douchy frat boys or silly sorority girls singing lame songs in large groups. These people were "professional" karaoke singers. And it seemed, almost everyone somehow knew each other from Philly karaoke circuit or from the Locust Bar itself. And well, any good dive bar has that quality. When it was my turn, the extremely casually dressed patrons were staring at me as I walked up in my slim fit pea coat, pinstripe dress shirt, form fitting jeans, and leather dress shoes. They were trying to figure out where I came from. It was obvious that I wasn't part of the regular crowd and nobody knew me here. As I grabbed the mic, I realized that my dad had never seen me karaoke. And growing up, whenever he watched me play baseball, or soccer, or run track, I always got nervous. But I brushed the anxiety off and started singing, "Get Up (I Feel Like Being a) Sex Machine Pt.1" by the legendary James Brown. It was tough to dance around since the place is cramped and the mic is not wireless (and had it been wireless the rating might have been higher). Regardless, I tried my best to sing, dance around, and "shake my moneymaker." The crowd was definitely into the song (and my antics). People were dancing. My dad was rolling his eyes (and smiling a little). My uncle was pumping his fist (and dancing a bit). At the end of the song, the crowd started to chant my name. "Archie! Archie! Archie!" If those people didn't know me then, they all definitely know me now.

text: FUBLE Diaries: Episode 4 * Just a brief disclaimer, to say that while I am not currently employed there (and it wasn't this location) I worked for Ruby Tuesdays for years. You are welcome to keep this in mind , when you read this..."review" Our damp day in Philly was behind us and after a rough few days for Jason, of travelling and hard living, he was ready to crash. Aside from the Arthritic condition, he also has a bum kidney, which takes alot out of him. Not wanting to impose on my family while he was sick (although I offered) , Jason preferred to get a room so he could rest up for the Main Event of the Eagles Game the next day. I figured the best bet, was to get a place near the airport, although with game 3 of the World Series set to begin that night, and a bunch of Yankees fans needing to rest their inflated heads, I wasn't optimistic. However, after utilizing an iphone ( There's an app for that!) he was able to get a pretty sweet room, for a decent price. The 2 other guys and myself, decided to pregame at Ruby Tuesdays, located in the same lot, to make a plan for the evening. Having worked there for years, i wasn't excited to be back in a Ruby Tuesdays. Nothing personal, I actually think their food is better than average (*wink @ DJ) but I think anyone who has left a place of employment can understand. Not to matter, we wouldn't be there for long...or would we. I tried to take notes on how these Alaskans operate. These guys walk into any place and after only a few minutes...own it! They are, however, armed with one of the best icebreakers Ive ever seen, " We're from Alaska." Its amazing how this gets peoples immediate interest. I'm thinking of having a fake McLovin ID made up, only with Alaska. This was how it went down on this particular evening. Dean, Mike and I sat at one end of the bar, and noticed a lovely blue haired Golden Girl, sitting at the other end. Without a word, Mike got up and began talking to the woman, who laughed, pointed at us and smiled. When Mike came back, I asked what he said . " I told her Dean was coming over to buy her a drink". It was then that we looked over, to see Betty White waving at us! Not wanting to disappoint, Dean walked over and bought her a Native Alaskan shot, The Duck Fart, which is a delicious combination of Kahlua, Baileys and Crown Royal. She loved it, and the flood gates opened. Turns out that entire side of the bar was her family, sons daughters, uncles, brothers, etc. These guys had befriended an entire clan, in about 2 minutes. What followed involved much laughter, back slapping, shots bought and good times. I distinctly remember that Dean was behind the bar making shots at one point. If you've ever worked at a corporate restraunt chain, you'll understand how rare a sight that is. These guys were not only allowed to do this, but were encouraged by the Managers with much fanfare. They became such good friends with the Management at Ruby Tuesday that if I ever need to get a job at RT again, I'm going to go through the Alaskans. So our pregame , became the Game itself. We ended up watching the entire World Series game there, and I'm afraid to know what they dropped there that night. I guess that one of the side effects of bar popularity that I cant afford. When all was said and done with this trip, we all agreed that that night at Ruby Tuesday's, was one of the highlights. Whod'a thunk?

text: Get to the point: Traditional, Quality, Fresh, Nigiri/Sashimi Focus, Reasonable Prices, Fan-freaking-tastic! ----- The owner and head chef, Seki-san, is a very traditional (trained in Ginza at Kyubei!), extremely experienced, and highly skilled Japanese sushi chef. His bar's focus is on nigiri-zushi/sashimi (which is excellent because it's mine also). He strives, and succeeds, at providing quality and freshness. At the same time, he is very amiable to making maki-zushi/rolls and even custom makis as the menu clearly indicates at the bottom to ask for any custom variations you desire. Seki-san originally worked at Sushi Garden and had a vision to start his own Sushi-ya. Thus Sushi King was born about seven months ago. By the way, King is an americanized word he used for easy recognition for the Japanese word kin = gold. Hence why the signage always shows the letter g in a different color. (Did you know this location has been the spot for many sushi-yas before Sushi King? Sachiko mostly recently had this location as a third restaurant.) I've recently took up sushi as a hobby/addiction about two years ago and have since been to 20+ sushi bars in the Tucson area (about ~60% of them). This is by far and above my absolute favorite to date. I'm a huge fan of nigiri-zushi/hand formed sushi. Seki-san's hamachi/yellowtail is always fresh and delicate. His saba/mackerel is smooth and light (Oh, he also finely chops shiso leaf for use between the neta and the shari which is more traditional also). The tamago/sweet egg omelet is just how I like it: not too sweet, not too "eggy". I don't think you can go wrong with anything here at the bar. His rice is just right also. Very subtle rice vinegar taste to a very soft and tender rice that sticks well and at the same time falls apart appropriately in the mouth. Have I mentioned he makes his own ponzu sauce for his sushi yet? I don't think many chefs do. And it's fantastic. A bright splash of sweet citrus combined with the salty soy base. I think such a clear contrast in the taste is only achieved by making it yourself as Seki-san does. I typically try to avoid most maki-zushi/rolls as I like to consider myself a sushi-traditionalist-in-training and most rolls are not considered traditional. But that said, I'm a proud American also and usually find myself indulging in usually at least one maki most times. My recent favorite is a negihama (yellowtail and green onion both chopped and mixed together with nori/seaweed on the outside). A very simple maki, but surprisingly easy to mess up if you don't keep it simple. Seki-san has the maki thing down perfectly also. His rolls are tight, thin and always well proportioned with all the ingredients involved. His negihama is a perfect example. Try one! Now, temaki-zushi/hand rolls are a whole other story. I've honestly not had many, but Seki-san inspired me to try one of his. I noticed he made some for a few other patrons and used a different technique from what I've seen used at all the other sushi-yas I've been too. Most use a conical shape to hold all the ingredients. Seki-san uses more of a cylinder shape with an small extra piece of nori to form the bottom which he holds in place with a small dab of rice. Hard to explain in text, but go and get one and you will see. Very interesting. I've tried one of his unagi temaki-zushi and it was fabulous. His nori is always very crisp and tasty. NB: When I say "traditional" I mostly mean small portions and simple ingredients. I have an issue with the typical attitude of people equating large portions and complexity to being worth while or good in general. I believe that each bite of sushi should be custom tailored by the chef to a singular experience in the mouth. Particularly with nigiri-zushi and maki-zushi. This is only achieved through small single-bite sized pieces. If you can't fit it all into your mouth at one time, the experience will vary too much and could easily not be what the chef intends. The complexity should come in the form of expertise which produces reliably consistent experiences and knowledgeable combinations. Through simplicity in design, beautiful presentations can be mastered. I think Seki-san produces on all of these desires for sushi that I have extremely well. However, I recognize many people only consider sushi "good" if it's received in large quantities. Please recognize I am NOT such a person. Additionally, please understand I sit almost exclusively at the bar and focus on the sushi. I almost never order kitchen food/ryori. I hope this location works for Sushi King well. I hope the past experiences sushi-yas have had here will not be the same this time around. I live to the South-East just outside of town and will drive 45 minutes to Seki-san gladly for sushi any day of the week. I hope you all will do the same to give it at least a try!

Another benefit of the Humane Society is that they have staff on the grounds 24/7, so if there is an emergency the animals are evacuated quickly. On the other hand, it was a Cornish hen, stuffed with raisins and pineapple (???) tenderly marinated in loving herbs and spices, and whiskey flamed at the table. Well, that settled it. The other dishes came out, followed by all of our generous bowls of sticky rice. Then, the waiter brought out a canister and set it on the table. You know those little devices used to glaze a creme brule? Yeah, this wasn't one of those. This was more like what you'd use to weld something in metal shop. Then, the waiter comes back out with my tiny chicken, and stands several feet from the table. He pours a significant amount of whiskey on it, and, with the whole restaurant now paying attention, lights it on fire. It burns for, no joke, like 35seconds. When it finally dies out, he walks it over, places it in front of me, and in a small and polite voice proclaims, 'Young Girl on Fire". There was laughter and applause. And this thing was DELICIOUS. Unbelievable. I even ventured to try the bizarre fruit & dried fruit stuffing. What's even more amazing was the price - usually when someplace is going to light your food on fire, or perform some other gesture that makes it more like 'dinner and a show', it seriously ups the cost. My young girl on fire cost me the same as the other entrees - most things seemed to be in the $15-$20 range. Want to mention something else cool - there were $4 cocktails. Now, we didn't partake in them this visit, so I can't comment on volume or quality, but it bears mentioning - $4 cocktails! And, they were color coded, much like the terror alert system. That way, when you get drunk enough, you can just say - 'Gimmie the Blue!' or "My young girl on fire set my Green aflame!' So, for those of you that haven't bothered to read everything, but want a quick informative recap, here's what this place has: 1) Reasonable Prices 2) Great Food 3) Humorous Dish Names 4) Flaming Entrees 5) Polychromatic Potables I cant recommend this place highly enough. Everything on the menu looks great, everything I tried was great... but you'll be disappointed if you don't make sure someone in your party orders the Young Girl On Fire.

Come into this corner spot in Dogtown, take a table -- the heated "patio" is a preferable option to the smoky inside section -- and before long you'll be looking over the menu at the appetizers. Andy's pick: either the "Dunk the Veggie" or the "Hot Poppers," which are both variations on the same theme: deep fried vegetables, cream cheese-filled in the latter case, served with dipping sauces. Yeah! If it's your first trip (or second or third, for that matter) to McDaniel's, you can't go wrong with the burger. The Seamus Cheeseburger ($7.50 or so) seems to be the crowd favorite: it's a BIG burger, overdiametered, served on a sesame seed bun and nested in an awfully big pile of crinkle-cut french fries served just right. My last visit I tried the chili and New England clam chowders. Both were okay, probably 3-star worthy, but were also the cheapest thing on the menu, and I wasn't very hungry. The beer selection here is also good. I haven't ordered one in a while, but nobody ever seems disappointed. Seamus McDaniel's, as far as I'm concerned, has the best non-chain burgers in the St. Louis area. I'm embarrassed to admit that Five Guys may still have a better formula, but if you gasped when I typed that, McDaniel's is, without a doubt, for you.

text: I've had lots of mediocre sushi in Tampa. From SB in Ybor City to CB near the stadium, there's a lot of just average... or restaurants trying too hard to be fusion. I grew up near Tampa, and every time I come back, there's only one requirement as far as dining -- I have to get in to see Ryo at Kaisen Sushi. Kaisen is a little known secret that Tampa has been hiding for years. Ryo initially opened over by Harpos, further south on Dale Mabry than their current location. I went in for the first time in 1999, and have been a repeat customer ever since, dining there sometimes twice a week. In all my years of eating at Kaisen, I've never once been disappointed. In fact, they know me by name now and I get that personal of service that keeps me coming back. Here are my highlights: Appetizer: Calamari -- I can't say enough about this stuff. It's not your typical frozen rings, this stuff is FRESH. They saute large chunks octopus, not just rings or tentacles, in a delicious sauce that has a mild tangy flavor to it. It's then topped with bonito flake, green onion, and a lemon. I could eat calamari appetizers as a meal and walk away satisfied... Stuffed Mushrooms -- Forget everything you know about stuffed mushrooms. Ryo takes large mushrooms, stuffs them with crab meat, tempura batters, and deep fries them. They're then coated with what I think is ponzu sauce for a delicious creation. Nigiri: One of my personal favorites is the zuke tuna. Ryo takes the best cuts of Tuna and marinates them in what I believe to be sesame oil, rice vinegar, and soy sauce, for about three days. The fish changes consistency and flavor, and becomes just ridiculously good. You have to try it. Ryo's fish selection and cuts are the absolute best in Tampa, in my opinion. He hand-selects everything, and he's committed to culinary excellence. You really can't go wrong. Rolls: My personal favorite, although not containing raw fish, is the Cynthia's Vegetable Tempura roll. The kitchen takes asparagus and sweet potatoes, tempura batters, then deep fries them. These scrumptious veggies are then rolled up and served with a side of ponzu sauce. It's HEAVENLY. The spicy tuna is by far the best I've ever had as well. Most restaurants pulverize the tuna or use shoddier quality of fish. Ryo takes his sushi tuna, cubes it, and mixes it with spicy sauce. You don't feel like you're eating some strange mush -- it has consistency, texture, and above all, great flavor. Dessert: I love the green tea ice cream. It's that simple. They also carry "Red Bean" ice cream, but I tend to stay away from that. It's a little too weird for me. For all you non-sushi lovers, they do a delicious cooked salmon and chicken teriyaki. I can't recommend Kaisen Sushi enough, that's plain and simple. If you're a first time sushi-er, or a seasoned expert, stop into Kaisen and prepare to be wowed. They also organize a yearly fishing trip, and I hear a lot of people have had a really good time on these excursions. You'll always see Ryo making sushi, and his Dad and sometimes his wife are there working to keep the place running smoothly. GO! NOW (unless it's Sunday or Monday)! DO IT! :-)

text: I'm not sure what to say about St V's. I registered to volunteer with Katrina Corps a few years ago, and knew nothing about the place or where I'd be sleeping until I actually arrived there. To use a closet. To keep our rooms. He owns a nice home down the way and stops in from time to time. "Sir Lickem" is the best. He's definitely an oddball, but the reason this place is better now is because of him. He does repairs, mows the lawn, paints, cleans the pool, etc. The staff all has problems. I'm sure they did things they weren't proud of to survive, but they continue to happen years after the storm. They all have interesting stories, especially Brandy and Taylor. I definitely didn't feel that safe here sometimes, especially when I knew about a young couple living 2 doors down from the stairs across the hallway. They had a baby girl together and sometimes you could see into their room because the door would be open. I heard them fighting one night and the male kept hitting the baby because she was crying non-stop and he screamed for her to shut up, so the mother put up a fight and he ended up turning on the mom and smashing her head against the wall and we heard her crying hysterically. My friend and I called the police, but they rarely do anything here. Too many bad reports and they fine them or shut the place down, so they don't. In the same week, our volunteer supervisor's van was broken into and his supplies were stolen. And for some reason we all thought it was Taylor. It made sense. They do have some roaches and rodents. Most of the rodents are in the courtyard or downstairs (I always caught small mice in the public bathroom off the kitchen, none in the rooms). In one room I stayed in, my friend and I had to wear HIGH heels to the bathroom and around the room. I didn't want to wear slippers or flipflops because I just had bad experiences with them. The waitress was able to tell me that the spicy sauce and saucy mayonnaise didn't have soy sauce in them. But then I asked if any of the sushi we wanted to order had something breaded in it. "Bread?", the waitress asked. "What is bread? I don't know what." "Panko?", my housemate asked. She still had no clue what we were talking about. When the eel maki came, it had a brown sauce on it, even though there was no sauce listed on the menu. When I asked the waitress what it was, she said, helpfully, "eel sauce". When I asked her if there was soy sauce in it, she said yes. One of the other makis - salmon or yellowtail, I can't remember - had something crunchy and suspicious-looking on the inside. Turns out when the menu said "scallion", it meant "breaded and fried onions". Boo! I normally don't run into any problems like this when I get sushi, so I was disappointed. The free shot of cinnamon iced tea at the end of the meal made me a little happier, but I'm also a person who likes the taste of Goldschlager, so I'm not sure if you'll feel the same way. This is not a place to bring your GFGF (gluten-free girlfriend)!

text: No doubt, Performance probably has the best prices in town on bikes, clothing, and accessories. I recently purchased a used road bike and needed to have the cranks changed out (it had power cranks/training cranks on it). The mechanics admitted they had never seen power cranks before, and after 15 minutes of loosening and tightening the crank bolt and literally hammering on the bottom bracket, they declared that the cranks were improperly installed, stripped, and could not be removed. They told me I had been ripped off, and then offered to sell me on of their Fuji bikes with a lesser grade of components. I took my bike home, and after 10 minutes of work, had the whole crank assembly and bottom bracket removed--in 15 minutes more I had the new BB and crank installed without problem. All they succeeded in doing was damaging the old cranks and BB with their hammering. I took my bike to them to have a professional mechanic, only to discover that I am more skilled then they are. Not sure if the problem was that they were simply incompetent, just desperate to sell me a new bike, or both.

text: Short Review: Avoid this place like the plague. Long Review: A while back, my girlfriend had some work pants that were a bit too long and needed them altered. Seeing as this place was near her job, she had them altered. After dealing with "Dawn", who seems (heh) to be the head seamstress, she vowed she would never go back. I didn't think it could have been that bad, so I was like "whatever." Fast forward to one week ago. A dress needed to be altered that was too long (she's short obviously). It had been a while and she had called around to various other places around town that do alterations. Alterations Connection had the most reasonable price. She grudgingly went back, and this time I accompanied her. The first thing that hit me were the posters around the store. Now, Reno is a bit of a redneck town still at heart, but their decor was a bit over the top describing all the reasons we would be shot if we did not follow their rules. This is a place where clothing gets repaired, not a bank. Not exactly welcoming. We waited a few minutes until Dawn came out of the back and asked "What do you want?" My girlfriend explained and after sighing, she showed my girlfriend the dressing room and went back in the back shop area. My girlfriend changed and Dawn wasn't back yet so I talked to her for a second. Dawn comes back out after a few moments, looks at my girlfriend and rudely points at the dressing platform while glaring. My girlfriend says ok. Behind her back, Dawn rolls her eyes at my girlfriend and walks out into the main area to "greet" the next customer. At this point, I'm thinking "All right, this is enough" so we decide to leave. She came back when my girlfriend changed back out of the dress and said "What'd ya change your mind?" Girlfriend answers with "Yes, I think you are very rude and we're going somewhere else." Dawn doesn't apologize (most likely because she knows it) and says "OK" in a sarcastic manner. An old Chinese proverbs states "If you want to get into business, learn to smile." I don't expect outstanding service everywhere I go, but to be treated flat out rudely for no reason other than we came to get a service and pay money for it speaks volumes about the longevity of a business's future. Hopefully, others hear about this place and they go under so some more qualified business can take its place. The only type of person who should go here is if they are a rodeo queen, because there were posters everywhere of her. Otherwise, be prepared to be treated like crap. In epilogue, we ended up finding another alteration place and they were extremely helpful and friendly for 2 dollars less. We definitely won't be back to Alterations Connections. Ever.

text: I've gotten takeout here three times, and thought this would be my go-to place for good, fast sushi (more variety than Lemongrass, but about the same distance). This third time is the final time. The first time, I popped in while my husband entertained our baby. I was told it would be 20-25 minutes. I asked if I could wait outside. I went back in around 30 minutes later, at which point the person with whom I placed my order ignored me, said something in Japanese to the chef, and turned to me to say that it was being made right then. I walked out with my food about ten minutes after that. The second time it was perfect. We were on our way home, I called ahead and ordered from the menu online, and it was waiting for me when I walked in. I thought the first time was a fluke and was very pleased. Grabbed their takeout menu and left happy. This time, however, I ordered from that takeout menu, and inexplicably got something completely random. I called to rectify the situation, but instead of working with me, the woman with whom I placed the order (same person from the first time, actually) looked at what she had written to prove that I had ordered the thing I had received. When I corrected it - it was a pronunciation issue - she continued to say that I had ordered this thing. I spelled the item I had ordered, and she said that it was not on the menu. Eventually I circled the item on the takeout menu and sent it with my very patient husband along with the random item she thought I had ordered. It turned out that the takeout menu contains things that are not, in fact, on the restaurant menu, and she had been going by the restaurant menu alone. The manager gave us what I actually ordered without extra charge (husband had paid for the random item, which was less than half the amount of what I'd ordered). So there was at least some attempt to rectify the situation, which is why they get two stars instead of one. But unless they (a) change the takeout menu to reflect their actual menu and (b) stop arguing when they screw up orders, I will not be returning.

text: A friend and I went over Labor Day weekend just to get out of the city. Neither of us had ever been to Reno before. Through hotels.com, we got a room in the "Montego" wing for $70. When we got our bill we, too, were charged the "resort fee", but it was part of the $70. When we arrived, I was wearing a polo shirt, cargo shirts and flip-flops. My feet were dirty and dusty from tramping around Lake Tahoe all morning. When we walked into the lobby, my friend said "oh-oh! Looks like you're overdressed!" And she was right. Trust me when I say that Old Navy is high-end to the people who were at this resort over Labor Day weekend. At least most everyone was wearing shoes. The Peppermill has recently had a very expensive renovation/upgrade. The public areas and casino/restaurants are about as over-the-top and tacky as you can get. It looks like Liberace threw up. Teletubby colors, gazillions of led/neon lights, "Tuscan" columns/marble, outer-space carpeting and sparkly/shiny surfaces everywhere. It was awesome in its hideousness! The Montego wing is connected via a skywalk from the main property, obviously the old part of the property (but it has been renovated). The skywalk looks like something one would expect at Disneyland: it has these funky bluish/purple lights that run the length of it. I joked that they were UV lights to sterilize the lesser Montego denizens before they were allowed back into the main property. Our room was clean and comfortable. Two very nice, soft queen beds, a large plasma screen, nice, large bathroom with granite countertop, tile floors and the standard blow/dryer, glassware, coffeemaker (in the bathroom. that always kills me) towels, soaps, etc. We did not notice any smoke smell (we were on the non-smoking level) as others have. The hallway did smell like a dirty bong at one point however. The casino is gigantic. Tons of slots (which I have little use for) and a fun/frenzied gaming area. The croupiers at the roulette table we parked at changed frequently - but all were fun and nice. I know, I know: roulette has one of the worst odds of any game in a casino. But, I can't help it. The cocktail waitress was there frequently as well, and drinks were decent (they are free, after all). Free parking in the spacious, easily-accessible parking garage. We went to the other casinos "downtown" - meh. Downtown Reno is a dump - Reno 911makes it look better than it really is. A bunch of hillbilly kids roaming the streets trying to be cool. Reno hipsters, I guess. Honestly, if I ever do return to Reno, I'll definitely stay at the Peppermill again - and not leave until I return home.
label: POS

My steak was good, although quite seasoned; and the fries, I regret to say, were seasoned within an inch of their lives. text: I want to like this place, I really do, but I have just about given up on Bala. Like others have said in their review, it is a great building. You can tell it used to be a great theater before its re-purposing into a cinema. There is staircases on each side that lead up to a balcony (you can't sit up there) and the ornamentation in the theater really is beautiful- the main theater with the chandelier has metal work all around it with an Egyptian theme. This place has good bones- that's about it. I have had several strange experiences at Bala that have made me want to rarely return. First, they used to offer a $5 matinee special for all films before 4. Great! Except no films would play before 4- all films started 4:30 at the earliest. If you don't want to offer a matinee, don't put it up there on your website. Now that they have raised their prices (which I will get to) to $8 bucks a ticket, they have some matinees. Who I believe to be the manager, Frank, is one of the worst customer service experiences a patron can have. He is rude when you ask him a question and has yelled in front of us (the paying customer) to his employees. Maybe it is time to find a new career? That being said, all of the other employees I have encountered have been nothing but professional and courteous at all times. On two separate occasions, the heat in certain theaters was not working. I understand that these things do happen from time to time, but when it happens twice, you should either close the theater all together until repairs can be made, or offer some sort of discount to another film in a theater that has working heat. Finally, the prices have jumped- a lot. During my most recent visit, however, I found that a ticket had jumped to $10 dollars- comparable to the bigger theaters nearby. This is just ridiculous. If I am going to spend $10 on a movie, I am going to go to a theater where I know I will get good service and have heat- two things Bala cannot always provide. While I want to support local business as much as possible, I won't support a bad business. For the same money I can go to KOP and see a film. If you are looking for a theater that serves a similar niche as Bala without the inconsistency and jacked up pricing, go to Bryn Mawr Film Institute- you will not be dissapointed.

When the waiter asked about the meal, my friend told him that the lobster tail was not very good, and the waiter said he would let the chef know. text: A refreshing breeze just blew through 20th and Sansom, and its name 'tis Noble. In the former digs of Cibucan (loved that place), then an Italian restaurant I never got the chance to frequent, Noble has taken up residence in the most gorgeous and delicious manner possible. Step inside and you'll know what I mean. Muted shades, subtle pieces of art on the walls and wood, wood, wood everywhere - it's airy, it's light, it's effortless Zen. It's coastal Washington State meets concrete inner city. I can't forget to mention the bar outfitted with a huge slab of shiny wood that seems totally inviting with its generous helping of stools and the mighty friendly and cool bartenders in green checkered shirts, ties and sleeve garters. (I know, sleeve garters! Love the throwback) Also love the indoor, outdoor table that frames the front part of the restaurant and opens onto the street. I know I keep tripping on service in my reviews, but I truly believe it can make or break the experience. Everyone was so damn nice at Noble and not fake Stephen-Starr nice either - I really enjoyed our server, she was quirky, uber informed (i.e. full of fun little facts like the wine I was drinking was from the first entirely solar-powered vineyard to what dish truly represented what the chef's signature style was), insightful and attentive without being intrusive. The pièce de resistance for Noble, of course, and what won me over, was the food. Each course precisely executed and beautifully presented. Started with the scallops (I know, kind of a boring choice, when you've got more exciting options on the menu but I was sharing it with my DOH who's got less than an adventurous palate) then moved on to the Black Sable (a fish, whose consistency and taste is very similar to seabass) and sweet jesus, I almost convulsed with delight. The temperature was perfect, the accoutrements were spot on. My dining companion had Free-range veal (and he dutifully remarked "Isn't that an oxymoron?") that was yummy but not as tender as he had hoped. (I'm blaming it on the free-ranging) Ended the meal with a trio of sorbet (delectable lemon-thyme, grapefruit and watermelon) and they were unexpectedly coupled with fresh from the oven little sugar cookies. Ingredients were fresh, everything was so thoughtfully and lovingly prepared, that much was evident. All this and the lovely ambiance did come at a price though - so with drinks (wine for me, beer for him, + after-dinner spirits), dinner bill for two came up to $130. Sure it's not an every week thing, but for a treat it's well worth your dime. I can't wait to go back and explore the rest of the menu - At the very least, I'll return as soon as I can to partake in the bar menu (yes, they do offer burgers!) and debate with the barmen on the benefits of sleeve garters.

text: First, I am kind of shocked I am the first to review this establishment. Second, I am REALLY shocked I haven't reviewed it yet, since I practically lived here the first 6 months of my son's life. I am OVERALL not a fan, but for convenience, I have limited baby shopping options. Buy Buy Baby is the shit and I would spend ALL my money there if I could, but it is well over an hour away and if you have read any of my other reviews, you know I don't like to drive much further than 3 miles to get somewhere....so even BRU is out of my way. BRU has the basics and a lot of crap you do NOT need or will EVER need for your child. Everything is comparable to what you would get anywhere else, but it does tend (from what i have heard) to be more expensive than Wal-mart (but that is one devil store I refuse to shop). For registering, I think it's a must do, b/c BRU is everywhere and Buy Buy Baby is still building their name and don't have nearly as many locations. The plus side about BRU is that everyone has heard of it and it's a trusted name...the downside is that it is a "trusted" name and generally is a terrible store. The staff is not well educated in products. They only (barely) know how to run the cash register. The return policy is outrageously annoying (SPECIAL TIP FOR ALL THOSE REGISTERING: Put everything you might never want on your registry and if you want, take it back for an in store credit. If it's NOT on your registry and you have no receipt. they will not give you any sort of credit. If you receive something that is not on your registry, you can EDIT it before you go into the store and get the credit, but if you don't, you are SOL). This is all a lot of information for a pregnant girl and seemingly unnecessary in my opinion. What is wrong with having a flexible policy especially for new moms?!?! Everything is difficult enough...by all means, make it as un-user friendly as possible. BRU's rewards program is also bunk. Supposedly the more you spend, the more coupons and treats you get. Not so much! It's just another way to over-spam your email account. Options are FAIRLY limited. Don't expect to find the likes of more upscale baby accessories like the Bugaboo or Uppa Baby Vista. They only carry more typical name brands....and typically extremely cheap product as well. That all being said, they have much of what you want/need. While the store may be disorganized and their staff is indifferent and useless, if you are in there long enough, you'll keep them in business and probably find what you are looking for. Yes, I keep going back, but only b/c my options are so limited in the Indy area....and I continually receive BRU gift cards which I cannot exchange for cash (dammit!).

text: Ya know what I'm sick and tired of, restaurants that don't seem to give a crap about pissing off customers, even regulars that they know. I've been coming here for years with no problems. Then last night we ordered some cheese steaks and fries. They told me 15 minutes for pickup but I gave them 25 minutes. When I got there I told the girl that always works the counter what I was there to pick up. She was frantically slapping some new meat on the grill and chopping it up. She said, "I'll be with you in a few minutes bud." Meanwhile another customer came in and got a whole bunch of cheese steaks and pizza. After that customer left there was a bag with 1 cheese steak and fries in it on the counter. I realized now that either one of my cheese steaks had just been given to the other customer or they forgot to make one of my two cheese steaks. The mother that works the place came up and asked to help me. I started to tell her what I was there for, thinking that maybe she'd want to ring me up, and the younger girl (pretty sure her daughter) interrupts me and says in a pissed off tone "I said I'd be with you in a few minutes bud." After waiting a few more minutes the cheese steak was finished and guess what, the mother rang me up after all, only she overcharged me for both cheese steaks. I was about to walk out when I asked the daughter for a menu and questioned her about the cheese steak prices being higher. She curtly responded to me that they had raised their prices and even though that was indeed the case they had STILL overcharged me $1 for both cheese steaks compared to the new menu. To top it all off the plastic lid of the french fry container was totally crushed in and the fries were barely warm. I just have no tolerance for this stuff anymore; rude behavior from employees, overcharging, lack of concern for the customer. When someone doesn't care and you're just $$$ to them, it's pretty obvious. I've worked at 3 restaurants in my life and you should ALWAYS treat the customer with respect and not play games with them, even if they're a jerk. So long Chiaro's, I'll be giving my business to Toscos or other area pizza shops from now on thank you very much.

text: Part I: I really wanted to fall in love with this dealership, and I did... at first. I've always been a domestic manufacturer kind of girl when it comes to cars. Hell, my father was a UAW (United Auto Worker) with the Ford plant in Gary, IN for over 30 years. He always drilled into the family to "buy Amercian", yadda, yadda, yadda. I should have heeded his advice but no, I had to learn the hard way. About a year ago the hubby and I took a ride over to Lexus of Chester Springs ready to make a purchase. We had just attended the Philly car show in February and of course we were all starry-eyed over the thought of a new car. Mind you, I had an '06 Pontiac that was completely paid off. What did I "need" a new car for? But that's neither here nor there at this point. We test drove a 2008 IS250, which was sweet, but then I found out that there was a faster version, the IS350. Sold! We were offered more than expected for my trade-in and the hubby used his skills to negotiate a reasonable price. We left the dealership deliriously happy that day, and I'm sure many of the police officers in Chester County were salivating at the thought of issuing me a speeding ticket in the near future. Unfortunately, this is where the bliss ended. Two weeks ago I was in a parking lot sitting in the car with the engine idling. Suddenly, the car started idling really rough; it was shaking and the RPMs were hovering at 0. I turned off the car, gave it a minute, and then tried to start it. No success, it would turn over. I knew it wasn't the battery because all of my accessories worked just fine (lights, stereo, windows, GPS, etc), and I had plenty of gas. I was at a loss, but good thing this happened only a few miles from my house. The hubby came out to meet me where I was stranded and agreed we needed to call for a tow. Here was my chance to use Lexus Roadside Assistance. They were great; a tow truck arrived within a half hour. The car was loaded on the flatbed and was on its way to the dealer. The towing company called us at home after to car was delivered to the dealer. Perfect. The next morning we went to the dealer since the car arrived after business hours and we wanted to talk to the Service Dept about what I experienced. The Service Advisor had no record of my car ever arriving the night before. I felt nauseous. My hubby just about popped a vein in the lobby and demanded that they find my car. He and the Service Advisor walked outside and found the car on the side of the garage, which was a HUGE relief. Only problem was that the key fob was not put in the night-drop, which is why the Service Dept had no indication that a car had arrived after-hours. Just to get things moving along, we gave the Service Advisor our extra fob and asked him to call us when they determine why my car broke down. In the meantime, I called the towing company to ask about the key fob. The driver of the tow truck said he couldn't find the night-drop so he left the key fob on the BACK BUMPER of my car, out in the open, in plain view. I guess it was a good thing that the car wouldn't start, not like anyone could have stolen it without a lot of effort. By mid-morning the Service Advisor called my hubby and informed him that upon initial review of the car it appears that a mouse made its way under the hood of the car and chewed through the wires that lead to the engine. I had never heard of such a thing, but what do I know? We were also told that this would not be covered under the warranty and could be pretty pricey depending on how extensive the damage was and the time/labor to rewire the car. All I could think was, "Buh-bye bonus that just appeared in my paycheck last week." A few hours later the Service Advisor called again and said their initial diagnosis may have been a bit premature and it was actually a valve spring within the engine that broke. The engine would need to be removed from the car, taken apart, and then repaired. At least this particular issue is clearly a mechanical malfunction (probably during manufacturing) and would be covered by the warranty. The parts were ordered and were expected to arrive the next day. Supposedly an engineer (or someone along those lines with that type of knowledge/expertise) from one of the Lexus US offices was informed of the broken valve spring and wanted to look at the engine to determine if there are any design flaws (whatever, it meant a lot of nothing to me at this point - I just wanted the car repaired). He was expected to arrive the same day as the parts. Stay tuned for Part II...

text: I don't know how I lived in Philadelphia for over two years never having been to this place, but I recently tried Sahara for dinner for the first time and have a new favorite for middle easten food in Philadelphia! Wonderful service, very reasonable prices (2 plates + diet coke + tip was $30), and very satisfying portions. My companion and I couldn't decide--the bottom line was that she wanted hummus--so we decided to share two plates. One was a chicken kabob dish that came with grilled veggies, salad, and herbed rice, the other was a falafel platter that came with hummus, tahini, raita-like yogurt, salad, and lots of pita. We were blown away. The salad was delicious--it was mixed with what had to be a mix of lemon juice and drizzle of olive oil and some herbs, but it was definitely fresh and not heavy at all. Both platers were delicious, and their falafel is some of the best I've tried in Philly. There was more than enough food, to the point that we didn't even touch the rice. And even though we left stuffed, we didn't feel gross or heavy afterwards since the food wasn't greasy (not even the falafel). This place definitely left an impression because my sister and I couldn't shut up about how yummy dinner was at the movie we went to that night, or even at brunch the next day. Will definitely go back. It's apparently BYOB, so I guess I'll be packing wine then as well :)

text: I originally reviewed this place as Giovanni's and no Giovani, because I am either dumb or the search function on Yelp is dumb. Either way, I've been going to Giovanni Pizza just up the street from my office for about a year now, I would think it's been around for a while. THE FOOD: Incredible...I am a pizza junkie, and I like those crazy specialty slices too, so for baked ziti and chicken pizza, sicilian meatlovers, BBQ chicken and buffalo chicken pizza, there is no substitute. And I've been to most of the area pizza joints, if only just to explore and compare. The only thing stopping me from eating this every meal until I turn into a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle is my own conscience, keeping me at bay. THE SERVICE: OK, this is what keeps my review from the full 5-stars-- and it's not even really the employees and their handling of customers. It's the process, and it's f---ed up. I write about it in my reviews all the time, if a place has to resort to calling out a customers' order ten times before they realize it and go to pick it up, something's wrong. Maybe it's the physical layout of the place-- narrow and uncomfortable where the ordering/pickup takes place, maybe it's the half-wit customers who will stand there and WATCH these guys call out their food, maybe it's me, the easily-irritated ignoramus of a reviewer. I think if they separated the eat-in's from the take-out's and gave the eat-in's a number and had their food brought to them, it would make things go smoother. THE PRICE: Totally worth it, worth the wait, worth the epic battle through a gauntlet of gluttons and gangstas, worth the mind-bending riddle of how/when you can give your $10 for 2 specialty slices and a snapple, you may finally emerge triumphantly with your food, like Harold & Kumar and White Castle...savor the spoils of victory my friend...savor them, you've earned it. THE BOTTOM LINE: Maybe I'm overdramatizing the experience, but I'm not overdramatizing the deliciousness...I prefer this over any other Pizza place in Center City right now. Go check it out!

text: Going to the Fox for me is always such a treat. Since I was a young kid, I've been requesting tickets to see the newest tour for Christmas and my birthday or really any other reason I can come up with. The best thing I ever saw here was in 2009 seeing Spring Awakening where we were sitting ON.THE.STAGE. It was the most incredible theater going experience of my musical nerd life. So, the last time I went to the Fox, it was to take my husband to see Wicked. I've seen it already and while it's become a little too popular for me, I knew it was something he'd enjoy because it's such a spectacular show to see live. The show did not disappoint - in fact, it was better than the first time I saw it with the original touring cast. But, I'm not here to Yelp about the show, amazing as it was. I realize that the ushers are there on a volunteer basis. My mom did it for a season or two. They're not getting paid and they often have to sit through the same show several times before it finally moves on (and not all the shows they sit through are as entertaining as you might think...my mom sat through Phantom of the Opera FOUR times. I would have died.) HOWEVER. The ushers that were working the show on Sunday, June 27 (at 2:00 pm) probably should have paid me back for my tickets. Clearly stated in every program, on lots of signs throughout the theater, on your tickets, and as GENERAL THEATER ETIQUETTE, people should expect to have to wait for a pause in the action to be seated if they show up for the show after it's already started. Then WHY, are ushers seating people while this show has already started, blocking the views of those of us who DID bother to arrive on time, and shining flashlights (which are supposed to be pointed to the ground at all times anyway) in MY FACE?! It's when stuff like this happens, that I just freaking wish the ushers would use a little common sense and perhaps take that moment to educate people on a little theatre etiquette. Don't even get me started on the Muny (i.e. it is never okay to SING ALONG with the actors onstage). This time around at the Fox I wasn't sitting in the best of seats, so had I been paying a little more, I probably would have complained. But, attention to everyone - it is RUDE to show up late for a show. Just like baseball, you're to wait for a pause in the action before you make your way to your seat. It's also rude to talk during a live performance. Sure, in a place like the Fox, the actors can't hear you, but I paid money to hear them, NOT YOU. I adore the Fox, I swear I do. I'll be going there for years to come and hope to bring my children there some day (once they're old enough to follow the rules above). But, I'd be lying if I said my last experience there was my favorite. Great show. Not-so-great ushers and patrons. Oh well.

text: Okay, I'm writing from the perspective of someone who regularly frequents other "Metro" transportation, primarily Chicago and Washington D.C. (I'm only reviewing the light rail. I have never used the buses or shuttles). By those standards, Metrolink is a sad and ailing relative. I agree 100% with the comment about the "honor" system. Why not put in turnstyles and guarantee 100% payment by all riders. The first time I rode Metro trains I was not aware of the "validation" requirement. WTF? How ridiculous is this system that doesn't allow you to purchase a fare card and use it over a span of time or add value? Additionally, the 1 line (with a spur) is a joke. Metrolink would be truly useful if a train went up to Alton, down to South County Mall to Arnold, out to West County. With the ineptitude, graft and overall mismanagement by the City and Metro board, you can't expect much more than we have though, so I guess it is as good as it will ever be. It will never make a profit, so it will never expand without massive Federal investment, which would be flushing more national treasure. All you need is one visit to D.C. or the Bay Area or Boston or Chicago or even Philly and you'll see how very narrow the Metrolink has set up their routes to prohibit large-scale ridership. It really does serve only a small fraction of St Louis City or County's residents and is almost simply a way to get airport folks to the downtown or out to Scott AFB. To complete my rant, I'll add--lack of public restrooms, security bordering on stoogery and recently reduced service, causing even longer waits. No thanks...I'll drive.

text: Came here for lunch the other day. The place was dead at 2pm, but I didn't mind. The bartendress was very friendly and she kept me entertained. I ordered the fish and chips upon her suggestion and was thoroughly pleased. The batter had a delicious, buttery quality to it and the the fish had a lovely creamy taste. Hard to describe, but I quite enjoyed it. The dish comes with fries and hush puppies which seemed like too many carbs, but still yummy. The fries are hand-cut and well seasoned. The hush puppies were the best I've had above the Mason-Dixon line and I couldn't help but think they'd taste amazing with vanilla ice cream. They've got quite a few of my favorite beers on tap including Allagash White and Monk's Sour Flemish Ale. The atmosphere is very warm with lots of dark wood and I'm sure it's a popular spot in the evening. The bartendress and I got into a conversation about UPenn undergrads trying to sneak in on the weekends and it seems they've got a pretty good system for keeping the wee ones out. Apparently, they've thwarted quite a few wily undergrads with fake ID's. I wouldn't say this place is mainly for UPenn students (whatever their age) but a place that's trying to provide more options for folks north of 40th street. It just so happens that many of those who live in that area are also students or employees of Penn (they are the largest employer in the city afterall). So pop by, grab a beer and a burger, and let the security staff take care of the interlopers.

text: I have to say that I cannot look at this place's lamely punned name without feeling a twinge of embarrassment on its behalf. Does the term "douchechills" apply here? I'm not sure. OK, now that I got that off my chest... We arrived for an earlyish dinner and were greeted by a hostess who seemed a little annoyed that we had shown up and needed a table and menus, too. Although the place was almost empty, we were seated cheek to jowl with another group, resulting in two parties with two servers having to yell over one another. The menu has a small list of drinks and a long list of dishes, and my friends and I had to ask some questions to make heads or tails of it - thankfully, our server was nice and super helpful. The water filling people and table bussing people were omnipresent and maybe too attentive, grabbing at plates that were still half full. If you ate at Du Jour, you know what the space looks like - just imagine everything painted purple and orange, plus a big, cool-looking, lit up communal table in the middle. I would like to offer a fist bump to whoever's in charge of the soundtrack. Lots of Cure, and was that Love & Rockets I heard above the din? Ah, my day just got a little better. Have you ever seen a potato leek spring roll before? I hadn't either, and I'll avoid them if I do again, because they tasted mostly like straight grease. The gingery Vietnamese roll was on the opposite end of the deliciousness spectrum, with lots of flavor and a kick-ass sauce that managed to be salty, sweet and spicy all at once. The main dishes were also really up and down in terms of quality - my friend's yellow curry was good. My fried rice (wait, "wok-fried tofu and vegetables") came out of the kitchen underseasoned, but that was quickly remedied with the tasty homemade soy sauce and chili oil on the table. Moo shu tofu was served an awesome hoisin sauce, but the tofu and vegetables themselves had a surprising, odd taste, almost like maple syrup, that nearly made me commit an uncharacteristic act of public spitting. Fresh, chocolate-filled doughnuts, on the house, ended the meal well. All in all, the inconsistent food, not-quite-smooth-yet service and highish prices make me wonder if this place will last any longer than its predecessor.

When all is said and done, Jose is good for a quick stop for a beverage before a show on Broad Street when Good Dog is too packed. text: I've reviewed Geno's - http://www.yelp.com/biz/genos-steaks-philadelphia#hrid:_NrO8jJP-vCBEtuehOxWtA I've reviewed Pat's - http://www.yelp.com/biz/pats-king-of-steaks-philadelphia-2#hrid:eVAW9xtyPJofcgd33XrsFA And while both of these icons of Philly cheesesteak goodness were nice - Jim's won the competition for me by a landslide!!! We were in the Philly area for an off site training, when my coworker casually mentions that he's craving cheesesteak. And as he's never been to Philly (?!?), he's never been to Pat's nor Geno's. With the hunt afoot, and I whisked him away for a taste test of Geno's (2 stars) and Pat's (3 stars). By this point, we've each had 2 cheesesteak in about 15 minutes. My coworker was pretty satisfied that he's had the "Philly cheesesteak experience" at this point, and from the sounds of his burps, pretty full to boot. But me, well I've been to Philly many many times, and neither Geno's nor Pat's really hit the spot for me. So, with a bit of whining, and some sad puppy dog eyes (and the promise to fix the SQL bug that he's been working on), I convince him to come with me to a THIRD cheesesteak joint - Jim's. Please keep in mind that this is our THIRD cheesesteak in about 30 minutes at this point. THIRD. So I hope you understand what high praise it is, when I say that my coworker not only wolfed down his Jim's cheesesteak - but whimpered for more (we ended up ordering another cheesesteak from Jim's and split it). Yes, we each ate 3 1/2 cheesesteaks, with the final 1 1/2 from Jim's. Yes, it's *that* good. What makes Jim's better then Geno's or Pat's? Some may say the toppings, others may point to the warmed bread. Me? I say it's love. As any good glutton knows, the difference between two practically identical dishes (or in this case, 3), isn't the ingredients - after all, a cheesesteak is constrained by the bun, cheese and meat - but of the love that goes into making it. Jim's? They load theirs up with an extra helping of love on each cheesesteak. Yes, I love that they are indoors (I hate the cold), and yes, I love that they have more toppings then just "wit" (I like mine with peppers and mushrooms as well as onions). But it's in the love that they put into the execution. Upon ordering, the cheesesteak-master lathers the bun with cheese, then HOLDS the bun, over the meat, letting the steam from the hot grill and the cooking meat to meld and blend with the cheese. Then he deftly tops with whatever you desire, before briskly wrapping it up. Delicious. The bread was so soft and warm. I got the cheesewiz (again), and it was so thick and creamy and perfectly held the finely chopped meat together. My coworker, again, got the provolone (our scoring model you understand), and the cheese was soft and gooey and stringy - like a perfect cheesesteak should. Of the three that we tried that night, it should come as no surprise that Jim's was BY FAR our favorite. High marks all around in all categories - service, options, quality of bun, meltiness of cheese, and the effort that went into the deliciously chopped meat.

text: DUNG BEETLES! Ok, now that I have your attention, Id like to talk to you about the Deleware Museum of Natural History. First, however, let me widen the scope. If you still arent convinced, know that they also give you a list of similar sites around the country where you can also go for free or at a discount. We have utilized this option numerous times while on vacation, saving hundreds of dollars over the years. Did I mention discounts? It also usually includes free parking and a discount at the gift shop, and if your kids are as greedy as mine, this is also useful. A little about me....I hate going into the city... to the point of it being an anxiety disorder. For the Franklin, Zoo or Aquarium, I always knew the exact route where I can get in and the *beep* out of the city with the least amount of exposure. Therefore I was delighted to discover a place where we could become members far away from dastardly Philly. I didnt even know the Deleware Museum of Natural History even existed. We came the first time to see one of our favorite local musicians, John Flynn do a kids concert. The DMNH is a very cool place. One of the things I like about it is that its chock full of stuff but you can see it all in one day. Places like the Franklin and the Zoo are also great but often, since there is so much to see, you have to make Sophies Choice to fit things in---CMON KIDS! BEARS OR LIONS! CHOOSE NOW! WE CANT SEE IT ALL! Smaller places like DMNH make it so you feel you didnt miss out on anything, but while still getting your moneys worth. Lest you think that going more that once will be boring, they have travelling exhibits usually 4 or 5 a year to keep it fresh ( coming up...BUGS!) They once had a great sports exhibit where I eventually let the other "kids" throw footballs into targets and pitched for speed. Here are some random thoughts that pop up when I think of DMNH... - The Dung beetles I mentioned...theres a large one pushing a (fake) ball of dung in the lobby and of course there is a picture somewhere of me pretending to "make" the dung. - There is a lifesize dinasaur skeleton. nuff said. - my favorite area is the aquatic section because in the hallway, the floor becomes plexiglass and reveals a reef under your feet. Its cool by itself but sit here for awhile and watch the toddlers who dont understand that its glass and not water. They wont walk on it! and when a mean parent (yes me) picks them up and puts them in the middle of it, their look of confused terror is priceless. - The cafeterias are clean and no snackbar, but the vending machines are plentiful. - not once since we have been going has it been so busy that you cant enjoy things like some places in the city. Ok, If you arent convinced yet your heart is as cold and black like Mr Burns. Its a hike, but its worth it , especially for the suburbanites. One thing more, if theres another sports exhibit, dont even try to score on the virtual Hockey Goalie cause that bastard is mine.

text: Ok, let me take a stab at Yakitori Boy/Japas. I like Yakitori Boy but I hate Japas. Since they didn't separate this establishment into two businesses, I have no choice but review them as one business and give it the lower average score. Philadelphia lacks izakayas and it's definitely business savvy for someone to fill the space. The thing is though that traditional izakayas are pretty inexpensive since the items they sell are usually cheap to make but since the concept of having an izakaya here in Philly is still exotic and they pretty much have a monopoly, we as consumers are paying primo for it. It's fine. I do enjoy having a huge menu of dishes to choose from and the food in general is pretty good, so I don't particularly mind. I generally get pretty good service accept on Tuesdays when they have the $1 yakitori and beer deal, the place would be packed wall-to-wall, then I know the attention span of the wait staff might suffer. One of the friendly waitress told me that the sushi chef has 30+ years of experience and the sushi is good. Again, the price might be a bit high for various items, so usually I do go on Tuesday. I'm sure we all have our favorite izakaya items but If you are a beginner, I recommend trying okonomiyaki, takoyakis, get a small bowl of udon/soba, and try the myriad yakitori according to your comfortable levels. Any chicken, beef, pork is good. I also like shishamo and chicken gizzard. Eat to your heart's content and be merry. 4 stars (And here's where my review of Yakitori Boy ends and my review for Japas begins) In the same establishment there's a karaoke bar upstairs named Japas where there is about a dozen of karaoke room of various sizes and a medium size open karaoke bar. You can other all the food items from Yakitori Boy and eat at the tables in the open area or in the rooms. Being the only decent karaoke bar in town, you can never get a room without booking hours or days ahead of time during weekends. But I'm not going to complain about their good fortune. What I dislike it's their asinine rules. You cannot seat at one of the table at the open bar unless you guarantee that you'll spend a certain amount of money there per hour. It's like a strip club, for a table of 4, you'd have to guarantee you'll be spending $60 an hour on food and drinks. It's easy to spend that amount when everything is overpriced but that's not it. A friend invited me to go to a gathering he's throwing at the karaoke bar. There's approximately 12 of us and some of us got there early, so we sat at the bar, ordered a lot of food and drinks, and when the rest of the party comes, the waitress informed us that the food and drinks we ordered at the bar cannot be counted toward the guideline of the table because we didn't order that at the table. We ended up spending way more than their requirements, but I certainly didn't feel welcomed so I didn't have any fun. Customer service is non-existent when your guest feel like their constantly being monitored. Drink-wise is way more over-priced than the food was at Yakitori boy or any place else I've been. 12 of us spent around $1000. It's a tourist trap with unfriendly rules. I can't in good conscience recommend it to anyone, unless you have money to burn. 1 star

text: What spicy (or not spicy if you prefer) heaven tastes like! First of all, I used to frequent Foxy's Red Hots for their super-cheap gyros years ago when they were here. A signal in my brain says "approach cautiously". But, an adventure is an adventure whether it ends up good or bad right?! And so adventure it is! Having lived in Thailand for several months, the bar was already set high. I had tried the good, the bad, and the "what the hell is that" while in Thailand. And whether it be served in a sit down restaurant, a night market, or in a banana-leaf bowl from a walking vendor on the third-class train, the majority of it was delicious. So I go for broke and order the Chiang-Mai noodle. Yellow curry plus noodles should equal contentment after all. Yep! Just like the Thai mama that I never had would have made it. A good start. I came back a few days later, dying to try the tom-yum noodle soup. And again, if I had not known that I was in some south country strip mall, I would have thought that I was being served food that was prepared in a much more distant location. Another thing about this place is the incredibly personable atmosphere. Sure, the first time or two they might not recognize you, but after a few times, you are always greeted with a hearty smile and a wave from whom I can only assume would be the owner. So, in closing, if you want to have a meal in a restaurant that is decked out in Thai decor and pay a premium for it, head to the Loop. If you want affordable Thai that is as authentic as it gets, then Zen is your place.

text: The End has long lived in the shadow of its larger counterpart, The Exit/In, which can be found just across the street. Despite The End's more modest digs, I find it to be more charming and an all-around better spot to grab a beer and see an unassuming rock show. The End is basically one room divided into three often cramped sections. The bar is toward the back and makes for a good spot to lay low and catch your breath if the place is more slammed than usual. Beer is dirt cheap, though the selection is modest. While you probably won't see the enormous touring acts that often grace The Exit/In with their presence, The End is an absolute must for popular local bands, and you can often catch comedy shows and DJs if you keep up with their schedule. Probably the most exceptional feature at The End, however, is the sound. Run by Bruce (you can't miss him), the mix at this little dive is possibly the best in Nashville. Speaking as someone who has played and seen shows all over the city, I have to tell you that you won't hear a more unadulteratedly clean and pure board mix anywhere. Being tucked right in the middle of Elliston Place makes for a good evening, and you can always skip down to the Goldrush or the Corner Bar for a shot if you're sick of swilling cheap beers. The End also has a nice but somewhat busted little patio for smokers. The door on the men's restroom, however, has never seemed to fully shut. I suppose that's just the price you pay at an authentic dive bar.

text: My wife and I went with our son to Cheeseburger Island Style for dinner. Figured we'd try somewhere new in town. Upon first entering the restaurant you won't get a good vibe about the atmosphere, its just simply TOO open and they need more walls. We sat down and ordered our food. We opted to order the coconut shrimp for an appetizer and share the black and blue burger. Our son ordered the Spaghetti and Meatballs. The shrimp came out pretty quickly and while they weren't the WORST I've had, they were still dry and semi-petrified. I don't agree with other reviews on here that they are good (sorry!). Either I had the only bad batch or others don't know what good coconut shrimp are like. The burger came out and I could tell just by looking at it not to be impressed. The patty was thin and small amount of blue cheese, onions and thousand island were at the top, maybe a tablespoon total. The bottom part of the bun was really soggy (weird considering the burger was dry). The flavor of the meat itself was bland and I had to use a lot of ketchup (bottle was empty and gross - hadn't been cleaned in who-knows-how-long). When asked we DID tell the waiter that the burger was dry but that we didn't want to bother returning it. The manager did come over but apparently didn't feel like asking us and just offered to take my plate. The kicker? There was a nasty old pineapple slice on the plate! It had a nasty thick dark ring around it. Ugh.. My sons spaghetti was gummy and without much sauce (asked for more). Didn't get his opinion on the meatballs. I've read others on here singing praises of the pulled pork sandwich - and perhaps that's what we should have ordered. HOWEVER - for a BURGER restaurant you would expect them to execute a burger properly but they are way off target. All said, it was $46 for: Coconut shrimp, 2 draught beers, order of Spaghetti/Meatballs and a split black and blue burger. In my opinion you could go across the street to Joe's or down the street to In-n-Out and get a MUCH better burger for a fraction of the cost. Needless to say I won't be patronizing this restaurant again unless they drastically improve their game. If yelp would allow 0 out of 5 stars I would have done that.

text: Maya Café was a recommendation from a local, working as a food demonstrator in Schnuks, my new favorite market. We were hungry and as happens many times while traveling, you wait too long between meals because you don't want to miss anything. This was the day of the wedding and we had just finished up with our groupon massages at Massage Lux....which btw, was fantastic. By the time we got out of there it was well past noon and we hadn't had a thing to eat all day; we were totally famished. The Maya Café is a unique, trendy, cool and artsy-vibe kinda place. The guy that works the bar and cash register also acts as the host and server during lunch hours; lucky for us because he really knows what to recommend as well as the history of the place. The cuisine is not necessarily Mexican but more of a south of the boarder Pan-Latin. We were told Maya's Margarita's are the best to be found in St. Louis area; they make their own mix with fresh squeezed juices. Multi-task guy was right; the Margarita's were awesome. We didn't want to eat too much because we were planning on a big meal at the wedding. My son asked for the best dish on the menu, according to our waiter that would be the enchiladas. He went with that. I chose chicken taco's (how original) DIL went with fish tacos and hubs went with Chile Verde. Everyone enjoyed their meal; but licking the plate was out of the question since we were in public. We had plenty to look at from our vantage point. I called it, "the voodoo wall". It was a three-dimensional art wall with all kinds of pagan and religious artifacts arranged in little cubbies. Very interesting. Dice, eight balls, statues of the virgin Mary, skeletons, crucifixes, good luck charms; quite interesting and a bit disconcerting I might even say. Lots of friendly folks were in and out while we enjoyed our meal and the casual non-hurried atmosphere of the place. All in all, good drinks, good meal, good company in a reasonably priced package. Kudos Maya Cafe-good job!

text: This small, almost nook of a restaurant pride themselves on preparing full gourmet meals - emphasizing local fresh meats and produce. And the tiny interior has been very carefully designed as a marriage of homey intimacy with upscale dining. The decor signals romantic casual dining, but draws a dress-for-dinner crowd (there is no jacket requirement). If only the food were as piquant as the setting. The menu is undoubtedly gourmet. It changes on a daily basis to reflect the chef's recent shopping. Bravo. But what does not change is the penchant of the chef to destroy his preparations with salt. I had the saltiest rissotto in memory here. And therein lies the fundamental problem with this romantic BYOB; the basic ideas are truly of-the-moment, but the finish lacks, well, finish. A creative chef has no room to mask technical deficiencies, and seasoning is what is unmasked at Pumpkin. The ingredients and the recipes promise far more than what is being delivered. Not all dishes are deserving of this somewhat harsh criticism, but gourmet fare cannot afford to be hit or miss, especially at prices rivaling even stalwart local gourmet cuisine. The waitstaff is entirely average at best, giving a somewhat affected performance that actually interferes with rather than embellishes the dining experience. Being aloof about the food is unjustified, and spilling water on me and my food is simply unacceptable. The menu is priced aggressively high, with a seating running easily into the $40-$50 range (including and depending on the wine(s) you bring). But then, that also increases the odds that your dinner companions at other tables, who will be sitting on your elbows, if not in your ear, share your values for a dining experience. I would not discourage spending an evening at Pumpkin - it is a bright spot in what seems to be a neighborhood renaissance. And the basic ideas that are being nurtured in this fresh genuinely gourmet restaurant may yet blossom. But for now, this is a night of adventure, rather than a regular visit.
